Removing waste from the
blood
Answers
1. Removing waste from the lungs
   The following table compares the composition of the air breathed into and out of the lungs.
     Gas                              Oxygen (%)               Carbon dioxide (%)                   Water vapour (%)                   Nitrogen (%)
     Air breathed in                          21                           0.04                          Usually <1%                            78
     Air breathed out                         16                           4                                     2                              78
   (a) Which listed gas is classified as a waste gas? ...............................................................................
                                                          Carbon dioxide

                                                   (b) Explain why the percentage of oxygen has decreased and the
                                                       percentage of carbon dioxide has increased.
                                                          Some of the oxygen has been used for respiration. During
                                                          respiration, carbon dioxide is formed and so the amount of
                                                          carbon dioxide in exhaled air is higher.

                                                   (c) The image on the left shows alveoli and blood capillaries.
                                                       Explain the importance of the close association of these
                                                       structures.
                                                          Alveoli have very thin walls and gases diffuse through these
                                                          walls from the lung into the blood or in the reverse direction. In
                                                          this way the exchange of gases is very rapid.



2. Removing waste from the kidneys
   Waste removal is also the responsibility of the kidneys. Blood is filtered and wastes leave the
   kidneys as urine. The following table provides data on the typical composition of urine.
                                                    %
     Component                                 (by weight)            (a) Identify the major component of urine. Water
     Water                                           95               (b) Urea is the major nitrogenous waste. Calculate the
                                                                          total nitrogenous waste in urine.         2.8%
     Urea                                              2.5
     Other nitrogenous waste                           0.3            (c) Glucose is initially filtered out of the blood by the
                                                                          kidneys but is reabsorbed and so is absent from the
     Salts                                             1.9
                                                                          urine. Explain why it is important that glucose is
     Other                                             0.3                not lost by the body.
                                                                            Glucose is an important energy source for cellular
                                                                            respiration.

   (d) A patient’s urine gives a positive glucose test. What information does this provide for
       a doctor?
       The kidneys are malfunctioning and further examination is required to find the reason (e.g.
       .........................................................................................................................................................
       high blood pressure).
       .........................................................................................................................................................

CHAPTER 4: Ecosystems

                                                                                                                                          Worksheet 4.7
                                                                                                                                      Science Quest 7: pages 163–165




Population overload
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class:
.................................................................................................................................

The European rabbit arrived in Australia with the First Fleet in 1788. In less than a hundred years, it
had increased to plague proportions. The damage caused by the rabbit is estimated to cost the
farming industry over $600 million per year. The success of the rabbit is due to a number of factors.
First, with land cleared for farms there is an abundance of food provided by grazing pastures.
Second, a female rabbit can produce four to six kittens every month. Third, rabbits are able to travel
long distances to find food and can tolerate drier conditions than many other animals.




A rabbit investigation                                                                          Year            Number of rabbits              Number of cats
A breeding pair of rabbits was introduced onto a                                                1984                    2                           –

The European rabbit arrived in Australia with the First Fleet in 1788. In less than a hundred years, it
had increased to plague proportions. The damage caused by the rabbit is estimated to cost the
farming industry over $600 million per year. The success of the rabbit is due to a number of factors.
First, with land cleared for farms there is an abundance of food provided by grazing pastures.
Second, a female rabbit can produce four to six kittens every month. Third, rabbits are able to travel
long distances to find food and can tolerate drier conditions than many other animals.

   time, shiny silvery coloured crystals grew on the surface of the copper wire. The experiment
   was repeated with a shiny magnesium wire in place of the copper wire. Once again silvery

        ....................................................................................................................................................
        ....................................................................................................................................................
        ....................................................................................................................................................
   (c) Explain why the crystals grew faster in the second experiment.

Worksheet 5.6



Corrosion and combustion
Answers
Corrosion
1. Corrosion is a process in which a metal or alloy is attacked by agents such as air and water,
   leading to the degradation and destruction of the material. The following diagrams compare the
   corrosion of iron and aluminium.
                                                              (a) As both metals are attacked, oxide layers form on the
                                                                  surface. The iron oxide is called rust. Use your
                                                                  knowledge of the activity series of metals to predict
                                                                  which metal (Fe or Al) will react with air and water
                                                                  more rapidly.
                                                                      Al as it is higher in the activity series than Fe.
                                                              (b) Iron continues to rust whereas aluminium stops
                                                                  corroding. Explain why this happens.
                                                                      The iron oxide (rust) layer is porous. Oxygen and
                                                                      water continue to penetrate through the rust layer to
                                                                      attack the iron beneath. This does not happen with
                                                                      aluminium oxide as the corrosion layer on the surface
                                                                      is non-porous.

   (c) Name a metal that is used to coat iron to prevent it from rusting.
       Zinc (process = galvanising)
       ....................................................................................................................................................
Combustion
2. In combustion reactions a substance reacts with oxygen and releases energy. The energy
   released can be in the form of heat, light and sometimes sound. The following diagram shows
   the blue flame of a Bunsen burner.
                                   (a) The Bunsen burner uses natural gas, which is mainly
                                         methane. Write the chemical formula for methane.
                                                            CH4
                                                    (b) The blue zone of the flame is a region of complete combustion
                                                        in which the methane burns in oxygen to produce carbon
                                                        dioxide and water vapour. Write a word equation and a
                                                        balanced formula equation for this combustion reaction.
                                                            Methane + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water
                                                            CH4 + 2O2  CO2 + 2H2O
                                                    (c) A yellow safety flame is produced by closing the air hole.
                                                        Explain why the flame turns yellow.
                                                            The methane burns poorly (incomplete combustion) due to
                                                            a lower air supply. The flame turns yellow due to the soot
                                                            (carbon) particles in the flame.

Dangerous water
Blackwater is a term given to water that
contains chemical and biological contaminants
(from faeces or toxic chemicals). Waterborne
diseases are among the leading causes of death
in developing countries. An estimated
2 million people die from water-related
diarrhoea each year. At least 10 per cent of the
total human diseases in many developing
countries can be attributed to diarrhoea and             Contaminated water is a major cause of death
intestinal worms produced from microscopic              in children who live in developing countries.
eggs found in contaminated drinking water.
Diarrhoea and vomiting can lead to extreme dehydration, shock and possibly death.
   Even in developed countries, water contamination is a problem. The US Environmental
Protection Agency reports that 90 per cent of the world’s water is contaminated in some way. There
is a variety of microscopic organisms that can contaminate water supplies and cause potentially
serious, even fatal, illnesses among wilderness travellers.
   Biologically contaminated water is water that contains micro-organisms such as giardia that, if
not killed, lead to intestinal disorders. Toxic water contains chemical contamination from pesticide
run‑offs, mine tailings and so on.

2. Now consider this information:

To recycle or to not recycle
Greywater is wastewater generated from washing dishes, laundry and bathing in homes. It makes up
50–80 per cent of residential wastewater. Greywater does not contain chemical and biological
contaminants. Greywater gets its name from its cloudy appearance and from its status as being
neither fresh (whitewater from groundwater or taps) nor heavily polluted (blackwater).
   If collected via a separate plumbing system, greywater can be recycled directly within the home
and garden. Recycled greywater of this kind is never clean enough to drink, but a number of stages
of filtration and microbial digestion can be used to provide water for washing or flushing toilets;
relatively clean greywater may be applied directly from the sink to the garden, because it receives
treatment from the soil and plant roots. Vegetables should not be watered with greywater.
   On 26 July 2006, 61.62 per cent of Toowoomba’s residents opposed the treating of sewage for
drinking water. Under the plan, wastewater would have been collected and put through a series of
purifying treatments, including ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and oxidation. The treated water would
be pumped into a dam, where it would rest for three to five years — enough time to convince the
community it is safe to drink.

CHAPTER 6: Inside the atom

                                                                                               Worksheet 6.2
                                                                                               Science Quest 9: pages 240–1




How big is an atom?
Answers
It is hard to visualise the size of tiny objects, like atoms and their nuclei. However, making
comparisons with something we are more familiar with sometimes helps.
     Use an everyday object to create an image that will help people to understand how small the
nucleus of an atom is compared with the size of the entire atom. Choose from the suggestions
provided or use your own ideas. Atoms vary in size, but for the purpose of this activity, assume the
nucleus of an atom is 100 000 times smaller than the size of the entire atom.
(a) If a marshmallow represents the nucleus of an atom, how big would the entire atom be? (Hint:
     You will need to measure the diameter or the length of a marshmallow.)
     Marshmallows vary in size. In this calculation, the marshmallow is 3 cm long. If the nucleus is
     3 cm on this scale, then the entire atom is 100 000 times larger.
      3  100 000
      300 000 cm
      3000 m
      3 km
(b) If one gradation on millimetre-lined A4 graph paper represents the nucleus of an atom, how
    many sheets of graph paper would you need to glue together to represent the entire atom?
     If the nucleus is 1 mm, then the diameter of the whole atom would be:
      1  100 000
      100 000 mm
      100 m.
     A sheet of A4 graph paper is 25 cm long, which is 0.25 m.
     Since 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400, 400 sheets of A4 graph paper would need to be glued together to
     represent the size of the atom.
(c) If a marble, representing a nucleus, is placed in the centre of a sports ground, how big would the
    sports ground need to be to represent the entire atom?
     If the marble nucleus has a diameter of 15 mm, then the diameter of the sports ground is
     100 000 times the marble’s diameter.
      15  100 000
      1 500 000 mm
      1500 m
      1.5 km
     Therefore, the sports ground would need to have a diameter of 1.5 km.

2. Read the following text and answer the questions below.
                                             Red giants
   Stars that have a mass between one solar mass and eight solar masses will evolve into red giant
   stars. Betelgeuse in the Orion constellation is a red giant star. During their lives, stars like our
   sun, fuse hydrogen atoms together to form helium. Since helium is denser than hydrogen, the
   helium that forms sinks to the core of the star. The star ‘burns’ the hydrogen in the shell that
   surrounds this core. When the amount of helium in the star reaches about 12%, the core
   collapses inwards under gravity leading to intense heating. The heat causes the outer layers of
   the star to expand outwards. The star can swell to one hundred times its original size. The
   surface of these giant stars begins to cool so that the star now shines with a red light.

It is hard to visualise the size of tiny objects, such as atoms and their nuclei. However, making comparisons
with something we are more familiar with sometimes helps.
1. Use an everyday object to create an image that will help people to understand how small the nucleus of
     an atom is compared with the size of the entire atom. Choose from the suggestions provided or use your
     own ideas. Atoms vary in size, but for the purpose of this activity assume the nucleus of an atom is 100
     000 times smaller than the size of the entire atom.
      (a) If a marshmallow represents the nucleus of an atom, how big would the entire atom be?
          (Hint: The length of a marshmallow is approximately 2 cm.)
          ..............................................................................................................................................................
      (b) If one gradation on millimetre-lined graph paper represents the nucleus of an atom, how many
           sheets of graph paper would you need to glue together to represent the entire atom?
          ..............................................................................................................................................................
      (c) If a marble, about 1 cm in diameter, representing a nucleus is placed in the centre of a
           sportsground, how big would the ground need to be to represent the entire atom?

Building with atoms
Imagine going to hospital to have an incredibly tiny machine injected into your body! The machine could
whiz through your body to heal a damaged knee or to fight a disease in your liver. A machine like this might
be a thing of the future, but research into nanotechnology is well underway.
  Nanotechnology is the science of using single atoms as building materials. Currently, scientists have been
able to use nanotechnology to build tiny machines, some of which have moving parts.
2. Imagine if a tiny machine (nanobot) was required to swim through a particular blood vessel, measuring
    1 cm in diameter. The size of the machine would be limited by many factors, including the number of
    atoms that could comfortably fit inside the blood vessel. How many atoms could fit side-by-side in this
    blood vessel? (Hint: Find out how big a typical atom is.)

Nature’s time machine
Answers

Secrets in the ice
Scientists may not have discovered a time machine yet, but they do have
a way of looking back over 300 000 years by looking at ice cores.
Scientists drill into the ice of Antarctica and collect samples from deep
down. Ice cores provide information about the Earth and the atmosphere
over hundreds of thousands of years.
    For thousands of years, snow has fallen in Antarctica. The snow
turns to ice, which builds up over time. Dust, gases and other
substances from the air become trapped. The trapped substances
provide information about what was in the air at the time the snow fell.
    By studying dust in the ice cores, scientists can work out when
certain volcanoes have erupted. They have linked radioactive
substances in the ice to nuclear disasters in various parts of the world.
The dust and radioactive substances were probably carried to Antarctica
by the wind.

Recycling carbon
Carbon atoms are found in the air, soil, rocks, oil and gas below the Earth’s surface, and all living
things. The number of carbon atoms on Earth always remains the same. When living things use carbon
atoms, the atoms don’t just disappear; they are recycled. The diagram below shows the recycling of
carbon. It also shows how humans have added to the amount of carbon dioxide in the air. We must take
care not to interfere with the natural recycling process.
1. How do animals get carbon as part of the carbon cycle?




   By eating plants and other animals

2. Explain two ways in which carbon that is contained within a plant can end up back in the air.
   Respiration and decomposing

3. Where in the carbon cycle is carbon stored for long periods of time?




                                       © John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd
    Underground as coal, oil or gas

4. Would the carbon cycle still take place if humans did not exist? Explain.
   Yes, animals would play the part that humans play in the carbon cycle.

5. How do humans add extra carbon dioxide to the air?
   By burning fossil fuel

CHAPTER 7: Chemical reactions

                                                                                    Worksheet 7.2
                                                                                  Science Quest 9: pages 258–61




Campsite chillout
Answers
Even while relaxing on holiday,
you can find exothermic and
endothermic processes going on
all around you.
1. For each of the activities
     shown on the illustration and
     listed below, state whether the
     process indicated is
     exothermic or endothermic,
     and then explain your choices.
     (Remember: an exothermic
     process results in thermal
     energy being given out to the
     surroundings, while an
     endothermic process requires
     thermal energy which is
     drawn in from the
     surroundings.)

     (a) The leaves use energy from the sun to make sugars for the tree (photosynthesis).
     Endothermic — energy is being absorbed.
     (b) Nuclear reactions in the sun warm the Earth during the day.
            Exothermic — energy is being released.
     (c) Sweat on a person's face evaporates.
            Endothermic — energy is being absorbed. Change of state: liquid  gas.
     (d) The gas barbecue burns.
            Exothermic — energy is being released
     (e) The eggs inside the saucepan cook to become hard-boiled.
            Endothermic — energy is being absorbed
     (f) Glasses fog up from the boiling water.
            Exothermic — energy is being released. Change of state: gas  liquid.
     (g) Insect repellent is liquid inside the can, partly gaseous as it comes out of the nozzle.
            Endothermic — energy is being absorbed. Change of state: liquid  gas.
     (h) Ice melts in a drink.
            Endothermic — energy is being absorbed. Change of state: solid  liquid.

2. Which of these processes can be classified as chemical reactions? Explain your choices fully.
     Chemical reactions are irreversible and involve the formation of a new substance.
     (a) Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water  glucose + oxygen
     (b) This is an example of a nuclear reaction in which the internal structure of the atom changes
         and different types of atoms are formed.
     (d) Combustion of methane: methane + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water
     (e) The proteins in the egg change (denature and coagulate). This is irreversible.

The nitrogen cycle
1. The following diagram summarises the nitrogen cycle in nature.

                                                                    important chemical in nature.

                                                                               DNA and so the nitrogen has to
                                                                               be available in food webs in a
                                                                               suitable nutrient form.
                                                                               (b)Identify two decomposers at point X.

                                                                            (c) Identify the ways that ammonia

                                                                               of decomposers; nitrates in the
                                                                               soil being converted by
                                                                               denitrifying bacteria; waste
                                                                               nitrogen from animals



   (d) Explain why ammonia does not build up in the soil.

    these bodies and break them down.
(b) Bacteria will grow on both living and non-living matter. They break down the matter and recycle
    nutrients.

Answers
Ozone and altitude
1. The following graph shows the ozone level (measured as the pressure of ozone in millipascals)
   as a function of altitude. Answer the questions about this graph.
                                        (a) What is the ozone level at sea level? About 3 mPa
                                        (b) At what altitude is the maximum ozone level?
                                              About 24–25 km
                                         (c) In what atmospheric layer is the maximum ozone level
                                             located?
                                              Stratosphere
                                         (d) Calculate the ratio of the maximum ozone level in the
                                             stratosphere to the maximum ozone level in the
                                             troposphere.




Ozone depletion
2. The following graph shows changes in the area of the ozone hole in the stratosphere above Halley
   Bay, Antarctica, for the same four-month period over three different years. The ozone hole is a
   region of the stratosphere that has severely depleted levels of ozone. Answer the questions about
   this graph.
                                                 (a) In which season of the year do the largest ozone
                                                     holes appear over Antarctica?
                                                         Spring
                                                   (b) Compare the area of the ozone holes over these
                                                       three years.
                                                         In 2004 the hole’s area was the smallest; in 2003
                                                         and 2005 the hole’s area was about equal.


                                                   (c) Determine the size of the ozone hole at the end
                                                       of September in 2004.
                                                         About 14 000 000 km2
                                                   (d) Studies in Chile showed a significant increase in
                                                       skin cancers since ozone holes first started to
                                                       appear in the mid-1980s. Explain why this
                                                       would happen.
                                                         The ozone hole lets more UV penetrate to the
                                                         ground, and UV exposure accelerates the
                                                         formation of skin cancer.

CHAPTER 7: Elements, compounds and mixtures

                                                                                                                                                 Worksheet 7.4



The periodic table — atomic
structure
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ................................................

As the early scientists discovered more and more elements, it became more important that they agreed
on names for the elements. Each element was given a name and a symbol. During their experiments, the
scientists also found that some of the elements had things in common. Because of this they decided to
organise the elements into groups.
   The person who finally worked out a system for sorting the elements into groups was a Russian
scientist called Dmitri Mendeleev. His system is called the periodic table and a modern version is used
by scientists today. A small portion of the periodic table is shown below.
                                                                                   The atomic number of an element is the number of
                                                                                 protons present in each atom. For example, all
                                                                                 hydrogen atoms have only one proton inside the
                                                                                 nucleus, so the atomic number of hydrogen is 1.




                                                                                       A simplified diagram of a hydrogen atom



   Atoms are electrically neutral; that is, the number of protons in an atom is the same as the number of
electrons. The atomic mass of an atom is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in
the atom.
   Complete the following table, using the information provided above. You might also like to
review the structure of an atom in your textbook.
                                                       Atomic                    Atomic                 Number of                Number of                Number of
  Element                    Symbol                    number                     mass                   protons                 electrons                neutrons
  Hydrogen
  Lithium
  Beryllium

Worksheet 7.5



Slowing global
warming — alternatives
Answers

                                      Wind power
                                      The wind is free and blows almost continuously; a series of wind
                                      turbines can supply a viable and reliable source of energy. It has the
                                      added advantage of being non-polluting. However, there has been
                                      controversy as wind farms can be quite noisy and some people think
                                      they spoil the aesthetics of the natural environment.


Photo: chuyu / 123RF




Nuclear power
Australia has vast reserves of uranium, the essential element
required to produce nuclear power. Enormous amounts of energy
can be harnessed through nuclear power generation, but the risks
are also great. Waste products and spent nuclear rods remain
radioactive for thousands of years, and if a reactor goes into
‘meltdown’ or these waste materials leak into the environment, the
results could be devastating.
                                                                            Photo: hxdyl / 123RF



                                            Hydro-electric power
                                            Hydro-electricity has been used for decades as an important
                                            source of electricity. The natural force of running water
                                            turns massive turbines, which produces electricity cheaply.
                                            It is also non-polluting. However, river systems must be
                                            dammed and this affects the natural environment. Larger
                                            tracts of land are often flooded in the process, resulting in
                                            the destruction of habitats.

Photo: Amornthep Chotchuang / 123RF




                                       © John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd
                                                                                             Worksheet 7.5

Biosphere 2
More than three decades ago, scientists first raised concerns that the Earth was heading for an
‘ecological meltdown’. Their solution was a project known as Biosphere 2. The aim was to replicate the
various ecosystems on the Earth, as well as its atmosphere, in a series of domes occupying
approximately 1.3 hectares.
    In 1991 the project reached fruition, when four men and four women took up residence within the
facility for two years. The project was plagued with problems, including the collapse of ecosystems and
the demise of several plant and animal species. However, a more serious problem was the inability to
sustain an atmosphere; falling oxygen levels and rising
carbon dioxide levels meant the project was doomed to fail
without external assistance.
    Perhaps what scientists really gained was an insight into
our future. If we continue to rely on fossil fuels, our climate
will continue to change and the atmosphere will continue to
deteriorate. We will not simply be able to prop it up from
another source. Alternative power sources such as
hydroelectricity, wind and nuclear energy are considered
sustainable, if somewhat controversial.                            Photo: James Mattil / 123RF

1. Explain what is meant by the term ‘ecological meltdown’.
    An ecological meltdown means that the ecology of the planet would be changed by increasing
    temperatures.


2. What was the aim of Biosphere 2?
    To replicate various ecosystems on Earth as well as its atmosphere


3. What important lessons do you think we can learn from the Biosphere 2 project? Justify your
   answer.
    That it is difficult to sustain an atmosphere without external help and that the future will look
    different for the production of energy

   you feel would help you decide which would be most effective in reducing global warming.

 1. In a chemical change one or more new substances are formed and the process is not easily
      reversible .
 2. The burning of a candle involves both physical and chemical changes. The melting of the
    wax is a physical change and the combustion of the wax vapour is a chemical change.
 3. In a chemical reaction the starting materials are called the reactants and the substances that
    are formed are called the products .
 4. Word equations can be used to describe the chemical change.
 5. Exothermic reactions produce heat.
 6. Endothermic reactions absorb heat from their surroundings.
 7. Acids are substances that neutralise bases to produce salts and water. Indicators can be
    used to determine whether a substance is an acid or a base.
 8. The pH scale is used to classify acids and bases. If the pH is less than 7, then the substance is
      acidic If the pH is above 7, then the substance is basic .
 9. Acidic gases such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide produce acid rain when they
    dissolve in rain. Acid rain can cause significant environmental destruction.
10. Indigestion can be relieved by using antacids , which neutralise excess acidity in the
    stomach.
11. When a fuel burns in the presence of air or oxygen heat is produced. If the fuel is a
    hydrocarbon, then carbon dioxide and water are formed unless the oxygen supply is
    limited.
12. Oxidation reactions involve the transfer of electrons from a reactant.
13. Not all oxidation reactions involve oxygen .

   (unbalanced) force and describe the resulting motion of the object. Assume north is up the page.
   (a)
                                                                                               The body will move to the left as the net
                                                                                               force is 20  10  10 N to the left (i.e.

                                                                                             The body will move at 45 to the right of

                                                                                             force is 7  2  5 N to the right (east). The

                                                                                                Worksheet 9.1



Identifying and classifying
minerals
Answers

Identifying minerals
1. Two common rocks are composed of
   the minerals shown in the images at
   right. Limestone contains calcite, and
   sandstone contains quartz.
                                                      Calcite                    Quartz

    The following table provides information about the properties of these minerals.
     Mineral          Colour             Streak (colour of powdered mineral)          Hardness           Lustre
     Calcite     Colourless, white                           White                          3       Dull to vitreous
                 Colourless, purple,
     Quartz                                                  White                          7           Vitreous
                     red, yellow
    (a) Explain how calcite crystals can be distinguished from quartz crystals.
        Quartz is much harder, so a Mohs’ scale hardness test will show the difference.

    (b) Pure quartz crystals are colourless. Explain the large variation in colour indicated in the table.
        Coloured impurities can lead to significant colour changes.

Creating a classification key
2. Use the following table to create a written classification key for these minerals.
     Mineral                         Colour                Streak                Hardness               Lustre
     Chalcopyrite                      Yellow          Green, black               3.5–4                 Metallic
     Chlorite                          Grey            White, green               2.2–5                  Pearly
     Galena                            Grey                 Grey                    2.5                 Metallic
     Haematite                         Grey             Red, brown                 5–6                  Metallic
     Magnetite                         Black                Black                 5.5–6.5               Metallic
     Pyrite                            Yellow              Green                  6–6.5                 Metallic

    2B. Streak is not grey..............................................................................................................go to 3
    3A. Mineral has a metallic lustre........................................................................................haematite
    3B. Mineral has a pearly lustre.............................................................................................. chlorite
    4A. Mineral has a hardness less than 5........................................................................chalcopyrite
    4B. Mineral has a hardness of 5 or greater............................................................................ go to 5
    5A. Mineral is black............................................................................................................magnetite
    5B. Mineral is yellow................................................................................................................. pyrite

 Scoria                             Pumice                                  Granite

   Obsidian: smooth, glassy black rock; non-crystalline

in the rock
Answers
Trapped!
1. The photo below shows an insect fossilised in amber.
                                     (a) Explain how this fossil formed.
                                                 The insect got stuck in tree sap oozing from a tree. It
                                                 eventually became encased in the sap. The sap was
                                                 eventually buried and hardened into a fossil over time.
                                           (b) Explain why there has been very little decay over millions
      Photo: falk / Shutterstock.com           of years.
                                                  The lack of air, water and decomposers has
                                                  ensured the preservation.

Fossils in a logical sequence
2. The evolution of life on Earth can be followed using fossils. In general, life appeared in its
   simplest form and then over billions of years more complex organisms evolved. Arrange the
   four drawings of fossils below in a logical evolutionary sequence using the letters A to D. ...............
                                                                                                  B, D, C, A




    A. Sabre-toothed        B. Trilobite         C. Pterodactyl             D. Early
       tiger                   (invertebrate)                                  amphibian


Reading the history
3. The following sequence of rocks was revealed in a road cutting. The events are listed in a
   random order. Arrange the events (using the letters A to K) in the correct sequence.
                                          A. Fine sandstone layer is deposited
                                          B. Shale deposited on top of coarse sandstone
                                          C. Sedimentary layers folded
                                          D. Land sinks and coal layer is deposited
                                          E. Rock layers fault
                                          F. Coarse sandstone deposited on top of conglomerate
                                          G. Land is uplifted and extensive erosion occurs
                                          H. Coarse sandstone deposited
                                          I. Dolerite intrudes through folded layers
                                          J. Uplift and erosion produces the present day landscape
                                          K. Conglomerate deposited
                                                     Sequence:      H, B, K, F, C, I, E, G, D, A, J

CHAPTER 5: Chemical reactions

                                                                                                                          Worksheet 5.6



Corrosion and combustion
Answers
Corrosion
1. Corrosion is a process in which a metal or alloy is attacked by agents such as air and water,
   leading to the degradation and destruction of the material. The following diagrams compare the
   corrosion of iron and aluminium.
                                                              (a) As both metals are attacked, oxide layers form on the
                                                                  surface. The iron oxide is called rust. Use your
                                                                  knowledge of the activity series of metals to predict
                                                                  which metal (Fe or Al) will react with air and water
                                                                  more rapidly.
                                                                      Al as it is higher in the activity series than Fe.
                                                              (b) Iron continues to rust whereas aluminium stops
                                                                  corroding. Explain why this happens.
                                                                      The iron oxide (rust) layer is porous. Oxygen and
                                                                      water continue to penetrate through the rust layer to
                                                                      attack the iron beneath. This does not happen with
                                                                      aluminium oxide as the corrosion layer on the surface
                                                                      is non-porous.

   (c) Name a metal that is used to coat iron to prevent it from rusting.
       Zinc (process = galvanising)
       ....................................................................................................................................................
Combustion
2. In combustion reactions a substance reacts with oxygen and releases energy. The energy
   released can be in the form of heat, light and sometimes sound. The following diagram shows
   the blue flame of a Bunsen burner.
                                   (a) The Bunsen burner uses natural gas, which is mainly
                                         methane. Write the chemical formula for methane.
                                                            CH4
                                                    (b) The blue zone of the flame is a region of complete combustion
                                                        in which the methane burns in oxygen to produce carbon
                                                        dioxide and water vapour. Write a word equation and a
                                                        balanced formula equation for this combustion reaction.
                                                            Methane + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water
                                                            CH4 + 2O2  CO2 + 2H2O
                                                    (c) A yellow safety flame is produced by closing the air hole.
                                                        Explain why the flame turns yellow.
                                                            The methane burns poorly (incomplete combustion) due to
                                                            a lower air supply. The flame turns yellow due to the soot
                                                            (carbon) particles in the flame.

Speeding up reactions
Answers
Boiling the billy
1. Making a pot of tea at a camp fire is known in Australia as ‘boiling the billy’. The camper wants
   to boil the water faster. An increase in the rate of wood burning will deliver heat to the water
   faster.
                                             (a) One method of increasing the combustion of the
                                                 wood is to add more reactants. How is the paper
                                                 fanning doing this?
                                                                            Adding more oxygen from the air at a greater rate
                                                                            than just diffusion

                                                                      (b) Increasing the surface area of the wood also helps.
                                                                            How has the camper achieved this?
      ............................................................................................................................................................
       Cutting the wood into small sticks, which have a greater surface area
      ............................................................................................................................................................

Changing the speed of the reaction
2. Calcium carbonate is the main chemical present in limestone. When hydrochloric acid is added
   to lumps of calcium carbonate, it fizzes and dissolves to form calcium chloride and water;
   gaseous carbon dioxide is also formed. The calcium chloride remains dissolved in the acid.
   (a) Write a word equation for this reaction.
         Calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid  calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
        ....................................................................................................................................................
   (b) A student used the following apparatus to study the speed of the reaction.
                                                                                           (i) Explain how the apparatus can be
                                                                                                  used to measure how fast the
                                                                                                  calcium carbonate is dissolved in
                                                                                                  the acid.
                                                                                                       The faster the reaction, the more
                                                                                                       rapidly the gas is evolved and the
                                                                                                       faster it depresses the liquid in the
                                                                                                       left arm of the U-tube. Liquid rises
                                                                                                       in the right arm and the scale can
                                                                                                       be used to measure the change at
                                                                                                       regular time intervals.
 (ii) Compare the observations when the experiment is repeated with powdered calcium carbonate
      instead of lumps of calcium carbonate.
       The rate will be faster. The effervescence will be greater as the powder has a greater
      ..........................................................................................................................................................
       surface area.
      ..........................................................................................................................................................
(iii) The student heats the flask to a higher temperature. How will the observations change
      compared with the experiment at room temperature?
       Increasing the temperature increases the rate and so fizzing will occur faster and the
      ..........................................................................................................................................................
       change in levels in the U-tube will be faster.
      ..........................................................................................................................................................

A huge variety of amazing creatures live in our oceans. Imagine you have been invited on board a
submersible craft that is capable of exploring the sea floor thousands of metres below the ocean
surface. As you descend, what changes will you observe in the animals and plants that inhabit the
ocean? Using the diagram above as a guide, write a brief description of how the plants and animals
change along your journey to the seabed. Think about the size, shape, colour and variety of
organisms at different depths. Write your descriptions in the table.

 Changes observed in animals

 As we travel deeper into the ocean, animals show adaptations for life in darkness, cold water and
 high pressure. Many of the animals would have large eyes, helping them see in the dark waters.
 Some will be small, dark and thin to help camouflage them. Other animals will glow in the dark.
 Because there is less plant food, animals in the ocean depths will not be as active because they
 have less energy available. Carnivores may have large mouths and jaws to capture prey with less
 energy expenditure. Once we get past the ‘twilight zone’, animals may not have eyes at all as there
 is no light this far down. Most animals at this depth will be invertebrates due to high water pressure.

Population overload
Answers
The European rabbit arrived in Australia with the First Fleet in 1788. In less than a hundred years, it
had increased to plague proportions. The damage caused by the rabbit is estimated to cost the
farming industry over $600 million per year. The success of the rabbit is due to a number of factors.
First, with land cleared for farms there is an abundance of food provided by grazing pastures.
Second, a female rabbit can produce four to six kittens every month. Third, rabbits are able to travel
long distances to find food and can tolerate drier conditions than many other animals.

Spot the pest
Answers
European settlers changed much of the Australian wilderness into farmland. They introduced new animals
into Australia for food, transport and companionship. Some of these tame (or domestic) animals escaped
and became wild. As feral animals, they preyed on native species and destroyed habitats. Some, such as
rabbits and foxes, were brought here to be hunted as sport. Others, such as rats, made their own way via
ships. Some animals have been introduced as a biological control for other pests.

2. Circle each animal you think has become a pest in Australia. Give reasons for your choices.
     Answers will vary. Examples are given.
     Dingo: predator of native wildlife
     Cat: pest when feral because it kills native wildlife
     Mouse: can cause social, economic and environmental problems when in plague proportions
     Dog: wild dogs prey on livestock such as sheep, cattle and goats. Predator of native wildlife.
     Pig: feral pigs cause agricultural damage through predation of newborn lambs, reduction in
     crop yields, damage to fences/water sources and competition with stock for feed by consuming
     or damaging pasture. They disrupt and damage native ecosystems because they dig up land.
     Horse: wild horses can damage native vegetation and impact on pasture and grazing land.
     Camel: feral camels in Central Australia damage native vegetation and affect pasture and
     grazing land.
     Northern Pacific sea star: damages marine ecosystem
     Cane toad: interferes with reproduction of native frogs; eats other native wildlife
3. Research one of these pests. Prepare a one-page report outlining why it was introduced to

   subsidise health care for the poor.
         Unfortunately, five years
   after it hit the market, new
   research uncovered evidence that
   prolonged use of Fatsoff caused
   fatal heart attacks in 2 per cent of
   users.
         Do you think that the
   production and use of Fatsoff
   should be banned? You will need
   to justify your answer. Consider the issue in terms of health, social and economic impact.

     What is Energy?                         Energy is what causes things to change.

There are many different types of energy. Here are just a few:

Type of Energy                            Changes Caused by this Energy
Heat                                      Change in temperature. e.g. a stove causes food to get hot.
Light                                     Nerve changes in your eye which allow you to see things,
                                                  or chemical changes in the film in a camera.
Sound                                     Vibrations in your ear which allow you to hear.
Electrical Energy                         Can cause a light bulb to glow and produce light,
                                                  or a stove element to get hot and produce heat.
Radio Waves                               Can cause electrical vibrations in an antenna.
                                          This allows reception of mobile phone, radio & TV programs.

     Two types of energy need special attention:                (learn these especially!)

 Kinetic Energy (KE)
 KE is the energy of a moving object. It causes the object to change its position by moving.
 If the moving object hits something, the KE can cause other changes, such as the damage
 done when moving cars collide.

 Potential Energy (PE)
 PE is energy stored in things, and not always obvious or apparent. There are 3 types:

           Gravitational PE is energy stored in an object in a high position. The energy is not
           apparent until the object falls down due to gravity. As it falls, it converts into KE.

           Chemical PE is energy stored in chemicals. The energy is not apparent until a
           chemical change occurs which releases the energy. Chemical PE is stored in
           chemicals like candle wax (can burn to release heat and light) or in a battery
           (can make electricity) or in petrol (can make a car move with KE).

           Elastic PE is energy stored in objects which have been stretched, compressed
           or twisted out of shape. When released, the elastic PE is released, often causing
           something to move with KE.
           e.g. When released, a stretched bow makes the arrow fly.

                                             Why Learn about Energy?
                                        Energy is the basic stuff of the universe.
                                      It powers all living things, all machines, the
                                            weather, the Sun... everything!


     Energy Transfers
 When energy causes a change, it always results in the energy transferring to a new
 form. Examples:
                                                                      converts to
                Stove:                       electrical energy                         heat
                                                                 converts to
              Car:             Chemical PE in petrol                                KE of moving car

                                           What is a Mixture?
              To understand mixtures, you need to know about pure substances.
    A substance is “pure” if it is made up entirely of particles that are identical to each other.

 Scientists have good

 that all substances
 are made up of tiny
 “particles”.
                                                Three different pure substances
   There are many different types of particles. The different types of particle are different from
    each other in their weight and density, in the way they cling together and in the way they
       combine with other types. You will learn about atoms & molecules in a later topic.
         For now we will represent particles simply by different shapes and shadings.

                 A mixture is NOT PURE.
 A mixture is a substance made up of 2 or more different

 What is Energy? (Revision)                     Energy is what causes things to change.
 There are many different types of energy. Here are just a few:

 Type of Energy              Changes Caused by this Energy
 Kinetic (in moving objects) Change in position because object is moving.
 Potential (stored)          Only causes changes when released in another form.
 Heat                        Change in temperature. e.g. a stove causes food to get hot.
 Light                       Nerve changes in your eye which allow you to see things,
                                     or chemical changes in the film in a camera.
 Sound                       Vibrations in your ear which allow you to hear.
 Electrical Energy           Can cause a light bulb to glow and produce light,
                                     or a stove element to get hot and produce heat.
 Radio Waves                 Can cause electrical vibrations in an antenna.
                             This allows reception of mobile phone, radio & TV programs.


                                           Waves Carry Energy
                    Many types of energy are carried as waves.
                   Waves carry energy from one place to another.
    Only the energy moves... substances do NOT move from one place to another.
  (A substance might vibrate as energy moves through, but it doesn’t go anywhere.)

               The substance vibrates as the wave energy passes through.
                    The substance is called the “medium” for the wave.
          Without a medium, the wave cannot exist, and the energy cannot move.

  It could be a bone, tooth or shell. It could be an imprint or a footprint or a burrow.

Variation and classification – the five kingdoms

Teaching notes

Give each group/pair a set of classification cards – there are keyword cards (below) and
picture cards (in the PDF). The picture cards are best printed in colour. They could be
laminated for reuse. The activity could be differentiated by removing some of the cards.


Suggested use:

  1. Ask the students to find the five kingdom cards and put to one side.
  2. Ask the students to match the remaining keyword cards with the correct picture.
  3. Ask them to group them into the five kingdoms.
  4. Then ask them to sort the animal kingdom cards into vertebrates and invertebrates.

Numbers in brackets refer to the picture number.

Correct use of the Bunsen burner
Task 1

Label the diagram of the Bunsen burner.




Task 2

Using the words and phrases in the box, complete the sentences below. Some of
the words and phrases may be used more than once.

1. The height of a Bunsen burner flame can be altered by .................................

2. The temperature of the flame can be altered by ............................................

3. The jet allows a ................................... stream of gas to enter the burner.

4. The inlet tube is where the ............................. enters the burner.

5. The flame is quiet, flickering and luminous when the air hole is ....................

6. The very hot flame burns a mixture of .......................... and .........................

7. To heat substances, you should use the flame with the air hole ....................

8. The hottest part of the flame (with the air hole open) is ................................

9. When lighting a Bunsen burner, you should make sure that the air hole is ....

10......................................................................................................................... A
   Bunsen burner should always be placed on a .................................................

just above the blue cone                                  open                                            gas
                  air                          turning the collar                                  narrow

               closed                                safety mat                       adjusting the gas tap

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012                         19235                                               Page 1 of 3
                                      Correct use of the Bunsen burner




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012   19235                      Page 2 of 3
                                          Correct use of the Bunsen burner

Answers

Task 1


                                                      chimney



            collar

                                                      air hole
               base
                                                                 gas inlet
                                                                 tube



Task 2

1. The height of a Bunsen burner flame can be altered by adjusting the gas tap.

2. The hotness of the flame can be altered by turning the collar.

3. The jet allows a narrow stream of gas to enter the burner.

4. The inlet tube is where the gas enters the burner.

5. The flame is quiet, flickering and luminous when the air hole is closed.

6. The very hot flame burns a mixture of gas and air.

7. To heat substances you should use the flame with the air hole open.

8. The hottest part of the flame (with the air hole open) is just above the blue
   cone.

9. When lighting a Bunsen burner you should make sure that the air hole is
   closed.

10. A Bunsen burner should always be placed on a safety mat.

Taboo – solids, liquids, gases

Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any of the
additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.


   1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each team).

   2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto different
      coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have all the cards back at
      the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

   3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

   4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile, and then
      describes the word at the top of the card without using the words below. The rest of
      their team must guess which word is described. Participants are not allowed to say
      ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

   5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the opposing team
      may challenge and the individual must move on to the next word.

   6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as possible to
      the players in their team (a longer time may be required to allow more descriptions
      to take place) before play passes to the next team. There are no penalties for
      wrong guesses.

   7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.
      Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each group.


This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other ways to
describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to reinforcing
the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could research
meanings of new terms.



Extension activity


   1. Each student puts a new vocabulary word at the top of a blank card.

   2. Each student then has to write a further five words which are associated with the
      keyword they have written at the top of the card.

Elements – what am I?


Teaching notes

This activity could be used with a whole class as a starter or a
plenary. The class could be split into teams or students could have
mini whiteboards which they hold up when they have decided on an
answer.

Read the statements out one at a time. If students guess the object
after one clue they get five points, after the second clue they get
four points, etc.

If the game is played in groups, each student could be given a set
of statements to test the others in the group.

As an extension students could write up with their own five
statements about an object and then play the game with a partner.

Earth and space taboo
Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the
keyword on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word
itself or any of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.


   1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each
      team).

   2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto
      different coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have
      all the cards back at the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

   3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

   4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile,
      and then describes the word at the top of the card without using the
      words below. The rest of their team must guess which word is described.
      Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no
      gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

   5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the
      opposing team may challenge and the individual must move on to the
      next word.

   6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as
      possible to the players in their team (a longer time may be required to
      allow more descriptions to take place) before play passes to the next
      team. There are no penalties for wrong guesses.

   7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
      point. Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each
      group.


This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding
other ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary
in addition to reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could
research meanings of new terms.



Extension activity
   1. Each student puts a new vocabulary word at the top of a blank card.


   2. Each student then has to write a further five words which are associated
      with the keyword they have written at the top of the card.

Earth and space – what am I?
Teaching notes

This activity could be used with a whole class as a starter or a plenary. The class could be
split into teams or students could have mini whiteboards which they hold up when they
have decided on an answer.

Read the statements out one at a time. If students guess the object after one clue they
get 5 points, after the second clue they get 4 points, etc.

If the game is played in groups, each student could be given a set of statements to test the
others in the group.

As an extension, students could write up with their own five statements about an object
and then play the game with a partner.

Designed for the job


  Imagine a clear plastic bag, or a balloon or a bubble, filled with water.
  Inside you push a squash ball, a few dried beans and some cling film, all
  scrunched up. You have made a model of a typical animal cell. Add a few
  dried peas, a smaller balloon, squeeze the whole lot into a cardboard box
  and you have a typical plant cell!

  However, most animal and plant cells do not look like typical cells
  because they have special jobs to do. Think of the Olympics and the
  competitors for each sport: a cyclist looks different from a weightlifter; a
  basketball player would not make a very good gymnast!

  Different cells have different jobs. In plants, palisade cells, found in the
  upper part of leaves, are green. The green colour is due to chlorophyll, a
  chemical essential for photosynthesis. The job of a leaf cell is to produce
  glucose from carbon dioxide and water using energy from the sun. A root
  hair cell is long and thin. This gives it a large surface area. Its job is to
  absorb water and minerals from the soil. Stomata are formed from two
  curved cells, rather like your lips. They can move to create an opening
  between them. This enables air to move in and out of the leaf.

  Animals too have a wide variety of cells. Sperm cells resemble tadpoles:
  both have long, lashing tails to help them swim. Sperm cells have plenty
  of mitochondria. Mitochondria provide energy for the long swim to the egg
  cell. The role of a sperm cell is to fertilise an egg. Under a microscope,
  nerve cells look like trees in winter. At one end, surrounding the nucleus,
  are lots of ‘branches’. There is a long, thin ‘trunk’ ending in a cluster of
  ‘roots’.
  The function of a nerve cell is to receive and pass on messages, in the
  form of electrical signals, to different parts of the body. Red blood cells
  are shaped like ‘donut’ peaches. They do not have a nucleus because
  they are designed to carry as much oxygen as possible. They are packed
  with a special, oxygen-carrying molecule called haemoglobin.




  1.   Use a blue pen to highlight all the words
       which identify a type of cell.

  2.   Now, using a green pen, highlight all the
       phrases which identify the structure of
       each cell (i.e. what it is made of).

  3.   Next, use a red pen to highlight all the
       phrases which describe a cell’s function
       (i.e. what it does).

Atomic structure – follow on cards
Teaching notes

This is a simple activity that students seem to enjoy. Once it is completed they will often ask, ‘Can
we do it again?’.
It is suitable for:
        whole class work
        group work
        individual work
        revision
        lesson starters
        lesson consolidation
        homework.

Instructions

Print out the two tables, ideally onto card so they can be used again. If multiple sets are produced,
print them onto different coloured card.
Each table needs to be cut down the middle and horizontally to create 32 individual cards, as
below.

                                                     Roughly

                                         Oxygen      elements
                                                     have been
                                                     discovered?


    1.    Distribute the cards between members of the group or class.

    2.    Students may place the cards in front of them or keep them hidden.

    3.    Explain that it is a bit like dominoes. A question is read out and someone within the group
         or class has the answer. They read out the answer followed by the next question.

    4.    Point out that the answer to the previous question is on the left hand side, in the shaded
         box, and that the new question is on the right hand side, in the unshaded box.

    5.    The student who receives the card with ‘start’ on it reads out the first question.

    6.    The students look at their cards. The one who feels they have the answer puts their hand
         up and reads it out. If it is correct, they will then read out the next question. Completed
         cards are placed face down on the bench.

    7.    Answers are included on p.4. In cases of poor literacy, you could intervene by reading out
         the next question.

    8.    The exercise continues until the ‘starter’ gives the final answer.

Other ways to use the resource

        It can be given as an individual exercise in class or for homework. The student could cut
         out and stick the cards into their exercise book, placing and numbering them in order.
         Otherwise, ask students to arrange the cards in sequential order in a pile. They can be
         quickly checked to see if task is done.

      Use the activity unexpectedly by asking the class to complete the exercise whilst being
       taught a different unit. This helps to refresh the memory.

Energy flow in an ecosystem

This activity outlines the flow of energy through a woodland ecosystem. It involves
Maths and Design.


     Every year 6.3 x 106 KJ/m2 of energy from the sun reaches a woodland ecosystem.

     A small amount of this energy is absorbed by plants during photosynthesis.

     Over the year, 2000 KJ/m2 of the energy absorbed by the plants is lost into
     their surroundings. However, 8000 KJ/m2 is used by the plants for growth.


1.       What type of plants do you think these are? Can you name any? Make a list.

2.       What is the total amount of energy absorbed by the plants each year?


     Over the twelve month period herbivorous birds consume 300 KJ/m 2 from the
     plants. They do this by eating leaves, fruits and seeds.

     Of this 300 KJ/m2, only 3 KJ/m2 is used by the birds to grow. The
     remaining 297 KJ/m2 is lost into their surroundings.


3.      How is this energy lost to their surroundings? (Think of yourselves on a cold
        winter’s day.)

4.       How efficient are birds at converting the energy they consume into new growth?


     Herbivorous mammals consume 500 KJ/m2.
     They use 5 KJ/m2 for growth and lose 495 KJ/m2 to their surroundings.

     Herbivorous invertebrates consume 1200 KJ/m2.
     They use 190 KJ/m2 for growth and lose 1010 KJ/m2.


5.      Which type of herbivore is most efficient at converting the energy it consumes
        into growth? Why do you think this is?

6.    What percentage of the plant’s annual growth is consumed by herbivorous
animals?


     Thrushes are birds which prey on invertebrates. Each thrush’s territory
     extends beyond the area of woodland in this example.


7.       Why do you think each thrush needs such a large territory?

8.      The information about energy flow through a woodland ecosystem is difficult to
        visualise when presented in this way.

        Can you design a more effective method of presenting the information in this
        example?

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012            19480                                Page 1 of 3
                                                   Energy flow in an ecosystem
      What extra information or data (not given in this activity) might help enhance
      and extend your work?




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012         19480                               Page 2 of 3
                                                    Energy flow in an ecosystem

Answers

1.    What type of plants do you think these are? Can you name any?

      Any trees, e.g. oak, beech, ash etc.; smaller shrubs and plants of the
      woodland floor, e.g. bluebell, bramble, grasses etc.

2.    What is the total amount of energy absorbed by the plants each year?

      2000 + 8000 = 10 000 KJ/m2

3.    How is this energy lost into their surroundings?

      Heat, excretion, movement, through reproduction.

4.    How efficient are birds at converting the energy they consume into new growth?

      3/300 x 100 = 1%

5.    Which type of herbivore is most efficient at converting the energy it consumes
      into growth?

      Mammals: 5/500 x 100 = 1%
      Invertebrates: 190/1200 x 100 = 15.8%

      Why do you think this is?

      Invertebrates are more efficient because they do not use energy to
      maintain their body temperature.

6.    What percentage of the plant’s annual growth is consumed by herbivorous
     animals?

      300+500+1200 = 2000
      2000/10 000 x 100 = 20%


7.   Why do you think each thrush needs such a large territory?

     The area of woodland in this example does not support enough
     invertebrates for a thrush to meet its own energy requirements.


8.   Can you design a more effective method of presenting the information in this
     example?

     A food chain or flow chart with arrows, which includes the energy data.

     What extra information or data (not given in this activity) might help enhance
     and extend your work?

     Secondary consumers
     The area of woodland
     Energy lost through death and decomposition

Capturing creatures

Teaching notes

Answers

Task 1

Pitfall trap: ground beetle, centipede, woodlouse
Pooter: shield bug, ladybird larvae
Sweep net: meadow brown butterfly, grasshopper, damselfly


Task 2

Mist net: swallows and house martins, wading birds, finches
Dart: elephant, tiger, rhino
Longworth trap: field mouse, bank vole


Task 3

Sound: bats, nightingale, bittern
Soft clay: otter, mink, water vole
Camera trap: Asiatic golden cat, pygmy hippo


There is a PDF of accompanying photographs for each task. Students could cut them up
or they could be given pre-cut sets to save time.

  Students could be asked to match the name with the methods of capture and animal
   pictures.
  Ask students to describe the capture methods by looking at the photos and to
   suggest the type of animals they could be used to catch.
  The photographs could be used as an alternative to the text based tasks.
  For a more challenging task students could be given all three sets of photographs
   and asked to sort them into groups according to the best methods of capture and
   identification (students will notice some overlap here which would lead to discussion).
   Ask students to explain their choices.

                                                                             Capturing creatures

To study a habitat or ecosystem you have to know which animals are living there.
Ecologists use keys to help them identify different organisms. But first they must capture
the animals.
