Chemical reactions – heating copper sulphate and heating cobalt chloride

Teaching notes
The resource is for use after the students have watched or carried out the two practicals -
heating copper sulphate and heating cobalt chloride.
The practical itself could be shown as a teacher demonstration or done as a class
practical. If it is not possible to carry out the practical, then there are several videos
available showing the reactions. The following videos are available at the time of writing:
      copper sulphate being heated and then rehydrated
       http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M6IIbZx7xvQ
      heating cobalt chloride
       http://www.youtube.com/watch?feature=endscreen&NR=1&v=oC3FtY29FUs
      rehydrating cobalt chloride
       http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1WCISnxqbas


Before carrying out the practical with students, an appropriate risk assessment
must be carried out. Please refer to CLEAPPS guidelines for full risk information.


Precautions
      Copper sulphate and cobalt chloride solids may irritate the eyes and skin.
      Water added to anhydrous solids produces heat.
      Substances should be heated in heatproof test tubes in the hottest part of a Bunsen
       burner flame.
      Eye protection should be worn and care taken in handling hot apparatus.
      Both chemicals can cause damage to the environment and should be disposed of in
       accordance with current CLEAPPS guidelines.

Answers

Heating copper sulphate

Before heating, the copper sulphate was blue in colour.

After heating, the copper sulphate was white in colour.

During heating it was observed that it changed from blue to white and a vapour was
given off.

The copper sulphate was left to cool and a few drops of water were then added. We
observed that it changed from white to blue and heat given off.

This is an example of a reversible chemical reaction.

Why do you think the arrow above points in both directions?

Because the reaction will go in both directions – it is reversible.

What does hydrated mean?

It contains water.

What does anhydrous mean?

It does not contain water.

Heating cobalt chloride

Before heating, the cobalt chloride it was dark pink in colour.

After heating, the cobalt chloride was light blue in colour.

During heating it was observed that it changed colour from dark pink to light blue and
a vapour was produced.

The cobalt chloride was left to cool and a few drops of water were then added. We
observed that it changed colour from light blue to pink and heat was given off.

This is an example of a reversible chemical reaction.

Both copper sulphate and cobalt chloride changed colour when water was added to them.

How could this be useful in the chemistry laboratory?

Since both change colour when water is added to the anhydrous chemical, they can
be used to test to see if a liquid is or contains water. Cobalt chloride is available as
papers which need to be heated to turn them blue and they will then turn pale pink if
the substance is water.

Answers


                             Statement                                    T/F?

  1. A molecule is a small group of atoms joined together.                  T

  2. Compounds are different types of atoms joined together.                T
  3. Neutrons have a negative charge.
     Neutrons have no charge.                                               F
  4. Compounds do not usually behave like the elements they
     contain.                                                               T
  5. In symbols representing elements, the second letter is always
     a capital letter.
     In symbols representing elements, the second letter is always          F
     a small letter.
  6. In pure substances the atoms are all the same type.
     In pure substances the particles, which can be atoms or                F
     molecules, are all the same type.
  7. The periodic table is a list of all known compounds.
     The periodic table is a list of all known elements.                    F

  8. Iron, potassium and calcium are metal elements.                        T
  9. Electrons are found in the nucleus of an atom.
     Electrons are found in the shells of an atom. / Electrons orbit        F
     the nucleus of an atom.

  10. Atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons.                    T

      Most of the mass in an atom is in its nucleus, which is made          F

  12. The centre of an atom is called the neutron.
      The centre of an atom is called the nucleus.                          F
  13. Sodium chloride is a common element.
      Sodium chloride is a common compound.                                 F
  14. Protons are so small that chemists say they have no mass.
      Protons are small and chemists say they have a relative mass          F
      of 1.

Connect 4 – genetics and inheritance

Teaching notes
This could be a starter, plenary or revision activity.
It can be carried out using scraps of paper, exercise books, with laminated
cards, or on an interactive whiteboard. There is a Magnet interactive resource
that can be used with the activity.
Working in pairs, students look at the words and phrases, trying to choose four
which are connected in some way. They agree on one or two sentences which
include the four words and explain the connection between those words. They
can then put up their hands; the class is stopped and everyone listens to the
connection. If the explanation is agreed to be valid, those four words are
scrubbed from the list and everyone has to start again with the remaining
words and phrases.
It is up to you to decide whether to continue with the game if a combination of
words does not match one of the suggested answers. You could praise
students for their ingenuity but urge the class to continue to search for a group
of four which matches the suggested answers; this way you will not be left with
a group of mismatched words at the end. (However, your class might enjoy
rising to the challenge of linking, for example, recessive, meiosis, clone and
Franklin!)

Suggested answers
                          sickle cell
   haemophilia                              cystic fibrosis      colour blindness
                          anaemia
   vegetative
                           asexual                clones             identical
  reproduction
       A                      C                      T                  G
  Levenne and
                           Franklin               Watson               Crick
    Chargraff
  chromosome                 DNA                   bases               gene
   homozygous           heterozygous             recessive          dominant
     meiosis               mitosis                haploid             diploid

Haemophilia, sickle cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis and colour blindness
are all examples of inherited diseases.
Vegetative reproduction is an example of asexual reproduction in which
the offspring are all clones and identical to the parent plant.
A,C,T and G are the four bases found in DNA. A always pairs with T and C with
G.
These people all worked on the structure of DNA. Levene and Chargaff
described the base pairs, whilst Franklin, Watson and Crick worked out that
the DNA molecule was a double helix.
Chromosomes contain DNA. Sequences of bases in DNA make up the code
for different genes.



© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012         19639                               Page 1 of 3
                                               Connect 4 – genetics and inheritance
Characteristics are controlled by pairs of alleles. If the alleles in the pair are
identical, the gene is homozygous; if they are not identical, it is known as
heterozygous. One of the alleles will be dominant and the other recessive.
Meiosis and mitosis are both types of cell division. Meiosis forms haploid
daughter cells whereas mitosis forms diploid daughter cells.
Of course, students may come up with their own combinations which are
equally as valid.

Light – an assessed practical

Teaching notes

Students appreciate opportunities to demonstrate their practical skills.

This activity is designed to be carried out over a period of 1 – 2 lessons at the end of a
topic on light.

If possible, keep group sizes small, 2-3 students, to ensure that everyone is occupied. To
make it manageable, assess each group rather than individual students.

Share with students what you will be looking for and explain that each skill is awarded a
mark out of 10 or 20.

There are a total of 100 marks.
30–39 = Level 3; 50–59 = Level 5; 80+ = Level 8


Apparatus

  ray/light boxes
  plane mirrors
  concave and convex mirrors
  a variety of transparent blocks
  prisms
  concave and convex lenses
  plain paper for diagrams


If the amount of equipment available is an issue then each group’s sheet could be marked
so that they each start with a different practical.

Please ensure you carry out your own risk assessment.


Skills development

  planning
  manipulation of equipment
  testing ideas
  developing problem solving strategies
  team work and communication

                           Sound waves travel through the air.


                       The small bones make the cochlea vibrate.

            The cornea bends (refracts) the light rays as they enter the eye.

                             Light rays travel through the air.


                     The light rays are bent (refracted) by the lens.


                          The light rays pass through the pupil.

Blood vessels

Teaching notes

This could be a starter, plenary or revision exercise.

A statement about a type of blood vessel is read out.

Students decide whether the statement refers to arteries, veins or capillaries.

They could work in pairs and write their answer on a mini whiteboard.

For a more active start to the lesson, they could physically move to different
parts of the room. Rather than the class moving en masse, you could select a
small portion of the class at a time to answer e.g. boy/girls only, people
wearing glasses etc.

On www.teachitscience.co.uk there is an interactive Magnet activity which will
randomly generate a statement and when double-clicked will reveal the correct
answer.


Statements about capillaries

      The vessel wall is one cell thick.

      They have a very small lumen.

      Glucose diffuses into tissues from these vessels.

      Oxygen diffuses from these vessels into surrounding tissues.

      They absorb amino acids and glucose (products of digestion).

      Waste products pass into the blood through vessel walls.

      They form a dense network around alveoli.

      White blood cells can squeeze out of these vessels.

      They form the glomerulus.

      They lie beneath the epithelium of villi.

      These vessels are very numerous in the placenta.



Statements about arteries

      Almost all of these vessels carry oxygenated blood.

      Blood is at high pressure in these vessels.
© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012         19675                           Page 1 of 2
                                                                    Blood vessels

      They have relatively thick walls.

      Their walls are elastic.

      Their walls are more muscular than other blood vessels.

      They carry blood away from heart.

      They have a pulse.

      They supply oxygen to heart muscle.

      In these vessels, red blood cells are rich in oxyhaemoglobin.

      These vessels carry bright red blood.

      The carotid is …

      The aorta is …


Statements about veins

      They carry deoxygenated blood.

      Blood travels through these vessels at low pressure.

      They have a large lumen.

      They will collapse if empty of blood.

      These vessels have relatively thin walls.

      They have valves to prevent back flow of blood.

      They are known as ‘varicose’ if valves have deteriorated.

      Blood plasma in these vessels contains more carbon dioxide.

      Body movements keep blood flowing through these vessels

      They have connections with lymph vessels.

      Three types are known as superficial, deep and systemic.

      The jugular is …

      The vena cava is …

Modelling the circulatory system

Starter

The PowerPoint or interactive could be used as a quick labelling activity to introduce
the modelling activity.


Modelling the circulatory system

Depending on the group the students could be asked to design their own simulation
using the following resources.

Resources
    –    2 large hoops
    –    100 red and blue cards
    –    2 boxes/bucket
    –    labels for heart, lungs and cells


Task

Assign students to a role: Lungs (1 person), cells (1 person), heart (2 people to hold
hoops), blood (rest of class or a smaller group).

Arrange students around the room (refer to animation on slide 4).
Students move around to represent blood flow – picking up red cards at the lungs;
going through the hoop (heart); dropping off the red cards at the cells and picking up
blue cards; returning back through the heart (hoop) to lungs and dropping of blue
cards.
The circulation will stop when all the blue cards are at the lungs and the red cards are
at the cells.


Discussion

There are many difficulties with this model. Get the students to recognise some of
them and suggest how the model could be improved. The following questions could
be asked to stimulate discussion.

Did the model show how oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood? – oxygen
in red blood cells, carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma.

In the model circulation stopped, why does this not happen in reality? – discuss that
concentration gradients are maintained in lungs due to gas exchange and blood flow
and in cells due to respiration.

Was the movement of the blood realistic in the model? – discuss network of blood
vessels.

Ask students to draw the model and evaluate it.

Reproduction and inheritance – question hunt

Teaching notes

This resource is a series of questions which become more demanding – ranging
from asking students to state/name something to asking them to explain a
more difficult concept.

It could be used in a variety of ways.

   1. The cards could be cut up and placed around the room (more than one
      set could be distributed) The students move round and find cards then
      record their answers on paper. They could be asked to find two of each
      type of question, e.g. state, define and explain. The cards could be
      photocopied onto different coloured card depending on the demand of
      the question. The task could be differentiated by asking different groups
      to find different numbered/coloured cards.

   2. The cards could be used as a quick starter where a student picks a card
      and reads out the question. Students discuss the answer in pairs and
      one pair is picked to suggest an answer. If the answer is correct, they
      choose the next card.

   3. The cards could be used as a team quiz where teams choose to attempt
      an easy/medium/difficult question. If they get it right, then they are
      awarded 1 point for easy, 2 points for medium and 3 points for difficult
      questions.

Suggested answers

 1.    Animal cell labelled: cytoplasm, nucleus, cell membrane.
 2.    Ovary.
 3.    Embryo.
 4.    Sperm and eggs.
 5.    Red blood cells.
 6.    Sexual and asexual.
 7.    28 days.
 8.    Chromosomes.
 9.    Organisms are chosen for their desirable characteristics and are bred
       together. Offspring exhibiting the characteristic are then selected to
       breed from.
 10.   Long tail, lots of mitochondria, head with genetic material.
 11.   Variation caused by environmental factors, e.g. diet, climate, soil type,
       flower colour, hair style.
 12.   Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a vacuole; animal cells do
       not.
 13.   Inherited variation is due to offspring receiving genetic information
       (genes) from their parents, e.g. eye colour, blood group.
 14.   The genetic code is altered in the lab.
 15.   The lining of the uterus builds up, then breaks down and is lost in
       menstruation.
 16.   Oxygen and nutrients move from the mother’s blood to foetal blood in
       the placenta. Waste moves from foetal blood to the mother’s. The
       umbilical cord joins the placenta to the foetus.
 17.   Sex cells contain half the chromosomes from each parent.
 18.   Tail for swimming, mitochondria to supply energy for movement, head to
       penetrate egg cell, genetic information to combine with egg cell haploid
       set.
 19.   There are only a few types of blood group. Discontinuous variation
       shows discrete variation.
 20.   The amniotic fluid cushions the baby against knocks. The baby develops
       inside the mother’s uterus. Waste products are removed via the
       placenta.
 21.   Frogs do not raise their offspring. Lots do not survive so are produced in
       large numbers.
 22.   Unknown long term effects.
 23.   They share the same genetic information.
 24.   Height shows an infinite amount of variation within the range of height.
       It is affected by lots of factors, e.g. genetic and environmental.

                                                     Carbon cycle jigsaw
Teaching notes

This jigsaw helps students engage with the carbon cycle. Students
often struggle to link processes together in science and the carbon
cycle can be difficult in this regard, particularly for lower ability
students.

As an initial task, students are asked (either individually or in pairs)
to cut out and put together the pieces of the carbon cycle. This
gives them some familiarity with the key parts and processes
involved.

Students can then use the jigsaw they have created to do individual
research on the carbon cycle. There is a worksheet that follows on
from the jigsaw activity (resource 19849, ‘Carbon cycle questions’).

The diagram can either be printed on paper each time it is used, for
each student/pair to stick into their books, or it can be printed on
card for multiple uses.

Page 2 shows the completed image, which could be used for class
discussion.

A jigsaw for the nitrogen cycle is also available (resource 19846,
‘Nitrogen cycle jigsaw’), along with a set of questions (resource
19847, ‘Nitrogen cycle questions’) and a consolidation activity
focused on improving exam answers and based on peer-assessment
strategies (resource 19848, ‘Nutrient cycles peer assessment’).

There are also two fully interactive resources, one for each of the
nutrient cycles, available from the Teachit Science Biology whizzy
things page:

http://www.teachitscience.co.uk/whizzybiology.

Electricity – pairs game

Introduction

A simple game designed to increase students’ confidence in the symbols of circuitry. Most
students have played ‘pairs’ at some time or other, so the rules are generally known to all.


Instructions

Divide the class into groups of between two and four players. Photocopy one set of the
sheets (as well as a sheet of answers) for each group. It is best to photocopy them onto
card or stiff paper that is thick enough so the typing cannot be seen through it!

Cut the sheets into individual cards. Remove any pairings not relevant to your group.

The aim of the game is to make pairs. A pair consists of symbol or graph with its
appropriate name. The answer sheet is given to each group to help them check the
pairings are correct.


Rules of the game

The cards are shuffled and spread out randomly face down on the bench.

The first player turns over two cards. If they are a pair, the player removes them and has
another go. If they are not a pair they are turned face down again. When the first player
has finished their go, play moves to the next player.

The winner is the one with the most pairs at the end.


Variations

One player can be nominated in each group whose sole responsibility is to check the
answers.

Groups of students can be formed according to their ability and different groupings of
cards given to them. The less able may find that sheets one and two are enough to start
with.

Also, with a bit of manipulation the names can be photocopied onto one colour of card and
the symbol or graph onto another. Therefore, when a student picks up a pair of cards they
are picking up two different colours. The game is faster this way.

Teaching notes

These questions were designed to be used with the jigsaw ‘The heart’ (19999). However,
they could be used with other heart diagrams. Some modification of the questions may be
necessary in this case.

Questions which are designed to provide more challenge are marked with an asterisk.


Suggested answers:

1) Right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, right atrium


2) For each bullet point, the following should be selected:
       atria
       receive blood into the heart
       a ventricle

Note: the word ‘atria’ is not used on the diagram, but this choice can be deduced and is a
literacy learning point.


3) Similarities:
       They are both ventricles
       They both receive blood from atria
       They both send blood out of the heart.

4) The chambers on the left of the diagram are named ‘right, the chambers on the right of
   the diagram are named ‘left’.

    *This is because if the heart was in your body, then the sides would be reversed – they
    would be on the correct sides.

Note: pupils usually understand the logic behind this better if they pretend to transplant the
heart diagram into themselves.


5) Differences:

    The left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right ventricle. The left ventricle sends
    blood out of the heart through the aorta rather than the pulmonary artery. The left
    ventricle is pumping out (oxygenated) blood to the body, whereas the right ventricle is
    pumping out (deoxygenated) blood to the lungs.


6) Oxygenated




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013              19998                                 Page 3 of 4
                                                                   The heart – questions
7) The blood is pumped to the lungs because it is deoxygenated, meaning it is low in
   oxygen. In the lungs, the haemoglobin in the red blood cells will be able to pick up
   oxygen.

Note: discourage pupils saying that the blood has no oxygen.


8) Valves.

    *This is important to make the heart as efficient as possible e.g. if blood could flow
    backwards, less blood may be in the ventricles to be pumped out and extra work
    would be needed to get the blood back into the atria. Blood might back up in the atria.
    Pupils sometimes find it useful for the valves to be equated to traffic police controlling
    the flow of cars.


9) *It leaves the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated), goes to the capillaries in the lungs
   (and becomes oxygenated). It returns to heart through the pulmonary vein and goes
   into the left atrium. It goes through a valve and into the left ventricle. It is pumped out
   of heart through the aorta.


10) The heart has two sides with two chambers on each. The top chambers are called
    atria. They receive blood. Blood then flows through valves into the ventricles (bottom
    chambers). Valves stop the blood flowing backwards. The right side receives
    deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava. This blood exits through
    the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
    The left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein
    and exits through the aorta to the body. The left ventricle has a thicker wall to pump
    blood to the rest of the body.

bullet points or extend the word limit!

Teaching notes
This jigsaw was designed to help engage students in learning the
structure and function of the heart. Whilst students are usually very
interested a heart dissection, they often struggle with naming the
structures and remembering the direction of blood flow.

As an initial task, students are asked (either individually or in pairs)
to cut out and put together the pieces of the heart. This gives them
some familiarity with the key parts and names involved.

Students can then use the jigsaw they have created to do individual
‘research’ on the heart.

A jigsaw of the circulatory system (resource 20000, ‘The circulatory
system – jigsaw’) is also available, along with a set of questions for
both (resource 20001, ‘The circulatory system questions’ and
resource 19998, ‘The heart – questions’) and a consolidation
activity focussed on improving exam answers and based on peer-
assessment strategies (resource 20002, ‘Circulatory system peer
assessment’).

The circulatory system

Look at a diagram of the circulatory system and use it to help you answer the
following questions.

1)   State the three types of blood vessels that make up the circulatory
system.

              

2)      State the name of the space which blood flows in a blood vessel.

        .....................................................................................................................

        .....................................................................................................................


3)      Complete the table to compare the relative sizes and structures of the
        three types of blood vessels. Choose from the options in brackets.

     Blood Vessel                                              Thickness of wall

        .....................................................................................................................

5)   Choose the correct words for these sentences. Underline your choice in
each bracket.

                   Most arteries carry (oxygenated/deoxygenated) blood.
                  Most veins carry (oxygenated/deoxygenated) blood.
                  In most networks of capillaries, the blood becomes more
                   (oxygenated/deoxygenated) as it travels through.

effectively.

      .....................................................................................................................

7)    Describe what happens to blood as it passes through the lung capillaries.

      .....................................................................................................................

Teaching notes
These questions were designed to be used with the diagram ‘The circulatory
system jigsaw’ (20000). However, they could be used with other diagrams of
the circulatory system. Some modification of the questions may be necessary
in this case.

Questions with a * are designed to provide more challenge.

Suggested answers:

1)    Artery, vein, capillary
2)    Lumen
3)    Complete table:

                        Size of lumen                                  Do they contain
                                            Thickness of wall
     Blood vessel            (very                                         valves?
                                            (thin/ thick/ very thin)
                      narrow/narrow/wide)                                 (yes / no)
        artery              narrow                  thick                    no
        vein                    wide                 thin                   yes
      capillary          very narrow              very thin                  no

4)    Veins take blood towards the heart. Arteries take blood away from the
      heart.

      * This can be remembered because ‘arteries’ begins with an ‘a’, and so
      does ‘away’, whereas ‘vein’ ends in ‘in’ and they take blood ‘in’ to the
      heart.

      Note: pupils may try to compare the structure of the vessels here. If so,
      this is an opportunity to remind them of the meaning of the word
      ‘function’.

5)    Choosing the correct words.
             oxygenated
             deoxygenated
             deoxygenated

       * The (pulmonary) artery which takes blood away from the heart to the
       lungs carries deoxygenated blood. It takes this blood to the lungs so that
       it can be oxygenated. As this blood vessel is taking blood away from the
       heart, it is called an artery.

       The (pulmonary) vein which takes blood into the heart from the lungs
       carries oxygenated blood. It takes this blood to the heart so that it can be
       pumped around the body. As this blood vessel it taking blood into the
       heart, it is called a vein.


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013         20001                                     Page 3 of 5
                                                         The circulatory system
6)   They have a very thin wall (just one cell thick) and so materials such as
     oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide can easily diffuse in and out of them.

     Note: It is also worth noting that capillaries are tiny compared to other
     blood vessels and so they can easily access cells.

7    As blood is passing through lung capillaries, it becomes oxygenated.

     Note: this is a basic answer. Pupils should be able to pick from the
     diagram that that this is a gradual process. They are likely to have already
     studied the blood, and so will be able to describe this in more detail i.e.
     each red blood cell contains haemoglobin. As the blood cell passes
     through the capillaries, more and more haemoglobin combines with
     oxygen to become oxyhaemoglobin.

8) * The haemoglobin in the red blood cells is likely to have given up most of
     its oxygen when it passed through the leg capillaries.

              The blood is deoxygenated.
              The blood now travels back towards the heart in veins.
              The valves in the veins help to stop the backflow of blood.
              The blood will enter the heart via the vena cava.
              Blood will pass through the right atrium into the right ventricle.
              It will leave and go to the lungs in the pulmonary artery.
              In the lung capillaries, the haemoglobin in the red blood cells
               becomes oxygenated again.
              The oxygenated blood enters the other side (left-side) of the
               heart through a vein (the pulmonary vein) and leaves in an
               artery (the aorta).
              The blood travels in this artery at high pressure to all areas of the
               body (including the leg muscle capillaries)
              The oxyhaemoglobin in the red blood cells will lose oxygen so
               that the cells in the tissues can respire.

9)    * A suggested full description in 100 words.

              The circulatory system transports blood around the body.
              The heart is the muscular organ that pumps the blood.
              Three types of blood vessels carry the blood.
              Arteries take blood at high pressure away from the heart and so
               have thick walls, but small lumens.
              Veins take blood at lower pressure towards the heart.
              They have larger lumens, but thinner walls.
              Veins have valves to stop blood flowing in the wrong direction.
              Capillaries are the smallest.
              They have walls that are only one cell thick.
              These features allow capillaries to easily exchange materials
               such as oxygen with nearby cells.

Task
A GCSE student called Donald was given a test about the      Examiner’s
circulatory system. Below are his answers. Read the            notes
questions and his answers carefully.

Mark Donald’s answers and annotate the paper to show
where and why you have awarded marks. Add notes to
show how Donald could improve his answers.

                   Circulatory system test

1. Name the main organ in the circulatory system. (1)

The heart.


2. There are three types of blood vessel. Tick the type of
blood vessel that is correct for each statement. (6)

                                              Capillarie
   Statement          Arteries     Veins
                                                  s

3. Where are valves found in the circulatory system?
Describe their function. (4)

Valves are found in the heart, where they stop blood
flowing in the wrong direction. They are also found in
blood vessels. In blood vessels, they do exactly the same
job – they stop the backflow of blood!

4. Describe the direction of blood flow through the right
© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012       20002                      Page 1 of 8
                                      Circulatory system peer assessment
hand side of the heart. (3)

Blood goes into the right atrium and then out from the right
ventricle.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2012      20002                     Page 2 of 8
                                                            Circulatory system peer assessment

5. How does a molecule of oxygen get from the capillaries
in the lungs to a muscle cell in your big toe? (4)

It’s quite easy. The oxygen gets into the blood in the lungs
and then it travels along the arteries to the big toe before
going into a capillary and escaping through its thin walls
into a nearby muscle cell!


*6. Compare the structure and function of veins and
arteries. (4)

Veins take blood into the heart, but arteries take blood
away from the heart. Veins have a big lumen and a thin
wall, and the blood travels through them at low pressure.
Arteries have a thicker wall because they carry blood at
much higher pressures.


7. Compare and contrast the structures and functions of
the two sides of the heart. (6)

Both sides of the heart have two chambers. Each side has
an atrium at the top and a ventricle at the bottom. In the
left atrium, blood enters from the lungs through the
pulmonary vein and then passes through the left ventricle
and out through the aorta. The left side of the heart pumps
blood to the body. The right side of the heart has a very
similar job, but it gets its blood from the body through the
vena cava and sends it to the lungs via the pulmonary
artery. Basically, both sides are pumps but they go to
different places.

He may score one mark for mentioning that they are found in the heart and that they
stop blood flowing in the wrong direction. Although he has correctly said that they are
found in blood vessels, he has not said which type of blood vessel (veins) they are
found in. Also, just saying they do the same job is not sufficient. He again needs to
refer to their function, saying that they stop the backflow of blood.

4) Although Donald’s answer is brief, he would score 2 marks.

He has correctly identified that blood enters at the right atrium. His answer would be
better if he described this as being at the top of the heart and that blood then flows
downwards before being pumped out from the right ventricle. He could gain an extra
mark for mentioning passing valves, or for mentioning the blood vessels that take the
blood in (vena cava) and out (pulmonary artery) of this side.

5) A lot of Donald’s answer repeats what was in the question. He would be lucky to
score even one mark.

Donald needs to recognise that the red blood cells carrying the oxygen go back to the
left hand side of the heart where they are pumped through the aorta into arteries.
They enter capillaries (he may score a mark here) and the oxygen diffuses out to the
muscle cells.

6) Quite a good answer! Donald would likely score three marks.

Donald scores marks for correctly comparing the function of arteries and veins. It is
good to see that Donald has used techniques that he has been taught to remember
the function – it doesn’t matter if the examiners see this! Donald has also correctly
compared much of their structure (e.g. thickness of wall). He could improve the
answer by mentioning that veins have valves. He could also compare the size of the
artery lumen to that of the vein.

7) The content of Donald’s answer is reasonable. He would score 4 marks.

In 6-mark questions, the responses are marked in bands of 1-2, 3-4, 5-6. In each
band, literacy is also considered.

He does give some similarities between the structure of each side (e.g. atria,
ventricles), so he fulfils the requirements for band 1-2.

To get 3-4 marks, differences in structure and function would be expected. Donald
has correctly given detail of each associated blood vessel that supplies the heart or
takes its blood away (e.g. aorta, pulmonary vessels). He has also stated the function
of the left hand side of the heart. However, he does not give the function of the right
hand side, simply stating that it pumps blood elsewhere.

Although Donald does not use capital letters properly, his spelling is very good and he
makes good use of a range of scientific words. Hence, he is awarded 4 marks.

To get 5-6 marks, a full and logical comparison would be expected. For this, the
omission already identified would be expected. Also, the inclusion of oxygenated and
deoxygenated blood would be expected as well as the presence of valves as being a
similar structure in both sides.

Overall, Donald would score (at most) 16 marks.

Plant pops
Teaching notes

This activity is designed to give students a sense of the challenges facing ecologists when
assessing the population of different plants.

This activity, with elements of a competitive game, is a useful alternative when a field trip
or access to the school field is not possible.

The aim is to assess the accuracy of using quadrats as a technique for estimating the
population of a plant species. The activity helps students understand the significance of
positioning quadrats randomly and that populations can only be estimated as it is not
possible in practice, to count all the individuals in an area.

However, this activity is not designed to be an accurate representation of how quadrats
are used in the field. It is a fun activity to do on a wet day which will get students thinking.

The activity is based on the game ‘Battleships’.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013              20087                                   Page 1 of 6
                                                                            Plant pops
Preparation

Equipment per pair of students:

     X2 sheets of blank grids
     stopwatch
     pencil

Each student should have a sheet of blank grids. The first blank grid on the sheet is to
record the distribution of the plants in their survey area. The second blank grid is their
record of the ‘throws’ they have made onto their partner’s sample area.

The grids represent plots of land. You could assign a specific habitat to the plots e.g.
saltmarsh, woodland, chalk downland, water meadow, heathland, sand dune.

A home learning task could be given as preparation for this activity. Students could find
images of a plant species linked to one or more of the habitats listed above. They could
write a description of the plant and it’s habitat in their own words, using more than one
source of information. They should write a list of references at the end.

Some suggestions of plants:

        Sea lavender Limonium vulgare – saltmarsh
        wood sorrel Oxalis acetosella – woodland
        wild thyme Thymus praecox – chalk downland
        creeping buttercup Ranunculus repens – water meadow
        tormentil Potentilla erecta – heathland
        eyebright Euphrasia sp – sand dune.

A follow-on home learning task could involve students finding out how ecologists working
in the field, ensure that they have placed their quadrats randomly; or they could research
other methods of surveying plants.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013            20087                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                                 Plant pops
The activity

 Explain to students that their grids represent areas of land and that they are going to
investigate the most effective way of estimating the population of a certain species of
plant, using a quadrat. For convenience, the ‘quadrat’ is the same size as one square on
the grid.

 From the beginning they will know the actual population size of the plant species. Explain
that there are constraints on ecologists working in the field and that they do not have the
resources to count all the individual plants in the area. How many random throws of the
quadrat will give the best estimate?

Play

  I.   Decide for the class what percentage of the grid is to be occupied by the plant
       species. Each square is 4% of the whole, so choose multiples of 4, e.g. 32% = 8
       squares.

 II.   Without showing others, students shade in the required number of squares on their
       first grid. The plants may be regularly spaced, clustered or concentrated in one
       small region.

III.   Player 1 gives coordinates for a square, player 2 puts a cross through the square on
       their coloured grid and says if a ‘hit’ has been made. Player 1 marks the square on
       their empty grid to show if it was a hit or a miss.

       Each turn represents one throw of the quadrat.

       Play continues as Player 2 now gives the coordinates for a square.

       In this initial game, play continues until all the plants have been found on one of the
       grids. Students need to time how long this takes.

IV.    Class discussion

       How long did it take them to find all the plants on one grid? How many ‘throws’ of
       the quadrat do they feel would have given a reliable estimate of the population?

       What do they feel is a reliable figure? +/– 5% or 10%? What might it depend on?

       Plants may not be evenly spread over the area of the grid. Will the reliability of their
       estimate compromised by the positioning of the plants?

V.     Now they are ready to investigate further. Students can decide to limit the number
       of ‘throws’ to what they feel is a reasonable number. Alternatively, they may decide
       to give themselves a time limit for the game. These conditions represent the
       constraints of time and money on ecologists working in the field.

VI.    Keeping the number of plants constant in each game, students play 3 games using
       the limited number of throws or time limit that they have decided upon.


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013             20087                                    Page 3 of 6
                                                                         Plant pops
       What percentage population estimate did each game produce? What is the range
       of their results?




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013         20087                               Page 4 of 6
                                                                               Plant pops
Further points for discussion

  a) Point 2, ‘without showing others, students colour the required number of squares of
     their first grid’ enables students to ‘throw’ their quadrats randomly.

       What would happen if they had seen their opponent’s grid with the plants drawn in?

       What did happen when they scored a ‘hit’? Did they concentrate their throws in that
       area?

       How could they ensure that all their throws throughout the game, were random?
       Why is this important?

       How could they investigate the effect of bias?

  b) The 5 x 5 grid is small to allow more than one game to be carried out in a lesson. It
     represents a sample area of the larger habitat.

       How would students use their results to provide an estimate of the whole habitat
       area? What would they need to know?
       How accurate would this estimate be?
       How could they test their ideas?

       If time allows, pairs of students could come together into groups to carry out
       investigations to test some of these ideas.

Microbes

Viruses

Viruses are even smaller than bacteria and are the cause of many diseases.
They are different from bacteria because they can only reproduce inside a
living cell. The common cold, chicken pox, measles, AIDS and glandular fever
are all caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not affect or harm viruses. Viruses
can be used to transfer genes into target cells.




Bacteria

Bacteria are so small we need a microscope to see them. They are single
celled organisms found in the soil, water and air around us. Harmful bacteria
can cause diseases such as scarlet fever, food poisoning and whooping cough.
Bacteria can reproduce and grow outside a living organism, and they can
reproduce very quickly: a small group invading the body does not take very
long to multiply into millions. They can be treated with antibiotics. Bacteria
have many uses, including the production of insulin and sewage treatment.




Fungi

These are simple organisms that feed off dead and rotting material. Organisms
that belong to this kingdom are moulds, yeasts and mushrooms. They used to
belong to the plant kingdom. Some fungi can cause rashes and often affect
nails, hair and mucous membranes. Ringworm, athlete’s foot and thrush are all
examples of fungal diseases. Fungi have many uses, e.g. yeasts are used in
brewing and baking; Penicillin is produced from the mold Penicillium.

Teaching notes

This resource is a good starting point from which to explore how to approach
extended answer exam questions.

The following link is a BBC learning zone clip that is a good introduction to the
advantages and disadvantages of stem cell research:
http://www.bbc.co.uk/learningzone/clips/stem-cell-research/6013.html.


Students could discuss the following questions in pairs or as a class.

 1) What do you think this type of cloning could be used for?

       2) Why will these cells, and the tissues and organs they form, not be
          rejected when put into the patient’s body?

 3) Evaluate the issues involved in the use of embryonic stem cells in medical
    research and treatments. Do you think stem cells from embryos should be
    used for medical research?

     Ask students to break their answer down into two sections:

     i) List all the advantages and disadvantages of embryonic stem cell research
        they can think of. Ask them to compare some of the advantages with the
        disadvantages. They should try to use link words such as ‘but’, ‘whereas’,
        and ‘however’.

     ii) Draw your own conclusion about the use of stem cells. You will need to
         justify your conclusion.

         Overall, I think ......... because………

Touch Testing
Aim
To find out which part of your body is the most sensitive to touch.

Method
  1. Work in pairs. Decide which areas of skin to test e.g. fingertip, forehead, knee, elbow etc.
  2. The tester randomly writes down a ‘1’ or a ‘2’ for each attempt in the 2 nd column of the table. The
     subject must not see.
  3. The tester gently presses one or two points (according to the table) against the subject’s skin.
  4. Tick the third column if the subject guessed correctly. Repeat steps 3-4 until all 10 attempts have been
     made.
  5. Total the correct answers. This is the subject’s score for that part of the skin.
  6. Repeat all the steps for a different area of skin.

                                                                 Touch Testing

Teaching notes


Duration

The investigation should take about 20 minutes, depending on how many body
parts are tested.


Equipment per pair of students:

   2 x worksheets
   1 x touch tester
   blindfold (or the subject can close their eyes)




The touch tester can be made by pushing two pins
into a rubber bung, 1cm apart.




Further discussion

Try to encourage students to test their fingertips – this should be the most
sensitive part of the body.

Discuss with pupils what detects the touch (receptors) and how you are aware
of it (nerve impulses to the brain). Discuss what makes some areas more
sensitive than others, i.e. a higher density of touch receptors.

Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?

Aim
To find out how the strength of a tube of paper (bone) changes as its length
increases. I will do this by hanging weights on the ‘bone’ until it breaks.

Independent and dependent variables
A variable is something in your experiment that changes. It may change
because you change it (this is the independent variable) or it could change
as a result of doing the experiment and you are going to measure this change
(the dependent variable).

Tasks
A.    For this investigation, write down the independent and the dependent
      variable.
          independent variable – the variable you are going to control.
          dependent variable – the variable that you will measure when you do
           the experiment.

B.    Draw a table to input the following data (choose the appropriate units for
      each entry);
          length of bone (there are 5 lengths to investigate)
          diameter of bone
          mass needed to break bone.

C.    You do not want any other variables to change. These are control
      variables and must be kept the same. Read through the method below
      and write down the control variables.

D.    Make five paper bones using the following instructions. The bones should
      be of different lengths – 20cm, 30cm, 40cm, 50cm and 60cm.
      1.   Take the longest paper (60cm) and roll it up tightly around a pencil.
      2.   Use a 5cm length of sellotape to hold the curled paper in place in the
           middle. Remove the pencil.
      3.   Measure the diameter of the bone accurately.
      4.   Mark the mid-point of the ‘bone’.
      5.   Repeat this for each of the bones.
      6.   Remember they should all be made using paper of the same width
           and rolled to the same diameter.
      7.   We will assume the thickness of each piece of paper is the same.

E.    Test the strength of the bones using the following
      method.
      1.   Set up the stands as shown in the diagram.
      2.   Rest the longest (60cm) bone on the clamps.

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013        20719                           Page 1 of 4
     Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?
    3.   Hang a 100g weight on the midpoint of the bone.
    4.   Keep adding weights until the ‘bone’ breaks (bends).
    5.   Record the data in your table.
    6.   Repeat steps 5-8 with the other 4 lengths of bone.
    7.   Draw a graph of your results and make a conclusion.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013    20719                        Page 2 of 4
     Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?

Teaching notes

Context
Students investigate how the strength of a tube of paper (bone) changes as its
length increases. They do this by hanging weights on the mid-point of the
‘bone’ until it breaks (bends). This investigation could feature whilst teaching a
topic on bones, joints or movement, but it is meant to build on their practical
skills. It requires students to do the following;

    -     identify an independent and dependent variable
    -     pick out control variables and understand why this is important
    -     draw a table for their results
    -     carry out an investigation in a methodical way and record accurate
          data
    -     draw a graph of the data with a line of best fit
    -      make a conclusion.

ISAs at GCSE level require students to understand and use variables.
The teacher can discuss the different types of variables with the students –
independent, dependent and control variables.

In this investigation the variables are;

         independent – length of bone
         dependent – mass required to break the bone
         control – diameter of bone, width of paper, length of sellotape,
          weights put onto midpoint of bone, paper thickness, overhang of bone
          on clamp.

Emphasis should be placed on the need to make the test valid. If more than
one independent variable were to change, the experiment would not be valid.

Equipment per group
         2 x retort stands, clamps and bosses.
         100g weights with holder and hook (wide enough to hang over the
          bone)
         5 x 5cm lengths of sellotape
         ruler
         5 sheets of paper (one each of the following dimensions):  20cm x
          21cm
          30cm x 21cm
          40cm x 21cm
          50cm x 21cm
          60cm x 21cm.


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013        20719                           Page 3 of 4
     Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?
The paper used in the experiment should be cut to size before the lesson and
preferably marked with an arrow to indicate the way it should be rolled up.

The investigation can get a bit noisy with falling weights so encourage your
students to put their hands under the weights to catch them.

Understanding our environment – learning grid

Teaching notes
This learning grid has been adapted from an idea from the book Outstanding
Teaching: Engaging Learners (Crown House Publishing) by Andy Griffith and
Mark Burns (2012).

This resource is designed for revision of OCR GCSE Gateway Science Biology
module B2, ‘Understanding our environment’, but can easily be adapted for
other specifications.

Equipment needed by each group

     -    2 dice
     -    learning grid
     -    set of keyword cards, placed face down
     -    pencils and paper
     -    play dough

Instructions

Students can play in pairs or groups of four.
Students roll a dice twice to get a grid reference.

They take it in turns to link the image to a keyword or explain the keyword.

The activity can be differentiated by asking students to:

A.       Give three key points related to the square.
B.       Make links between their square and another.
C.       Talk for a minute on the keyword/image.

Alternatively on their first go they could give A answers, on their second go
they do B etc.
Or the teacher could allow 5 minutes when everyone gives A answers. Then
using the Teachit timer they could get everyone to swap to B and then change
to C a few minutes later.

When students land on one of the following squares they take a keyword from
the pile.


                    Students act out a keyword for the others to guess.

Teaching notes

This is intended as a quick starter activity (5 minutes) to stimulate a discussion about variation and what factors it is caused by, i.e.
inherited and environmental factors. It should be used sensitively and with students who will be supportive of each other.

Once the activity is completed ask the students:

   1) If they managed to fill in all of the boxes, it’s quite likely that they have not been able to. Can they explain why?

   2)    If anyone found someone who had all of the same characteristics as themselves. This might happen if there are identical twins in
        the group!

   3)    Ask for their ideas as to why everyone is different.

   4)    Ask what they notice about the characteristics to introduce the idea of features being inherited and dependent on the
        environment.

   5)    The students could group the characteristics depending on whether they are inherited or affected by the environment.

Taboo – stem cells and cloning

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any of the
additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.

1.    Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each team).

2.    Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto different coloured
      paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have all the cards back at the end
      of the activity in order to reuse them.

3.    The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

4.    An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile, and then
      describes the word at the top of the card without using the words below. The rest of
      their team must guess which word is described. Participants are not allowed to say
      ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

5.    Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the opposing team
      may challenge and the individual must move on to the next word.

6.    Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as possible to
      the players in their team (a longer time may be required to allow more descriptions
      to take place) before play passes to the next team. There are no penalties for
      wrong guesses.

7.    For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
      point. Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each
      group.

Science in the news – living ear grown in lab

Teaching notes

This task can be used when covering cells, tissues and organs with GCSE students or high achieving
KS3 groups.
It is based on the article from The Week magazine called ‘Living ear grown in lab’. Further information
and web links can be found at http://www.nhs.uk/news/2013/08August/Pages/Artificial-ear-grown-in-
lab.aspx.
All links were available at the time of publishing.


Starter
As an interesting stimulus show the class the famous image of a human ear grown on a mouse's back
(http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/1949073.stm). You may also like to show them a video
(http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LHHe_q3DNas).
Ask the students to discuss in pairs why they think scientists have done this and feedback their ideas.
Explain that some people have lost ears through injury or because they were born without them (you
might like to show a suitable image at this point) and this kind of research is helping to work out ways
of building human tissue in the lab to help such people. It is called tissue engineering. The image
shown at the start shocked the world when it was released in 1997. Since then, tissue engineering is
making progress and the same team have recently announced improvements to the human ears they
are engineering.


Main
Students complete Task 1. If you have access to microscopes and slides with cartilage then students
could use them to take a look at some cartilage and draw what they observe.
Go through the answers with the students:


Answers
                                                                         1.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014                  21674                                        Page 1 of 7
                                   Science in the news – living ear grown in lab




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014   21674                               Page 2 of 7
                                                   Science in the news – living ear grown in lab

2. Cartilage is a tissue because it is made up of one type of cell (chondroblasts). The ear is an organ
   because it is made up of several different tissues all working together to perform a function.
3a. Cartilage in the outer ear contains mostly elastin in its extracellular matrix so it is flexible.
3b. The cartilage that makes up the rings around the trachea contain mostly collagen so it is strong
    enough to hold open the trachea so air can pass through.
4. Titanium was used because it is lightweight so the ear would be light enough to wear and also it is
   non-reactive. This is important so it does not react with the cells.
5a. The rat's immune system would have attacked the foreign cartilage cells and rejected the ear if it
    had a functioning immune system.
5b. If the ears are to be used in humans then the patient's immune system would have to be
     suppressed or the ear would be rejected. With a weak immune system the patient would be at
     risk from infections.
5c. To avoid this problem the replacement ear would have to be made using the patient's own
    cartilage cells.

Then ask students to work in small groups to complete Task 2. They should cut out the cards and use
the information to answer the question: 'How close are we to building replacement outer ears?'

Ask students from each group to read out their statement. Discuss with the class what steps the
researchers need to take next.



Plenary
Discuss with the students the need for scientists to develop techniques to build other replacement
body parts such as whole organs. Talk about why this is more complicated and why. For example,
organs are made up of many tissues working together, they require a blood supply and connection to
the nervous system.
Ask the students to consider the question: 'How close are we to building replacement organs?' Ask
them to stand in a line to form a continuum to show where they think we are in this endeavour.



Homework idea
Ask the students to do some research into other teams that are working in the field of tissue
engineering and summarise their work in their own words. For example, another recent news story
reported that a team have grown a miniature human brain (see http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-
23863544)

Science in the news – the abominable snowman’s DNA

Teaching notes

This task can be used when learning about classification and evolutionary trees with
GCSE students.
It is based on the article from The Week magazine called ‘The abominable snowman's
DNA'.
Further information can be found at (links all available at time of publishing):
http://www.theblaze.com/stories/2013/10/17/mystery-solved-dna-test-finds-reasonable-
explanation-for-identity-of-abominable-snowman/


Starter

To add an element of mystery to the lesson, show the class a video or an image of a
possible abominable snowman, or yeti, sighting:
http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zZFHxqesLo4
http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-2278024/The-clearest-sighting-Yeti--elaborate-
hoax-schoolboys.html
Discuss with the students if they think these sightings are real and what they think a yeti
might be.
Then ask them to discuss in pairs what evidence would they need in order to prove that
yetis exist. Suitable answers might be samples of fur, footprints, good quality photographs
or video.
After hearing their feedback, discuss how their ideas could prove the existence of the yeti
and also its limitations. For example, if some fur was found, how could it be proved that it
belonged to a yeti?


Main task

Inform students that an Oxford University Professor has collected what could be evidence
for the existence of the yeti and their task today is to analyse it.

 He has extracted some DNA from two hair samples found in two different mountainous
areas where yetis are thought to live and worked out the DNA sequence. He has found
they are exactly the same, so from the same species, but are they from the yeti?

 Ask students to work in small groups and hand out each group a paper copy of the 'yeti'
DNA sequence. Also give them copies of 'human', 'gorilla', 'polar bear' and 'brown bear'
DNA sequences which should be photocopied onto acetate. They should follow the tasks
given on the worksheet. Students place the acetate copies on top of the 'yeti' sequence
and also on top of each other to compare them and help them to answer the questions.
The matching sequences are shown at the end of the resource.
© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013              22037                                 Page 1 of 13
                             Science in the news – the abominable snowman’s DNA
 Go through what they have found. They should have seen that the polar bear and the
brown bear are most closely related (they share seven sequences). The human and
gorilla share three sequences. The mystery animal is equally related to both the polar
bear and brown bear which suggests that it would be a bear-like creature and not human
looking as many 'sightings' of the yeti suggest.
Explain that this is a simulation and in real life the DNA sequences would be much longer
(thousands of bases long) which makes the comparison more accurate.
 Tell the students that the professor also sequenced DNA from an ancient bear and found
a 100% match to the mystery animal - so it looks like the yeti could be a species that was
thought to be extinct.
 Introduce the idea of common ancestors. They would have seen from the DNA
sequencing task that all the animals have one sequence in common which suggests that
they all share a common ancestor. Display a mammalian evolutionary tree
(http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:An_evolutionary_tree_of_mammals.jpeg) which
shows the orders of Primates (apes belong to this order) and Carnivora (bears belong to
this order). Ask the students to place the common ancestor of these two orders on the
evolutionary tree.

 Display a bear evolutionary tree
(http://bix.ucsd.edu/bioalgorithms/downloads/bookfigs/fig.10.7.pdf) and ask the students to
place where they think the ancient bear, and therefore the 'yeti', goes.


Plenary

Ask the students to read the article from The Week magazine for further information and
then discuss in pairs:
      If this is a species that we thought was extinct, why haven't we discovered it before?
      Can we be sure that this is the 'yeti' that people have claimed to have seen. Why?
       What further evidence is needed?
      Why is it important that the professor publishes his findings in a scientific journal?


Homework idea

Ask the students to use ideas about natural selection to write an explanation of either:
How the brown and polar bear evolved from this ancient ancestor
or
How the ancient bear may have evolved to become the human-looking 'yeti'

Could the mystery animal be a yeti?
Scientists are able to extract DNA from tissues and
sequence it.
Comparing the sequence of bases in a sample of
DNA allows them to compare the DNA of organisms.

Closely related organisms will have sequences that are
similar.

a 100% match to the mystery animal - so it looks like the yeti could be a species that was
thought to be extinct.
 Introduce the idea of common ancestors. They would have seen from the DNA
sequencing task that all the animals have one sequence in common which suggests that
they all share a common ancestor. Display a mammalian evolutionary tree
(http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:An_evolutionary_tree_of_mammals.jpeg) which
shows the orders of Primates (apes belong to this order) and Carnivora (bears belong to
this order). Ask the students to place the common ancestor of these two orders on the
evolutionary tree.

 Display a bear evolutionary tree
(http://bix.ucsd.edu/bioalgorithms/downloads/bookfigs/fig.10.7.pdf) and ask the students to
place where they think the ancient bear, and therefore the 'yeti', goes.


Plenary

Ask the students to read the article from The Week magazine for further information and
then discuss in pairs:
      If this is a species that we thought was extinct, why haven't we discovered it before?
      Can we be sure that this is the 'yeti' that people have claimed to have seen. Why?
       What further evidence is needed?
      Why is it important that the professor publishes his findings in a scientific journal?


Homework idea

Ask the students to use ideas about natural selection to write an explanation of either:
How the brown and polar bear evolved from this ancient ancestor
or
How the ancient bear may have evolved to become the human-looking 'yeti'

Teaching notes
This resource has 16 ‘milestones’ in the study of the DNA molecule. Included is the work of Crick,
Franklin, Watson and Wilkins. Also included are important contributions by other scientists.
The information can be used in several other ways.
    Enlarge the statements and give one to each pair of students. Ask the students to add them
     to a ‘washing line’ timeline. Other major events of the century could also be added.
    Ask the students to find the names of the seven scientists in the statements. They could then
     group the statements into piles according to the scientists. Ask students to write a summary
     of each scientist’s contribution to the development of the DNA model.
    Ask students to draw a concept map to show the links between the scientists, their work and
     the development of the DNA model.
    Working in pairs, students write a short script in which the scientists explain their contribution
     towards the development of the DNA model. They could make paper finger (or pencil)
     puppets of each of the scientists using the photos (they could try to find a photo of Erwin
     Chargaff) and perform their script. They could video their presentations to show to the class
     later.


Snakes and ladders teaching notes
To give students a better understanding of the timescale of this work give students A3 pieces of
paper and ask them to draw their own game board, 10 x 10 squares, starting around 1900 and
ending around the year 2000 (they will need to allow three squares for 1951).

Answers

Task 1



1914 X-ray crystallography was used to find the position of atoms in simple molecules, the first
structure to be determined was that of table salt.
1934 Rosalind Franklin attended one of the few schools in London where girls were taught
science.
1940s Erwin Chargaff found that the number of A and T bases were the same, as were the
number of C and G bases.
1942 Oswald Avery proved that DNA, and not the protein part of chromosomes, was responsible
for inheritance.

1945 Atomic bombs are dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan with devastating effects.

1946 Linus Pauling and Maurice Wilkins turned away from studying nuclear science and began
to study biological molecules.

1950 Wilkins took the first ever images of the DNA molecule.

1951 Linus Pauling discovered that the molecules of some proteins have a helical shape.

1952 Rosalind Franklin had become an expert in the technique of x-ray crystallography. The
famous image ‘Photo 51’ was taken (by Gosling a research scientist, supervised by Franklin).



© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014                 22248                                       Page 6 of 7
                                                                Development of the DNA model

1953 Wilkins showed ‘Photo 51’ to Crick and Watson without Rosalind Franklin’s permission.

1952-3 Crick and Watson made numerous models of the DNA molecule; first out of cardboard
and then of metal plates and brass rods.

1953 Crick and Watson revealed their double helix model of DNA.

1958 Rosalind Franklin died of cancer at the age of 37.

1960 Wilkins completed seven years of work in order to check and verify Crick and Watson’s
model of the DNA molecule.
1962 Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins received the Nobel Prize for Medicine
for their work on the structure of DNA.
1990s Modern NMR spectrometers can show biological proteins interacting with other
molecules.



Task 2

 1.        Crick and Watson revealed their double helix model of DNA in 1953. Why was the Nobel
           Prize for Medicine not awarded to them until 1962?
           The Nobel Prize was not awarded until 1962 because it took other scientists, most notably,
           Maurice Wilkins seven years to check and verify the work of Crick and Watson.

 2.        ‘Photo 51’ provided Crick and Watson with crucial information about the structure of DNA.
           Why do you think Rosalind Franklin was not awarded a Nobel Prize, along with Crick,
           Watson and Wilkins in 1962?
           She was not awarded the Nobel Prize as it is not awarded posthumously and Rosalind
           Franklin died at the age of 37 in 1958.

 3.        Pauling and Wilkins began their careers researching the structure of atoms. What do you
           think made them change to studying biological molecules instead?
           They moved away from studying atoms after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and
           Nagasaki. They were concerned about the further development of nuclear weapons,
           developments which involved research by many scientists. Indeed, Linus Pauling became a
           prominent peace activist and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

      2. Watson and Crick (Watson on left) and DNA molecule.
      3. Linus Pauling and a helical protein (collagen).
      4. ‘Erwin Chargaff’ and paired bases.
      5. Oswald Avery and cell, nucleus, chromosome, DNA to represent his discovery that DNA is
         responsible for inheritance.
      6. Maurice Wilkins and an x-ray diffraction camera from the 1950s.

Insect pollinators and the world food supply

Teaching notes

Make 4 copies of each information sheet.

Give one information sheet to each pair of students. They should read and summarise the
information on their sheet using pictures and a word limit of 12 words. Students then
circulate around the room explaining their poster and finding out about three other threats
to insect pollinators.

During this time keywords/concepts could be added to the questions on the whiteboard.

                                  Information sheet 1

Agricultural intensification
The term ‘agricultural intensification’ describes what has happened to farming practices
over the last 60 years. Only one type of plant is grown in each field. Herbicides are used
to kill any other plant which may grow on the land. Even when the crop is grass e.g. for
silage or grazing, only a few species will be found growing in the field and almost no
flowering plants. For many farmers this is the most efficient method of production.
However, agricultural intensification has reduced the availability of flowering plants and
nesting sites for insects, birds and mammals. The UK has lost 97% of its wildflower
meadows since the 1930s. Such changes affect wild insect pollinators because they are
totally dependent on wild flowers growing in the landscape.
Flowering crops such as oilseed rape produce a super abundance of flowers over a very
short period of time. For there to be enough insects in the environment to pollinate the
flowering oilseed rape each farm needs to have natural, wildflower rich areas to support
bumblebees, butterflies and other insect pollinators when their crops are not in flower.
To overcome this problem in the USA, large numbers of honeybees and their hives are
transported around the country. The bees are taken to orchards as the trees come into
blossom. When the fruit has set the hives are moved to newly flowering orchards. In
recent years many hives in the USA have suffered the devastating colony collapse
disorder (CCD) in which all the adult bees simply disappear from the hive. CCD may be
linked to the practice of transporting bees over large distances or to pesticides.




                                  Information sheet 2

Pests and diseases

Pests and diseases are the main threat to honeybees, particularly an introduced parasitic
mite called Varroa. Varroa infestations can be treated but the mite is beginning to show
resistance to some treatments.
Most beehives in Britain are managed by amateur beekeepers in their spare time.
Beekeeping associations provide training but the quality depends on the expertise of local
volunteers.
The impact of pests and diseases on other pollinating insects has not been well studied,
but is probably less severe than on honeybees as they are particularly exposed to new

The history of prosthetic limbs

Task

Cut out the statements and put them in chronological order.
Answer the following questions.
  Which period has seen the greatest development in prosthetic limbs?
  Why do you think this is?




         Blacksmiths in the Middle Ages sometimes made limbs of iron to replace
                those lost by knights in battles, jousts and tournaments.



         In 2007 research into a motorised ankle joint designed to mimic normal
                               movement was carried out.



        A Dutch surgeon, Pieter Verduyn, refined the design of prosthetic legs by
                    adding hinges and a leather cuff in the 1690’s.



       A prosthetic foot was designed in 1987 to include a carbon fibre shank and
        heel spring which enabled the whole foot to flex, absorb and then return
                               energy to the moving limb.



      A prosthetic toe made of wood and attached by leather straps was discovered
                          on a 3000 year old Egyptian mummy.



         Anaesthetics, developed in the 1840’s, and sterile surgery improved the
       success and effectiveness of amputation operations. Prosthetic limbs were
                    still made of wood and metal in Victorian times.


           Double amputee, Oscar Pistorius qualified for both the Olympic and
          Paralympic Games held recently in London, using carbon fibre running
                                       blades.



       In 2006, a man was able to control his prosthetic lower leg by thinking about
       moving it. Signals from his sensory nerves were relayed to the artificial limb.

                                                          The history of prosthetic limbs

Teaching notes and answers

It may be helpful to have a discussion about artificial limbs before or after the sequencing
activity.

Class discussion
If a person loses a lower limb (e.g. members of the armed forces, children who have
stepped on a land mine, road traffic accidents) what do they want a replacement artificial
limb to do?
    give you normal movement, change gait , climb stairs, play sport
    be comfortable to wear, easy to attach, not too heavy, not to rub
    look good/natural
    easy to maintain/ hardwearing
    for a child: easy to replace as child grows

A useful video clip is the following from the BBC, ‘Prosthetic limbs give military amputees a
new lease of life.’ (Nov 2013, http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-25116869 (link available at
the time of publishing)).



A prosthetic toe made of wood and attached by leather straps was discovered on a 3000
                              year old Egyptian mummy.

 Blacksmiths in the Middle Ages sometimes made limbs of iron to replace those lost by
                      knights in battles, jousts and tournaments.

A Dutch surgeon, Pieter Verduyn, refined the design of prosthetic legs by adding hinges
                           and a leather cuff in the 1690’s.

 Anaesthetics, developed in the 1840’s, and sterile surgery improved the success and
 effectiveness of amputation operations. Prosthetic limbs were still made of wood and
                               metal in Victorian times.

  A prosthetic foot was designed to include a carbon fibre shank and heel spring which
enabled the whole foot to flex, absorb and then return energy to the moving limb in 1987.

 In 2006, a man was able to control his prosthetic lower leg by thinking about moving it.
           Signals from his sensory nerves were relayed to the artificial limb.

 In 2007 research into a motorised ankle joint designed to mimic normal movement was
                                      carried out.

Double amputee, Oscar Pistorius qualified for both the Olympic and Paralympic Games
            held recently in London, using carbon fibre running blades.
