Treating heart disease
Task

Look at the information sheets about different methods for treating heart disease. Use the information to fill in the table.

           Method                     Description                         Advantages                        Disadvantages




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016                                  27263                                                         Page 1 of 7
                                                                      Treating heart disease

Information sheets


  Artificial valves - what are they?
  It’s a device implanted in the heart of a
  patient to replace their faulty valve.
  By Stif Komar (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0
  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia
  Commons


  Artificial valves - advantages
        No rejection

  Artificial valves: disadvantages
        Can damage red blood cells, so
         patients need to take anti-clotting
         drugs.


  Biological valves – what are they?
  They are based on valves taken from
  animals, such as pigs or cattle. They are
  treated with chemicals to stop your body
  rejecting them.
  By Stif Komar (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0
  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia
  Commons


  Biological valves – advantages
        No need for blood thinning drugs as
         they don’t damage red blood cells.

  Biological valves – disadvantages
        Valves can harden and need replacing.



  Stents – what are they?
  Stents are used to treat narrow coronary
  arteries. The stent is pushed into position
  using an x-ray, the balloon is inflated,
  expanding the stent, and then removed,
  leaving the stent to open up the artery.

  Stents – advantages
        Lowers risk of infection as major
         surgery
         not required.

  Stents – disadvantages


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016                              27263                Page 2 of 7
                                                  Treating heart disease

       Fatty deposits can build up again.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016          27263                Page 3 of 7
                                                     Treating heart disease


  Bypass surgery – what is it?
  A surgical procedure used to treat coronary
  heart disease.
  It transplants a vein from the leg to divert
  blood around narrowed or clogged parts of
  the major arteries to improve blood flow and
  oxygen supply to the heart.
  Around 20,000 coronary artery bypass
  grafts are carried out in England every year.

  Bypass surgery – advantages
       No rejection risks.
       Very effective treatment.

  Bypass surgery – disadvantages
       Major surgery, so involves risks.




  Statins – what are they?
  These are drugs which lower cholesterol
  levels by stopping the liver producing as
  much.
  Patients can also change their diet to help
  reduce cholesterol.

  Statins – advantages
       They reduce cholesterol which helps
        slow down the build-up of fatty layers
        in the arteries.

  Statins – disadvantages
       They have possible side effects, e.g.
        liver damage.
       Patient has to remember to take them
        regularly.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016             27263                Page 4 of 7
                                                   Treating heart disease


  Artificial pacemakers - what are
  they?
  Some people can’t control their heart rate.
  Artificial pacemakers can be fitted under the
  skin. A wire is passed from a vein to the
  right atrium. This sends electrical impulses
  to the heart to control the heartbeat.

  Artificial pacemakers – advantages
       Major surgery not required, so not very
        risky.

  Artificial pacemakers –
  disadvantages
       The immune system can reject the
        pacemaker and it will need replacing.
       The pacemaker may sometimes
        malfunction.


  Heart transplants – what are they?
  A heart transplant is an operation to
  replace a damaged or failing heart with a
  healthy human heart from a donor who
  has recently died.
  Heart transplants are rarely performed in
  the UK, mainly due to a lack of suitable
  donors.
  There were 197 heart transplants
  performed in the UK between 2012 and
  2013.

  Heart transplants – advantages
       A better quality of life (improved
        strength, energy & stamina).
       More normal lifestyle day to day
       An improved chance of a longer life.

  Heart transplants – disadvantages
       Major surgery (anaesthetic risks,
        bleeding, clotting, infection)
       Anti-rejection drugs needed for life
       A shortage of donors.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016           27263                Page 5 of 7
                                           Treating heart disease




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016   27263                Page 6 of 7
                                                                                   Treating heart disease
Teaching notes

Copy the information sheets, cut them up and spread round the room. Ask students to
find the information to fill in the table with.

Ideas for differentiation

For students who need more support:

      the table could be partially filled in
      don’t cut the information sheets up
      students could work in groups and find information for just two methods each.

For more challenge ask students to:

      create their own table
      research the advantages and disadvantages themselves
      remove the headings from the information sheets.


Going further

Students could try this specimen exam question (question 5) from AQA for new (9-1)
GCSE.

Antibiotic resistance – news story
Read the article below which features a news item from 13 th January 2017.



    A superbug that could not be treated with 26
    different antibiotics has killed a woman in the
    USA
    The 70-year-old returned to the USA from India in August last year with
    an infected swelling in her pelvis. The infection arose after the woman
    broke her right leg. She was seriously ill when she arrived at the hospital
    in Nevada – her immune system was going into overdrive in an attempt
    to fight the infection causing inflammation throughout her body.

    Eventually, she died from septic shock.

    Samples of the infection taken from the wound were sent for testing to
    the Centre for Disease Control.

    They showed she was infected with a bacterium called Klebsiella
    pneumoniae – which normally lives in the gut without causing any
    problems. However this sample proved to be resistant to all 26 available
    antibiotics in the USA, including the group of drugs known as
    carbapenems used as a 'last resort' to treat drug-resistant infections.
    This superbug produces an enzyme which makes them resistant to
    carbapenems.

    The young and old are most at risk of antibiotic-resistant infections. This
    is because these two groups have low immunity, making them more
    susceptible to infection.

    Such resistant bacteria are primarily created in hospital conditions.
    Antibiotics are used to kill bacteria, but some antibiotic-resistant bacteria
    propagate, spreading throughout medical centres, and beyond.

    Each year in the United States, at least 2 million people become infected
    with bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics and at least 23 000 people
    die each year as a direct result of these infections.

    Prof Laura Piddock commented:

    "In circumstances such as this, where doctors are faced with the inability
    to treat a life-threatening infection, they need the flexibility to use
    antibiotics licensed for use in other countries and shown to be active in
    the laboratory against the patient's infecting bacterium."

    Dr David Brown, chief scientist at Antibiotic Research UK, said: "It is still
    quite unusual for a bacterial infection to be resistant to such a large

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017         28034                                Page 1 of 5
                                              Antibiotic resistance – news story

    number of antibiotics. However, the ease of global travel does mean that
    such cases will increase."




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017      28034                             Page 2 of 5
                                                Antibiotic resistance – news story

Task

Using the information above and your own understanding of how antibiotic-
resistant bacteria evolve, answer the following questions.

   1. Which people are most at risk to resistant infections and why?

   2. How many types of antibiotic are available in the USA?

   3. Why are some potentially useful antibiotics not available to doctors
      treating patients with infections?

   4. What do you know about Klebsiella pneumoniae?
       Extension: Why might doctors be particularly concerned about this
       bacterium?

   5. Describe how antibiotic-resistant bacteria might be 'created' and spread
      in a hospital environment.
       Extension: If you were in charge of infection management in your local
       hospital what procedures would you put in place to prevent the spread of
       resistant bacteria? What role can you play in helping to reduce antibiotic
       resistance?

   6. Using numbers with one significant figure, estimate the percentage of
      people who recover from infection by antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

   7. How might cases of infection by drug resistant bacteria be increased by
      global travel?
       Extension: How could this risk be reduced?

   8. Describe how the rise of antibiotic resistance provides evidence for the
      process of evolution.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017        28034                             Page 3 of 5
                                                            Antibiotic resistance – news story

Suggested answers
1. Young and elderly people are most at risk. They have low immunity to infection and disease.

2. 26 types

3. Prof Laura Piddock implies that different countries have different antibiotics available to
   doctors. Antibiotics have to be licensed for use. Perhaps if an antibiotic is available for use in
   one country doctors in other countries should also be free to use it.
   Some may be licensed to treat one or two specific infections only but they may have been
   shown to be effective against other bacteria in the lab. Perhaps these should be made
   available without going through all the stages in drug development.

4. It is a bacterium. It is found naturally in the gut. It is normally harmless. Some forms are
   resistant to antibiotics.
   Extension: It's a very ubiquitous bacterium which is found in lots of people. It could pose a
   serious risk to people if the ability to produce the enzyme which renders carbapenems
   ineffective, is passed on to other bacteria and becomes widespread.

5. The idea of mutation producing new strains some of which are resistant to antibiotics. These
   are not killed when exposed to antibiotics. They survive, reproduce and percentage of resistant
   bacteria in population increases.
   Extension: Possible answers might include – scrupulous hygiene management and cleaning
   routines; reduce number of visitors; treat cases that do not involve wounds, surgery etc. in a
   different hospital; reduce the number of operations e.g. no cosmetic surgery.
   Your role could include taking care not to spread infection; looking after your own health by
   cleaning teeth, eating well; not taking antibiotics for minor infections; taking the full course of
   prescribed antibiotics; deciding to become a research scientist in this field!

6. 2 000 000 cases

   (20 000 ÷ 2 000 000) x 100 = 1% deaths therefore 99% survive.
   23 000 deaths = 20 000 deaths (1 significant figure)


7. Cases such as the woman from Nevada introduce new, resistant forms of bacteria into a
   country and its hospital environment.
   Extension: Taking antibiotics to the patient rather than moving the infected person. Not allowing
   an infected person to travel if they have a resistant strain unknown in their destination country.
   Preventing infected people from travelling e.g. a person with TB unless they can prove
   themselves free of infection.

8. Bacteria reproduce at a fast rate. Mutations in bacteria produce new strains. Resistant strains
   are not killed by antibiotics so survive and reproduce – passing the resistant gene/ mutation to
   the next generation.

Conservation of mass
We are studying the reaction between marble chips (calcium carbonate) and
hydrochloric acid. Write a balanced equation for the reaction.

           calcium          hydrochloric           calcium    carbon
                    +                                       +         + water
          carbonate            acid                chloride   dioxide


Prediction

Write down what you think will happen and explain why.

Method

1. Pour 25 ml of 1 M hydrochloric acid (HCl) into the conical flask and weigh it.
  Record the result in the first column of the table.
2. Weigh out 4 g of large marble chips (calcium carbonate). Record the mass in
  the second column.
3. Add the masses of the reactants together, record the answer in the third
  column.
4. Place the marble chips into the acid and swirl.
5. When the reaction stops (fizzing stops) re-weigh the flask. Record the mass
  in the fourth column.
6. Calculate the mass difference in the last column.


Results

Teaching notes

Before the lesson copy the cards and cut them up, so that each card has a question
and a forfeit on it.

Equipment per team (team size 3-4 students)

      10 question/forfeit cards

      10 paper cups

      1 ping pong ball

Ask each team to arrange their cups facing each other as below:




      Put a ‘question-forfeit’ card in each cup.

      The teams then take it in turns to throw a ping pong ball into their opponents’
       cups.

      When a ball lands in a cup, the throwing team answers the question in the cup.

      If they can’t answer the question correctly, they must do the forfeit. The cup is
       then taken away.

      If they answer the question correctly the team scores 4 points. If they do the
       forfeit they score 2 points. If they fail to do either the other team gains 3 points.

      The game ends when a team has had all its cups removed.

      The winning team is the team with most points.

      As a follow up, ask students to keep the questions that they couldn’t answer in
       a pile. They then need to use their notes to find the correct answers. Build up a
       definitive set of answers as a class.

Teaching notes
Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any of the
additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.

 1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each team).

 2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto different
    coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have all the cards
    back at the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

 3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

 4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile, and then
    describes the word at the top of the card without using the words below. The rest
    of their team must guess which word is described. Participants are not allowed to
    say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are
    permitted.

 5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the opposing
    team may challenge and the individual must move on to the next word.

 6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as possible to
    the players in their team (a longer time may be required to allow more
    descriptions to take place) before play passes to the next team. There are no
    penalties for a wrong guess.

 7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.
    Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each group.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other
ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to
reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could research
meanings of new terms.



Further activities
 1. Each student is given a blank card to put a keyword onto. They then write a
    further five associated ‘taboo’ words underneath. Collect the cards and use as a
    class or group activity.

Teaching notes

Students could be given the game to play in small teams with one of them as
the question master. Each team will need 10 coloured counters or hexagons to
place on the grid when they get a question right.

The object of the game is to complete a path across the board. One team
should make a path from left to right and the other teams should go from top
to bottom. The original TV game pitted one contestant (on the shorter path (top
to bottom)) against a pair (going left to right).

Teams take it in turns to choose a hexagon. If they get the question correct
they place a coloured counter over the hexagon. The team that wins is the one
that makes a complete path from one side to the other.

The grid can be used on an interactive whiteboard. Click and drag the coloured
counters to cover the appropriate hexagon when a question is answered
correctly.

Energy clock
Task

Throughout the day and night, you are constantly using energy. This energy is
released by the process of respiration inside your cells. Respiration is the oxidation of
foodstuffs to release energy.

Different activities require varying amounts of energy. Intense physical activity
requires most energy but even when sleeping you need energy to maintain body
temperature, heart rate, breathing etc.

The table shows various activities and the amount of energy needed by an average 15
year old for such activities.




                                                      Energy needed each hour
                      Activity
                                                                (kJ)
Sleeping                                                           250

Sitting, resting, listening to music                               300

Reading, gaming, texting, watching TV                              350

Writing                                                            400

Studying, eating                                                   450

Washing, dressing                                                  600

Walking                                                           1000

Cycling, jogging                                                  1400
Playing active games e.g. football, swimming,
                                                                  1500
rugby


Make up a list of all your activities for a particular day and then draw your own
Energy Clock like the one shown below.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2018           29926                                  Page 1 of 2
                                                                           Energy clock




Using your energy clock and the table for energy values for different activities,
calculate how much energy you use up in an average day.

Most teenagers use between 8 000 to 12 000 kJ each day.

How active is your day?

Teaching notes

Students could be given the game to play in small teams with one of them as
the question master. Each team will need 10 coloured counters or hexagons to
place on the grid when they get a question right.

The object of the game is to complete a path across the board. One team
should make a path from left to right and the other teams should go from top
to bottom. The original TV game pitted one contestant (on the shorter path (top
to bottom)) against a pair (going left to right).

Teams take it in turns to choose a hexagon. If they get the question correct
they place a coloured counter over the hexagon. The team that wins is the one
that makes a complete path from one side to the other.

The grid can be used on an interactive whiteboard. Click and drag the coloured
counters to cover the appropriate hexagon when a question is answered
correctly.

RP Microscopy revision activities

Aim: Revision of the Microscopy required practical (RP), relating it to the content of
the specification, including maths skills and working scientifically.

Keywords: resolution, magnification, mitochondria, ribosomes, eukaryotic,
prokaryotic.

Starter activities


1. Setting the scene – how to use a microscope

   This activity is a recap of KS3 skills and puts into context the content and skills
   needed at GCSE. In pairs, ask students to describe how they would use a
   microscope to observe a biological specimen.

   They could use the following key words: specimen, slide, eye piece, coarse
   adjustment knob, fine adjustment knob, objective lens, magnification, light/mirror,
   stage, cover slip.


2. Magnification and microscopes PowerPoint (30133)

   Use slides 2-7 to recap magnification and to practise using the magnification
   equation.

1. Marking cells

   Give students a range of actual images of cells viewed under a microscope, from
   the selection provided on pages 5–10. If laminated, the images could be written on
   with wipeable markers and used again. The activity could be used as a class
   activity on the IWB with students annotating the images on the board.

   NB The magnifications given are correct when the images are 10 cm wide when
   printed out.

    Suggested further activities could include:

          The examples given are all eukaryotic cells. Ask students to describe the
           differences that they would expect to see in an image of a prokaryotic cell.

          Ask students to make labelled drawings of 2-3 cells from the images, they
           should include the magnification of the image.


    Differentiation

    There is a range of different images (pages 5-10) from simple cheek cells to
    more complex tissues. Give students the most appropriate images for the level
    that they are working at.

Plenary activities

1. Microscopy – taboo (pages 12-13)

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
at the top of your card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any
of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card. Before the lesson, copy
and cut up the taboo cards; each group of students will need a set.

 1. Students work in groups of at least four. Give each group a set of cards. Each
    group then splits into two teams.

 2. The cards need to be shuffled and placed face down.

 3. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile and
    describes the word at the top of the card without using the ‘taboo’ words. A
    member of the opposing team could sit by the clue-giver so that they can
    challenge if a taboo word is used. The rest of the clue–givers team must guess
    the word being described. Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or
    ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

 4. Should the clue-giver be correctly challenged or if their team correctly guesses
    the word then they must move on to the next card.

 5. Each clue-giver is allowed one or two minutes to describe as many words as
    possible to the players in their team before play passes to the next team. There
    are no penalties for a wrong guess.

 6. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other
ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to
reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

Suggested further activities could include:

      In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, ask students to revise the
       meanings of the keywords.

      Give each student a blank card to put a keyword onto. They then write a further
       five associated ‘taboo’ words underneath. Collect the cards and use as a class
       or group activity.

Who am I – solid, liquid or gas?
Task

Read the statements below.
For each statement decide which state of matter has made it.
Hint: Some statements could be made by more than one state of matter.

        1. I have a fixed volume.

        2. If I am cooled to my boiling point I will condense.

        3. I can take the shape of whichever container I am poured into.

        4. My particles move freely and randomly.

        5. If I am heated to my boiling point I will evaporate.

        6. My particles vibrate around a fixed position.

        7. My particles can spread out to fill whatever space they are in.

        8. If you heat me, my particles will gain energy.

        9. I have a fixed shape.

        10.         I have a fixed volume, but not a fixed shape.

Skeletal system – comprehension
Task

Read the text in the box and then answer the questions.
 The skeletal system is a body system made up of bones along with cartilage,
 ligaments and tendons. There are 206 bones in the adult human body, which
 make up a skeleton. Bones are living tissue that can grow and repair itself.
 The skeleton has four main functions: support, protection, movement and the
 production of red blood cells.

 Without the support of the skeleton, the body would be completely floppy
 and limp. Having a skeleton gives the body support and holds the organs in
 place.

 The skeleton protects the organs because the bones are strong and hard.
 The rib cage protects the lungs and heart. The vertebrae of the spine protect
 the nerves of the spinal column.

 Muscles attach to the bones by tendons and this allows the bones to move
 when the muscles contract. Where two bones meet there is a joint.

Questions

1. Along with bones, what makes up the skeletal system?

   ..........................................................................................................................

2. How many bones are there in an adult human skeleton?

   ..........................................................................................................................

3. Is bone a living tissue?

   ..........................................................................................................................

4. What are the four main functions of the skeleton?

   ..........................................................................................................................

5. What would the body be like without a skeleton?

   ..........................................................................................................................

6. Which bones protect the lungs and heart?

   ..........................................................................................................................

7. What is the job of a tendon?

   ..........................................................................................................................

8. What is the term to describe where two bones meet?

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019                          33506                                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                                      Skeletal system – comprehension

   ..........................................................................................................................




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019                          33506                                                 Page 2 of 3
                                               Skeletal system – comprehension
Answers

1. Along with bones, what makes up the skeletal system?

   Cartilage, ligaments, and tendons

2. How many bones are there in an adult human skeleton?

   206

3. Is bone a living tissue?

   Yes

4. What are the four main functions of the skeleton?

   Support, protection, movement, and the production of red blood
   cells

5. What would the body be like without a skeleton?

   Floppy and limp

6. Which bones protect the lungs and heart?

   The rib cage

7. What is the job of a tendon?

   To attach muscles to the bones

Separating iron filings from sand
Magnets are used for recycling because they can attract certain types of
metals from the recycling pile.
The metals that magnets attract are iron, nickel, and cobalt. It can also attract
steel because steel has iron in it!
In your investigation, you will use a similar idea in removing iron filings from
sand.

Aim
To investigate how a magnet can extract iron filings from sand and to calculate
the percentage of iron in the mixture.
You will need:
       eye protection
       a bar magnet
       a small plastic bag
       a mixture of iron filings and sand
       a top pan balance
       a calculator
       two small plastic containers
       paper weighing boat.

Method

   1. Measure the mass of the plastic container and record it on the table on
        page 2.
   2. Set the top pan balance to ‘zero’ with the container still on it. If you are
        unsure how to do this ask your teacher.
   3. Weigh out approximately 10 g of the sand and iron filing mixture and
        record the exact mass to 2 decimal points.
   4. Remove the plastic container from the top pan balance.
   5. Put the bar magnet into the small plastic bag and work it through the
        sand and iron filings.
   6. Taking care not to get the iron filings on your fingers, place the iron
        filings removed from the mixture into the other small plastic container.
   7. Repeat steps 5 and 6 until you have removed as many of the iron filings
        from the mixture as you can.
   8. Measure the mass of the sand without the iron filings and record your
        result in the table.

Variation and identical twins
Task – version A

Read the description of a pair of identical twins.


 Mateo and Felipe are identical twins. Mateo is five minutes older than his
 brother. Today is their 30th birthday.
 'Feliz cumpleaños, big brother.' Felipe can speak fluently in both Spanish and
 English. Mateo only speaks English but with a strong Scottish accent which
 sometimes confuses his brother.
 When they were very young, family circumstances forced the boys apart.
 Mateo went to live with his father, a football coach, in Edinburgh, Scotland,
 whilst Felipe remained with his grand-parents on the family olive farm in
 Andalucia, Spain.
 Both young men have dark brown eyes and black hair. Mateo's hair reaches
 his shoulders and Felipe's is very short. They have a wide gap between their
 two front teeth.
 When he was a toddler, Felipe used to roll up his tongue and poke it out at his
 grand-mother's parrot, Loro, which he did not like. Mateo broke his leg when
 he was eight and learnt from the doctor that his blood group was O+. In
 Andalucia, when Felipe was told about the accident he decided to send his
 brother a keyring carved in the shape of a bull. Whilst wrapping the present,
 he noticed his fingerprints on the sticky tape and wondered for a moment, if
 they were identical to Mateo's.
 When he was seventeen years old, Mateo applied to do sports science at
 university. He was amazed to learn that Felipe had chosen to do the same
 course in the same city! They decided to share a flat with two friends. At first,
 their friends had no problem telling the twins apart as Felipe had very dark
 skin whilst Mateo's face was pale. Felipe was also one centimetre taller than
 his brother.
 The friends soon decided to join a gym. They were very competitive! It was
 discovered that Felipe had a greater grip-strength than his twin and could
 work out for longer on the rowing machine. But Mateo always beat his brother
 on the squash court.
 Today, they both support Manchester United and like to wear beanies when
 it's cold. Mateo won't admit, even to his twin, that he is afraid of birds. Felipe
 regularly plays the guitar and their grand-parents describe him as 'the
 musical one'. Mateo doesn't play any instruments but he does sing opera and
 Ed Sheeran songs very loudly in the shower!


When you first see identical twins, they can be hard to tell apart. This is
because much about the human body is controlled by genes and identical
twins have identical genes.

As well as (usually) having the same birthday, they also share the same
physical features, such as eye colour.

But, as you have read, Mateo and Felipe are not exactly the same. How people

Instructions

Have 5 different colours ready (they don't have to be identical to those listed
below). Choose pens or pencils which make a thin line. These will help you
draw around the words you select so you can still read them easily.

Pink – circle all the physical features the twins have. Now draw a table with
two columns, one for Mateo and the other for Felipe. Record all their physical
features.

Green – In your table, circle the physical features which are different in both
boys.

1. Why do Mateo and Felipe have some features which are exactly the same?
2. Can you explain why some of their features are different?
    Brown - circle the coincidences.
    Orange – circle the other skills and attributes they have between them.
    Draw a second table with two columns and list all the orange-circled words.
    Blue - In both tables, circle any physical features and skills which can be
    easily measured.
3. Are any of these blue-circled words 'measured' in words or letters
   (qualitatively)?
4. Using numbers will give you quantitative measurements which can be
   easily compared. What units would you use to measure the other blue-
   circled features and skills?
5. Look at your second table. What skills and attributes do you think the twins
   share and what is your evidence for your conclusion?
6. Which features or skills do you judge to have an equal genetic and
   environmental influence? Explain why you think this.


For further research or home-learning:

    a. Can Mateo also roll his tongue? Explain your thoughts.
    b. What blood group is Felipe? Outline your evidence.
    c. Are their fingerprints identical? Why do you think this?

Task – version B

Read the description of a pair of identical twins.


 Mateo and Felipe are identical twins. Mateo is five minutes older than his
 brother. Today is their 30th birthday.
 When they were very young, family circumstances forced the boys apart.
 Mateo went to live with his father, a football coach, in Edinburgh, Scotland,
 whilst Felipe remained with his grand-parents on the family olive farm in
 Andalucia, Spain.
 Both young men have dark brown eyes and black hair. Mateo's hair reaches
 his shoulders and Felipe's is very short.
 When he was seventeen years old, Mateo applied to do sports science at
 university. He was amazed to learn that Felipe had chosen to do the same
 course in the same city! They decided to share a flat with two friends. At first,
 their friends had no problem telling the twins apart as Felipe had very dark
 skin whilst Mateo's face was pale. Felipe was also one centimetre taller than
 his brother.
 The friends soon decided to join a gym. They were very competitive! It was
 discovered that Felipe could work out for longer on the rowing machine. But
 Mateo always beat his brother on the squash court.
 Today, they both support Man. United and like to wear beanies when it's cold.
 Felipe regularly plays the guitar and their grand-parents describe him as 'the
 musical one'. Mateo doesn't play any instruments but he does sing opera and
 Ed Sheeran songs very loudly in the shower!

Teaching notes and suggested answers

The aim of this resource is to promote a better understanding of how physical
features and other attributes such as sporting skill are influenced by both
genes and the environment. It does this through to prompting discussion,
questions and ideas from the students.
The text has been reduced and questions adjusted in version B to open the
topic to students who need more support.

 Mateo and Felipe are identical twins. Mateo is five minutes older than his
 brother. Today is their 30th birthday.
 'Feliz cumpleaños, big brother.' Felipe can speak fluently in both Spanish and
 English. Mateo only speaks English but with a strong Scottish accent which
 sometimes confuses his brother.
 When they were very young, family circumstances forced the boys apart.
 Mateo went to live with his father, a football coach, in Edinburgh, Scotland,
 whilst Felipe remained with his grand-parents on the family olive farm in
 Andalucia, Spain.
 Both young men have dark brown eyes and black hair. Mateo's hair reaches
 his shoulders and Felipe's is very short. They have a wide gap between their
 two front teeth.
 When he was a toddler, Felipe used to roll up his tongue and poke it out at his
 grand-mother's parrot, Loro, which he did not like. Mateo broke his leg when
 he was eight and learnt from the doctor that his blood group was O+. In
 Andalucia, when Felipe was told about the accident he decided to send his
 brother a keyring carved in the shape of a bull. Whilst wrapping the present,
 he noticed his fingerprints on the sticky tape and wondered for a moment, if
 they were identical to Mateo's.
 When he was seventeen years old, Mateo applied to do sports science at
 university. He was amazed to learn that Felipe had chosen to do the same
 course in the same city! They decided to share a flat with two friends. At first,
 their friends had no problem telling the twins apart as Felipe had very dark
 skin whilst Mateo's face was pale. Felipe was also one centimetre taller than
 his brother.
 The friends soon decided to join a gym. They were very competitive! It was
 discovered that Felipe had a greater grip-strength than his twin and could
 work out for longer on the rowing machine. But Mateo always beat his brother
 on the squash court.
 Today, they both support Man. United and like to wear beanies when it's cold.
 Mateo won't admit, even to his twin, that he is afraid of birds. Felipe regularly
 plays the guitar and their grand-parents describe him as 'the musical one'.
 Mateo doesn't play any instruments but he does sing opera and Ed Sheeran
 songs very loudly in the shower!

Discussion points

1. Why do Mateo and Felipe have some features which are exactly the same?
    These features are controlled by their genes and their genes are identical.

2. Can you explain why some of their features are different?
    These have been affected by their environment: hair can be cut; skin tone
    is affected by exposure to sunlight and Mateo lives in Scotland whilst Felipe
    spent his childhood in Spain; grip-strength depends on practice – Felipe has
    lived on a farm and may have helped out, making his grip stronger. This
    may also have given him greater endurance. Mateo may be better at
    squash because this indoor sport is one which can be done regularly in a
    colder, wetter climate.
3. Are any of these blue-circled words 'measured' in words or letters
   (qualitatively)?
    Eye colour; hair colour; tongue roll; blood group; fingerprints; skin colour

4. Using numbers will give you quantitative measurements which can be
   easily compared. What units would you use to measure the other blue-
   circled features and skills?
    Hair length – cm; gap between teeth – mm; height – m and cm; grip-
    strength – Kg, N or mmHg (often with a dynamometer); work-out – hours,
    mins, sec; squash – no unit as such just number of winning games.

5. Look at your second table. What skills and attributes do you think the twins
   share and what is your evidence for your conclusion?
    Share sporting ability as they can beat each other, although in different
    sports possibly due to their different exposure to physical activity when
    young; also father is a football coach, so they will have inherited and share
    some of his genes. Both like football but why the same team? Is this simply
    a coincidence?
    May both have a fear of birds – Felipe 'did not like' the parrot; Mateo doesn't
    admit his fear of birds.
    Both may be equally musical as one plays guitar and other sings opera with
    confidence.

6. Which features or skills do you judge to have an equal genetic and
   environmental influence? Explain why you think this.
    Language – humans genetically predisposed to communicate with
    language.
    Type of language and accent – result of environment.
    Musicality – genes may complement each other to bring about a strong
    musical potential.
    Instrument and skill – heavily dependent on environment.
    Sporting ability – as above.

                                                              Reflections – ray diagrams
Teaching notes

There are two different versions of the activity. Students should know the rule for
reflection before doing this activity. Provide students with protractors, rulers and sharp
pencils.

Ask students to measure and write in the angles of incidence and reflection.

If half the class complete sheet A and the rest complete sheet B then students could
peer assess each others diagrams. They should look out for the following marking
points:

         rays drawn with a ruler
         the normal clearly drawn at a 90o angle
         rays should touch the surface of the mirror
         arrows should be drawn in the right directions
         the angle of incidence should equal the angle of reflection.

 Question 1: Draw a parallel circuit with a light bulb on each branch, a 12 V cell and an ammeter to measure the current in each
 branch.

                                      correct symbols used

Current – picture it!
Task

   1. Read carefully through the text.
   2. Put the images in the order that they appear in the text.
   3. Glue the images in the spaces provided on the worksheet and quote a small
       part of the text that you are linking the image to – this cannot be more than
       eight words! Next, say why you are matching the image to that piece of text.



        When you think about the word ‘current’ what is the first thing that
        comes to mind? Perhaps the current in a river or something present-
        day?

        The current of a river is the flow of water. As the current flows from high
        ground to low ground it can carry things with it, like leaves, twigs and
        even boats. Current can only flow from high ground to low ground.

        Current in an electrical circuit is very similar, it also flows and carries
        electrical charge. The electrical current that flows in one direction is
        called direct current. Just like a river, it cannot flow backwards and
        forwards, it can only flow from one side of the battery to the other.

        As long as the current flows through the wires and cell any components
        in the circuit, like lightbulbs or buzzers will work. However, it is very
        important that there are no breaks in the electrical circuit because if
        there were, the electrical charge would not be able to flow back to the
        cell.

        We can think of the cell as being responsible for ‘pushing’ the current
        around the circuit. A bigger push from the cell will mean that more
        current can flow.

        To measure the current we use a piece of equipment called an
        ammeter, and it is placed in the circuit so that it can measure the
        current that flows through it. An ammeter measures current in units
        called ‘amps’ or ‘amperes’. Amps are given the unit symbol, A, for
        example, 10 A is 10 amps. Remember that the ammeter must be part of
        the circuit and not on the outside of it.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019             33744                                     Page 1 of 6
                                                                        Current – picture it!

        The amount of current that leaves the cell must be the same as the
        amount of current that returns to the cell. No matter where we measure
        the current in a series circuit, it will always be the same.

Additional questions

   1. Why is current like a river?
   2. Why is current not like a river?
   3. What unit is current measured in?
   4. What piece of equipment is used to measure current?
   5. What can cause current to stop flowing around a circuit?
   6. Describe how current moves around a circuit.
   7. Describe how to correctly place an ammeter in a circuit.
   8. If current is flowing at the same rate around the circuit predict what might
       happen to it if another cell is added.

Teaching notes

This activity is best used to consolidate learning after students have set up a series
circuit and measured current.

The first activity will force students to actively engage with text while justifying their
selections.

It is important to tell students that it is not the order in which they put the images that
is important, but their justification for why.

Teaching notes and answers
This activity is most suitable for lower to middle achievers after they have been introduced to current, voltage and
resistance.
The task asks students to sort 12 statements into their relevant categories, current, voltage or resistance.
It is very important that at this stage their work is checked, otherwise, they may be using a powerful technique to
rehearse, recall and link incorrect information.
After their work is corrected they are asked to complete a blank mind map.
Students then rehearse their knowledge by using their mind map to tell their partner about current, voltage and
resistance and how they link together – and then they listen to their partner’s explanation. Usually at this point,
some questions may arise or, if you’re luck some “what ifs”. Ask students to scribble down any of these points on their
mind map for clarification later.
Then, in silence, students try to recreate their mind map without looking.
As a final task, you could then ask students to write a short paragraph on what they have learned.

                                                                       Word equations
Task 2

Read the descriptions below of different chemical reactions.
Use the information to write a word equation for each reaction.

1. A mixture of flour, sugar, and eggs is baked to make a delicious batch of
   biscuits.

2. A small piece of magnesium was dropped into hydrochloric acid.
   Hydrogen gas and magnesium chloride was produced.

3. Hydrogen and oxygen react together to form water.

4. Methane burns in air (oxygen) to produce carbon dioxide and water.

5. Chlorine and methane react to form chloromethane and hydrogen
   chloride.

6. A small piece of iron was left in outside for a week and become rusty.
   Rust is called iron oxide.

7. Copper and sulfur were heated over a Bunsen burner. At the end of the
   investigation, the copper had a bluish coating on the surface.

8. After copper sulfate (blue liquid) reacts with magnesium a small amount
   of an orange substance appears at the bottom of the beaker and the
   solution becomes clear.

9. A small piece of magnesium is held over a Bunsen flame. After producing
   a very bright light a white ash is left over.

10.   A small piece of sodium was dropped into some water. The sodium
   formed a ball, fizzed, and moved across the surface of the water. A gas
   was produced that popped with a lighted splint, but the sodium could no
   longer be seen. When the liquid was tested it turned Universal indicator
   purple.

11.   When living things respire their cells use oxygen and a sugar called
   glucose. These react together to release energy for the organism. Carbon
   dioxide and water are produced as waste products. During
   photosynthesis, this reaction is reversed. (Show both equations).

12.   Hydrogen peroxide and a manganese catalyst are added to a beaker.
   A drop of washing up liquid is added (only to form a foamy lather, it does
   not play a part in the reaction). Lots of bubbles start to form and when a
   glowing splint is put into the foam it relights.

Thermal decomposition
Sometimes when chemicals are mixed they react to form a new substance and
sometimes a chemical will just need heat to break apart.
The word thermal means heat and another way of saying breaking down is
‘decompose’ – so thermal decomposition means to break down with heat.
One example of this happening is chalk. The chemical name for chalk is calcium
carbonate and when heated it breaks down into a chemical called calcium oxide and a
gas called carbon dioxide.

decomposition.

Adapting creatures
Teaching notes
The idea behind this resource is to explore the concept of natural selection and
to explain in general why species evolve and why some become extinct. All the
information to run the activity is below. The additional PowerPoint structures
the activity for use on a whiteboard and includes images and links to clips.

Keywords
Adaptation, evolution, extinction, natural selection, offspring, reproduction,
species, survival of the fittest

Teaching sequence
Step 1
Begin with a few images of familiar species e.g. whale, camel, fish, frog, bird
   What are they?
   How do we know?

Step 2
Then show images of animals which have unusual adaptations (ones that might
be useful to the creatures described below) e.g. flying fish, giraffe, lungfish,
nocturnal aye-aye; video clip of darkling beetles in Namib desert or male
Namaqua sandgrouse collecting water in their feathers youtu.be/Of2Mu_D18I0 .
    Can students suggest how these adaptations arose?

Step 3
There are lots of crazy creatures in the world. Students are going to illustrate
their own species of animal, however it must have features which enable it to
live in the way described.
        A camel which lives in a very cold desert where all the trees are tall.
        A species of nocturnal frog which lives on a foggy beach.
        Fishes who live in ponds which dry up for 6 months of the year.
        A flightless, tree-climbing, fruit-eating bird.
Students work in pairs or small groups, each person in the group chooses a
different creature to illustrate. They draw their animal and add notes about its
adaptations (colour could be added later at home). Allow 10-15 minutes.
Show and discuss the finished creatures.

Step 4
Then throw a big problem into the mix…
E.g. imagine a whale which vacuums up swarms of flying insects. What would
happen if all the swarming insects suddenly vanished? If the change was too
quick for the species to adapt to then it may become extinct.
What change, linked to habitat or diet, would drive their species towards
extinction?
But, what if the problem was more minor?
    What if the swarming insects began to fly a little higher – out of the reach
       of many whales?
    How might this type of whale species alter over time?

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019        33937                              Page 1 of 2
                                                               Adapting creatures
Step 5
Students return to groups.
Possible changes are shown on the board.
Here are a few suggestions.
    For the camel the trees become taller
    For the frog the foggy spells reduce
    For the fish the ponds become drier for longer
    For the bird the fruit begins to develop at the very tips of the twigs
Students will mostly think about visible changes to their creatures’ body.
Encourage them to consider physiological as well as morphological changes
(depending on what they have covered so far in the syllabus).
E.g. the whale may require more energy to leap higher, may begin to have
more red blood cells to carry more oxygen.


Students alter their creatures and/or add annotations.

Then pose the questions:
   Why did the trees in the camel’s habitat become taller?
   Why did the fruit tree begin to produce fruit that was out of the tree-
     climbing birds reach?

Step 6
Show images of poison arrow frogs; poisonous mushrooms with names like
'destroying angel'; spines on an acacia; the trunk of a monkey puzzle (choose a
spikey one!). They all have defences against being eaten.

The swarming insects and the trees don't want to be attacked by the students'
creatures – it is not an advantage for them.
    Can they suggest adaptations which they might evolve to prevent them
      being eaten?
The problems which arose for the frog and the fish were not the result of a
feeding relationship but the result of a change in climate.
    What would students do to protect their creature and its food source from
      environmental change?

Step 7
Extension questions:

      What measurements could students take over time to show the
       evolutionary change that has occurred in their animal species? E.g. mass
       of muscles used by whale to rise above the water.

      What measurements could be taken to show the main factor which has
       driven this adaptation? E.g. average height the insect swarm flies at.

Photosynthesis word challenge
Teaching notes
The aim of this challenge is to make links between a word, image or sound
prompt and the topic of photosynthesis.
The activity helps students explore and extend their understanding of
photosynthesis. It is also useful to highlight misconceptions.
The activity is described here with some examples.
Prior learning: Leaf structure, testing for starch, process and word equation
for photosynthesis.


Running the activity
Students work in groups of two or three.
To keep things moving, have a time limit on responses. Use Teachit Timer (free
to all) to structure the session.
At its simplest:
Students are shown a word prompt and each group has to make a connection
between it and the topic of photosynthesis.
To add more challenge:
      Generate a random number, between one and twelve.
      Select a structure card from a set of three, 'Words', 'Connections’ or
       'Steps'.
The structure cards give the following instructions:
      Words - make a link to photosynthesis using the specified number of
       words.
      Connections - make the specified number of links between the word
       prompt and photosynthesis.
      Steps - using the specified number of short sentences or phrases (joined
       by words such as 'because') get from the word prompt to photosynthesis.


For example:

Word prompt                       Animal
Random number                       2
Structure card                    Steps

In this round, students must link the word 'animal' to the topic of
photosynthesis in two steps.
E.g 'a rabbit' (one step) 'because it eats plants which carry out photosynthesis'
(second step)

                                                           Photosynthesis word challenge
Make it random:
Each group receives a set of word-prompt cards, a set of structure cards and
two dice.
Groups work independently of the class.
They can bring their best links to the class for discussion.
Or ...
Pre-prepared:
Have a presentation ready to use with the class (see the PowerPoint for
examples).

Modelling DNA and chromosomes
This craft based activity is fun and many useful observations and questions can
arise from it.

Students make two simple models:

      One is a paper ladder to represent a short length of the DNA molecule
       and is used to show the helical structure and illustrate the notion of a
       gene(s).

      The second is a paper chain which represents a chromosome. It is used
       to show how the long, thin DNA molecule shortens and condenses as it
       coils up to form a chromosome.

You will need:
      lined a4 paper
      scrap paper
      scissors
      sticky tape.


Ladder instructions

Cut one A4 sheet in half lengthways.
Take one piece and fold in half, lengthways. If the paper is lined it's helpful to
have the margin on the outside so it is visible.
Start at one end and cut out a block two lines deep, cutting from the fold along
a line and up to and along the margin.
Move along the sheet a distance of two lines. Leave these intact and cut out a
block of the next two lines, up to the margin.
Continue up the length of the sheet, removing about 8 blocks.
Opening the sheet will reveal a ladder.


Paper chain instructions

Simply make a long paper chain. Get students to make sections and then join
them together to make one long chain.
Use scrap paper or coloured paper, each link should be about 1-5 cm wide

Show students two or three 3-D animations of DNA molecules. Mute the video
so students are not overwhelmed with keywords.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019         33948                               Page 1 of 3
                                                Modelling DNA and chromosomes
Using the ladders

Below are some suggestions for questions and things to do with the ladders.

1. What does the ladder represent?

2. Students can colour sections, three or four rungs long, to represent individual
   genes. Students then have a go at twisting their ladders. How well does this
   show the structure of DNA compared to other models and diagrams they
   have seen?

3. The rungs of the ladder usually collapse so the helix is difficult to see – how
   can they solve this? (Students may suggest things like using short strips of
   sticky tape to reinforce each rung and joined two or more ladders together).

4. Some 3-D animations show the DNA molecule 'unzipping' and two new
   strands forming. How could they use their ladder models to illustrate this?


Using the paper chains

Below are some suggestions for questions and things to do with the chains.

1. What does the chain represent?

2. Which parts might be said to model genes?

3. Are the ladder and the chain actually showing the same thing?

4. Which is a more accurate model of the double helix? Why?

5. Now, twist the chains. (Hopefully, each link is stuck together firmly). What
   happens to the chain? Show a 3-D animation which illustrates this.


Further questions

1. If you had a giant model cell, where would you put the ladder or chain you
   have made?

2. When would you coil up the chain to show the formation of a chromosome?

3. When would you open up your ladder to create two copies of the DNA
   molecule?




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019        33948                              Page 2 of 3
                                               Modelling DNA and chromosomes
Suggested answers

Using the ladders

1. What does the ladder represent?
   A short length of DNA molecule; DNA with a couple of genes; double helix
   structure of DNA

4. Some 3-D animations show the DNA molecule 'unzipping' and two new
   strands forming.
   How could they use their ladder models to illustrate this?
   They could cut them up the middle of the rungs and new T-shaped pieces of
   paper added to make two new ladders

Using the paper chains

1. What does the chain represent?
   A single chromosome and how it becomes more visible under microscope
   when it coils up.

2. Which parts might be said to model genes?
   Each link of chain.

3. Are the ladder and the chain actually showing the same thing?
   Ladder represents a small section of the chain.

4. Which is a more accurate model of the double helix? Why?
   Ladder shows the 'backbone' of DNA molecule and cross-pieces. Chain has
   links which pass through one another.

5. Now, twist the chains. (Hopefully, each link is stuck together firmly). What
   happens to the chain?
   Shortens; thickens

Questions

1. If you had a giant model cell, where would you put the ladder or chain you
   have made? Inside the nucleus

2. When would you coil up the chain to show the formation of a chromosome?
   When cell is preparing to divide.

3. When would you open up your ladder to create two copies of the DNA
   molecule?
   During process of cell division when chromosome is making a copy of itself

Modelling variation activity
Teaching notes
In this activity, students make simple 'organisms' from different materials.
Working in pairs, they use the same material to make a population of
organisms by following very simple rules.
When they have made their population they study each individual and note
down any differences between them. This reveals variation within the
population.
Students look at the differences and try to decide what environmental change
these particular individuals may be better adapted to.

Keywords
Adaptation, offspring, population, reproduce, species, survive, variation
(continuous and discontinuous variation).
The idea is to demonstrate how variation within a population may help
individuals of the same species survive when the environment changes.
As an extension it can be used to illustrate continuous and discontinuous
variation.

Activity
1. Choose an organism from the following suggestions for students to make.
   Give them a certain amount of time to make their population e.g. 60
   seconds. Challenge students to make them as identical as possible.

Organism 1
Work in pairs (to represent parents and shows that variation occurs even
amongst offspring who share the same parents).
Using modelling dough, students make as many pea-sized balls of dough as
they can in the given time.
Organism 2
Cut out very simple winged shapes from paper strips folded in half. The shapes
should be no larger than 2 cm2 when opened out.

Organism 3
Using the back of a pair of scissors, paper-curl (pre-cut 1cm wide strips from
width of A4 sheet) paper strips.
2. Next, they decide broadly which habitat their organisms live in.
    Are they herbivores, carnivores or omnivores?
    Are they a prey species for other organisms?
    Are they camouflaged?
    Are they nocturnal?
    Do they hibernate?
When they have their population they carefully study each individual and make
a note of any differences such as size, shape, smoothness, colour. Can they
group them?
Now, they decide an environmental change which might favour the more
unusual individuals.

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019       34808                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                     Modelling variation activity
E.g. Small pea shapes may survive better should there be a shortage of food in
their habitat; darker peas may have an advantage if the climate becomes
wetter and more cloudy.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019      34808                             Page 2 of 3
                                                       Modelling variation activity
Extension - continuous and discontinuous variation
Students decide which forms of variation in their population can be described
and measured by using numbers and units and which can only be described
using words and the number in each category tallied.
They can collate their data and share with other pairs who made the same
creature.
Bar charts and histograms can be drawn.
Discuss the differences in bar charts and histograms e.g. bars are not touching
on the chart because the categories are quite separate and distinct
(discontinuous variation) whereas a histogram shows continuous variation and
the bars are touching.
Discuss how charts can be used to show which part/proportion of a population
shown on the graph may survive to pass on genes to its offspring, should a
particular environmental change occur.
Discuss the effects of rapid changes in climate on species in evolutionary
terms. There may not be sufficient variation in a population to allow it to adapt
to a decrease in precipitation, for example.
To stimulate discussion, there are video clips available showing penguins which
breed on the rocky shores of South Africa. Due to rising sea temperatures the
fish stocks that they feed on are moving further away from the shore making
harder for the penguins to feed. The population has declined by 60% since
2004.

Marie Curie
Marie Curie (1867 – 1934) biography A




                                  Maria Salomea Sklodowska was born in
                                  Warsaw, Poland, on November 7th 1867. She
                                  was the youngest of five children – three older
                                  sisters and a brother. Her mother was a
                                  headmistress and her father taught maths and
                                  physics. He introduced the subjects to Maria
                                  when she was a child. When Maria was young,
                                  Poland was ruled by Russia. Maria’s family
                                  didn’t like the rules the Russian government
                                  made, however. For example, it was against
                                  the law to speak Polish and it was illegal for
                                  girls to go to school. Maria was clever and
                                  curious so her parents decided to send her to a
                                  secret school, where she did extremely well.

 Unfortunately, however, not everything in Maria’s early life was easy. In
 1877, when Maria was just 10 years old, her oldest sister died from typhus
 and in 1979 her mother died of tuberculosis. Maria and her family were
 heartbroken. Maria finished school when she was 15. She and her sister,
 Bronya were both interested in scientific research and after school, they both
 desperately wanted to go to University. The University in Warsaw, however,
 only allowed men to attend at the time. Women were allowed to go to
 University in other countries, but that was very expensive. So Maria and
 Bronya promised each other that they would take turns working to pay for
 the other to travel abroad to study. Maria thought that every child should be
 educated, so for almost 5 years, she secretly worked as a governess and a
 tutor, illegally teaching poor children to read. She sent the money she earned

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019         34893                           Page 1 of 14
                                                                  Marie Curie
 to Bronya, who attended University and became a doctor, which was almost
 unheard of for women at the time.

 In 1891, Maria moved to Paris. She changed her name to Marie because it
 sounded more French. She studied at the Sorbonne, a famous University,
 where she earned a degree in physics, maths and chemistry. Later, she
 gained a master’s degree in physics and then yet another degree in maths.
 Marie was so poor while she was there
 that she had to live on bread and tea and she
 sometimes fainted from hunger!

 While she was in Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, a physics
 professor. They soon fell in love and were married in
 1895. Marie worked with her husband in scientific
 research to investigate x-rays, radioactivity, and how
 atoms work. In 1898 Marie and Pierre discovered two
 new substances, called polonium (named after Poland)
 and radium. In 1903, they won a joint Nobel Prize for
 their work in physics, making Marie the first woman ever
 to win the award.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019      34893                          Page 2 of 14
                                                                        Marie Curie
 Marie and Pierre had two children – Irene born in 1897 and Eve, born in 1904.
 Sadly, in 1906, when Eve was just 2 years old, Pierre was killed when he was
 knocked down in the street by a horse drawn carriage. Marie was devastated
 but she decided to take over Pierre’s work. She became the first ever female
 professor at the Sorbonne University, and she won a Nobel Prize of her own
 for her work in chemistry in 1911. Soon after this, doctors found that
 radiology could help with curing cancer.

 Then, in 1914, the First World War started. Marie realised if military doctors
 had access to x-ray machines, they could make better medical decisions and
 save more lives. She helped to develop mobile x-ray machines and put them
 into ambulances, which she herself drove to the wounded soldiers on the
 front line.




 These vehicles became known as ‘Little Curies’ in Marie’s honour and they
 helped over one million soldiers during the war. She trained doctors and
 taught them how to use this new life-saving equipment and in 1921, she set
 up the Curie Institute in Paris. It is still an important cancer research centre
 today.

 Marie didn’t realise it, but the radioactive substances she worked with were
 very dangerous. As a result of working with them for such a long time, Marie
 developed leukaemia, a blood disease, and died on 4th July 1934, aged 66.

 Marie’s discoveries of radium and polonium have changed science and
 medicine forever. Her work meant that x-ray machines became more useful
 and were used more by doctors. They continue to be used today to detect
 broken bones and other problems, helping doctors to treat and cure their
 patients.

Winning Science
Put the winning design on display and ask the children to use
science to explain its success.

Aiming High
Find a high position at the top of a staircase or on top of stage
blocks to maximise the difference between recorded results.

Test Flights
Introduce time limits for each step of the investigation or limit
the number of test flights allowed.

Reverse, reverse!

See if children can find a way
to reverse the direction
of rotation.

Z--. LOS

Finale
Film the final of the class competition.

Chinook Craft
Can children find a way to make a double helicopter in the
style of a Chinook?

Slow Down

Invite children to make anything out of 1 A4 sheet of paper
that will take longer to fall to the ground than the winning
design.

Grand Finale

Invite each class winner in the school to fly their helicopters
in a Grand Final against the other class winners to determine
a school champion.

Twinkl’s mission is to ‘help those who teach’ and although

That’s why we employ our own team of experienced

With such high-quality versatile content at your fingertips,

delivery.

innovation is what makes Twinkl Secondary Science such an
incredible teaching tool.

Find a Friend: Specialised Cells Activity

Teacher Instructions

This activity is good for consolidating or checking learning in a plenary or for revision.
Cards can be printed out A4 or A5 and laminated for repeated use.

How to use:
There are 3 types of card:

orange - diagram (with a part labelled as X);
blue - name of a part;
green - description or function of a part.

Give each student in the class one of the cards. This can be random or differentiated by giving easier
cards to weaker students and more tricky cards to higher ability students. Unused cards can be put onto
a table for students to go to if they can't find their ‘friends’. Where there are more students than cards,
give one card to a pair of students.

Students should then move around the room and find their two ‘friends’ with the matching diagram,
name and function. This encourages discussion and students that are unsure can get help from their
peers.

Once the students have found their friends, the cards can be stuck onto a board, wall or window to form
a display that students can refer to if necessary.

Modelling Tectonic Plate Movement
 Aim: To model the Earth’s tectonic plate movement.


Equipment:
                                                          Safety Information
• Safety goggles
                                                          Hot syrup – risk of burns, may
• Large 1l beaker                                         spit when boiling.
• 300ml treacle                                           Wear goggles at all times. If burnt,
                                                          put area under running cold water for 10
• Biscuit (halved)
                                                          minutes and inform teacher immediately.
• Tripod
                                                          Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• Gauze
                                                          Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
• Bunsen burner                                           immediately.
• Heat proof mat                                          Bunsen – risk of burns.

                                                          Tie back hair, handle with caution.

                                                          If burnt, put area under running cold water for
                                                          10 minutes and inform teacher immediately.


Method:
Step 1: Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram

Step 2: Pour the treacle into the beaker

Step 3: Lay the two halves of the biscuit onto the treacle, with
a small gap between them

Step 4: Light your Bunsen burner on a safety flame (hole closed)

Step 5: Move the Bunsen burner underneath the tripod
(remember: to safely move a Bunsen burner while it is lit, hold
it where the rubber tubing connects to the base)

Step 6: Gently heat the treacle with a blue flame until it begins
to bubble

Step 7: Observe the biscuits carefully, do not let the treacle boil
too much

Step 8: Remove the heat to control the bubbling of the treacle




                                                  Page 1 of 2
                                                                           Modelling Tectonic Plate Movement



                   In 1912, meteorologist Alfred Wegener describe his theory of continental drift, and
                   the idea that the different continents would have fit together like a jigsaw puzzle.
                   He couldn’t explain how though, and it was about 50 years later that the theory
                   of plate tectonics arose.



Questions:
 1. What does the treacle represent in this demonstration?

 2. What do the biscuit halves represent in this demonstration?

 3. How does the heated treacle cause the biscuits to move?

 4. Use the model to describe how earthquakes occur.




                                               Page 2 of 2
                                                                           Modelling Tectonic Plate Movement

Answers:
 1. What does the treacle represent in this demonstration?
    The molten magma layer of the earth

 2. What do the biscuit halves represent in this demonstration?
    The tectonic plates which make up the earth’s crust

 3. How does the heated treacle cause the biscuits to move?
    As the treacle is heated from underneath, the particles gain more energy and begin to move faster
    and further apart, making the area of treacle less dense. The less dense area of treacle floats
    upwards and into the underside of the biscuits. As more treacle rises up the top layer of treacle is
    forced to move sideways and with it carries the biscuit. The heat is being transferred
    by convection.

 4. Use the model to describe how earthquakes occur?
    As the tectonic plates pass one another they rub at their boundary and cause friction. When the
    forces become unbalanced then the plates will jerk past one another, causing an earthquake.

 alkaline or neutral.

 oxide and sulfuric acid.

                        Producers and Consumers

  A producer is a living thing that makes its own food from
  sunlight, air, and soil. Green plants are producers who make
  food in their leaves.

  A consumer is a living thing that cannot make its own food.
  Consumers get their energy by eating food. All animals are
  consumers.

  A decomposer is a living thing that gets energy by breaking
  down dead plants and animals. Fungi and bacteria are the
  most common decomposers.
