Investigating Leaf Adaptations
Aim: To observe adaptions in leaves.

Equipment:
• Ruler

• Sample of leaves grown in full sunlight                Safety Information
                                                         Plants – possible allergen
• Sample of leaves grown in shade
                                                         Wash hands after handling.
• Calculator (optional)



Method:
Step 1: Measure the width and length of each leaf
(make sure you know which leaves were grown in
the different conditions)




                                                                                             width
Step 2: Record the results into a suitable table

Step 3: Calculate the area of each leaf (area = length
x width)

Step 4: Find the average values for the area of each
type of leaf                                                                  length



Questions:
 1. What is the function of a leaf?

 2. What is the difference between the length of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?

 3. What is the difference between the width of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?

 4. What is the difference between the area of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?

 5. Are your results reliable?

 6. What type of data have you collected?
                                                                              Investigating Leaf Adaptations


Answers:
 1. What is the function of a leaf?
    The leaves contain a lot of chlorophyll, which is a green pigment that absorbs sunlight for the
    process of photosynthesis.

 2. What is the difference between the length of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?
    You would expect the leaves grown in shade to be longer.

 3. What is the difference between the width of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?
    You would expect the leaves grown in shade to be wider.

 4. What is the difference between the area of leaves grown in shade and grown in light?
    You would expect the leaves grown in shade to be larger.

 5. Are your results reliable?
    Answers may vary. This is a reasonable sample size as it provides a good range to take an
    average, without being so large a sample size that it takes too long to collect data.

 6. What type of data have you collected?
    Continuous data

Mouldy Bread
 Aim: To investigate factors which cause mould/fungi to grow


Equipment:
                                                          Safety Information
• 4 slices of bread
                                                          mould/fungi – harmful, risk of
• 4 re-sealable food bags                                 aerosol if opened.
• 2 paper towels                                          Keep the bag sealed, observe through the
                                                          transparent sides.
• Water

• Marker pen and labels

Method:
Step 1: Stick a label on each bag and write your name on it.

Step 2: Put a slice of bread in the first bag. Seal and label as ‘dry/light’.

Step 3: Put a slice of bread and a damp paper towel in the second bag. Seal and label as ‘damp/light’.

Step 4: Put a slice of bread in the third bag. Seal and label as ‘dry/dark’.

Step 5: Put a slice of bread and a damp paper towel in
the fourth bag. Seal and label as ‘damp/dark’.

Step 6: Put the first two bags (‘light’) onto a sunny
windowsill.

Step 7: Put the third and fourth bags (‘dark’) into a
dark cupboard.

Step 8: Leave the bread at least five days.




                                                  Page 1 of 3
                                                                                             Mouldy Bread


Questions:

 1. Draw a sketch of each slice of bread. Estimate the percentage coverage of mould/fungi per slice.




     Dry/light conditions              %                       Dry/light conditions              %




     Dry/light conditions              %                       Dry/light conditions              %




 2. Which conditions caused the most mould/fungi growth?

 3. How might you store food to avoid decay and mould/fungi?




                                                Page 2 of 3
                                                                                            Mouldy Bread


Answers
1. Draw a sketch of each slice of bread. Estimate the percentage coverage of mould/fungi per slice.




    Dry/light conditions              %                       Dry/light conditions              %




    Dry/light conditions              %                       Dry/light conditions              %


Sketches should be accurate to their different, observable results. Students should indicate the
presence of mould/fungi by shaded areas/dots, etc.

The percentage coverage should be estimated from the grid – each square is equivalent to 4%.

2. Which conditions caused the most mould/fungi growth?
   The most growth should be found on the bread stored in the damp/dark conditions.

3. How might you store food to avoid decay and mould/fungi?
   Food should be stored in a cool and dry area to limit mould/fungi growth and decay.




                                               Page 3 of 3

Preparing Red Cabbage pH Indicator
 Aim: To understand how indicators work.


Equipment (to prepare the indicator)
                                                               Safety Information
• Safety goggles
                                                               Acids and alkalis - causes
• Red cabbage
                                                               irritation to skin, eyes and
• Grater or knife                                              respiratory organs. Harmful if
                                                               inhaled or swallowed.
• Boiled water (kettle)
                                                               Wear goggles at all times.
• Filter paper                                                 Glassware / grater – risk of cuts.
• Funnel                                                       Apply pressure to wounds and inform
                                                               teacher immediately.
• 2 x 500ml glass beaker
                                                               Boiled water – risk of scalds or burns.
Equipment (to use the indicator)                               Rinse all burns with cold running water
• 5 x 250ml beakers                                            for 10 minutes and inform your teacher
                                                               immediately.
• Marker pen

• 5 chemicals to test (choose from):

     • Ammonia (NH3)

     • Baking soda

     • Sodium carbonate

     • Lemon juice

     • Vinegar

     • Seltzer water (carbonic acid, H2CO3)

     • Hydrochloric acid

Method
 1. Step 1: Grate or chop the red cabbage into small pieces

 2. Step 2: Fill the 500ml beaker with the chopped cabbage to about the 400ml mark

 3. Step 3: Pour boiled water over the cabbage up to the 500ml mark

 4. Step 4: Leave to stand for at least ten minutes until the water has changed colour

 5. Step 5: Carefully filter off the chopped vegetables and collect the solution in the other
    500ml beaker



                                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                                           Preparing Red Cabbage pH Indicator


                      How does it work?
                      Red cabbage contains a pigment molecule which changes colour depending on
                      the pH of a solution.

                      Very acidic solutions cause the pigment to turn red.

                         Neutral solutions cause the pigment to turn purple.

                         Alkali solutions cause the pigment to turn green / yellow.



Questions:
 1. Colour the table to complete an indicator scale for the red cabbage indicator.


     pH              2                4              6             8              10              12

   Colour           red            purple          violet         blue         blue-green   green-yellow



 2. Use your indicator scale and choose 6 chemicals to test their pH:
    a. Number the small beakers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5
    b. Pour 20 – 50ml of the cabbage solution into each of the smaller beakers (how much you add
    will depend on how much solution you managed to filter from the cabbage mix)
    c. To each beaker add a different solution to find its pH
    d. Record your results in the table


     Chemical name               Colour change                   pH               Acid, alkali or neutral?

 Answers

 2. Use your indicator scale and choose 6 chemicals to test their pH:

Using a Light Microscope
 1. Always carry a microscope with two hands. Hold
    the microscope by the arm with one hand, and
    place your other hand underneath the stage to
    support it.

 2. Turn the object lens to the lowest magnification
    (usually X4 or X10) until you hear it click.

 3. Place the microscope slide you want to observe
    on the stage, and ensure it is secured with the
    stage clips.

 4. Using the coarse adjustment knob, slowly lower
    the objective lens until it is close to the slide,
    but not touching it. Make this adjustment while
    viewing the microscope slide from the side and
    not through the eyepiece lens.

 5. Look through the eyepiece lens and adjust the
    mirror and / or light to find the brightest level.

 6. Slowly turn the coarse adjustment knob so that
                                                         Photo courtesy of euthman (@flickr.com) - granted under creative commons licence
    the objective lens goes up (away from the slide),
    whilst observing through the eyepiece lens for
    the image to come into focus.

 7. Use the fine adjustment knob to view the image
    more clearly.



Remember:
• DO NOT let the lens touch the slide – it could
  damage it.

• Only clean the lens with specially designed cloths.

• Look through the eyepiece lens with one eye.

• The image you see is flipped vertically and
  horizontally, so bear this in mind when moving
                                                         Photo courtesy of studiobeerhors (@flickr.com) - granted under creative commons licence
  the slide to a more central position on the stage.

Your Heart
The heart is a muscle in your chest made up of four chambers:

•   the right atrium;

•   the left atrium;

•   the right ventricle;

•   the left ventricle.

Your heart is protected by your ribs and pumps blood around your
body. This is what happens:

Your blood ‘picks up’ the oxygen from your lungs and then it travels
to your heart. The heart pumps or pushes the blood around your
body by using the muscles in its walls. These muscles contract
to push the blood around the body. Arteries carry the blood to
every part of your body so your muscles and organs can use the
food and oxygen to make them work. Veins carry blood back to
your heart when all the oxygen has been used so the blood can be
pumped back to your lungs again to ‘pick up’ more oxygen.

body. The blood travels through                to return to the heart. Blood collects                from
the lungs then returns to the heart to begin the cycle again.

Where Do Bacteria Live?
 Aim: to take bacterial swabs and determine conditions for bacterial growth.


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Petri dish with nutrient agar
                                                         Cultures – possible bacterial
• Sterile cotton swabs                                   infection risk

• Coloured permanent marker pens                         Handle sealed Petri dishes only.
                                                         Dispose of in biohazard marked bags. Wash
• Ruler
                                                         hands after handling.
• Clear sticky tape
                                                         Glassware – risk of cuts if broken
• Incubator
                                                         Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
• Location class list                                    immediately.


Method:
Step 1: Your teacher will assign you a location from where to collect your sample.

Step 2: Without removing the lid, turn your Petri dish upside down and label the perimeter with your
name and the date.

Step 3: Using a ruler, carefully draw a line across the middle of the Petri dish to divide it into two
halves. On one half, write the name of the location from where you will collect your sample, and label
the other half as ‘control’.

Step 4: Remove the swab from the packaging, taking care not to touch the end. Gently rub the swab on
the assigned location.

Step 5: Quickly but carefully open the lid of the
Petri dish – just wide enough to fit the swab in –
and rub the swab over the agar in a zig-zag pattern
in the half labelled with your location. Take care
not to mark the agar, or to rub onto the half marked
as control.

Step 6: Replace the petri dish lid and secure on four
sides with sticky tape. Leave some gaps to prevent
anaerobic bacteria growing.

Step 7: Place your Petri dish, upside down, into
the incubator. This helps to prevent condensation
occurring, and allows easier identification of the
plates when checking them.


                                                 Page 1 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?

Step 8: Examine your Petri dish again after one day, two days and then five days. Record all observations
on your result sheet.

Step 9: Your teacher may also conduct a control* investigation to measure bacteria from the air.


 This could be done by simply leaving a Petri dish of agar open and exposed for a specified time
 length e.g. one hour, then sealing and incubating with the other Petri dishes.




                                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?
Location Class List
Teacher note: Suggested are several locations and space to add in your own. You may decide for students
to investigate a location each or to work in pairs, depending on your class size. We recommend assigning
the students to a location and them displaying the list to the class.

        Location description                           Students investigation this area

1       Classroom desk

2       Lab sink plug hole

3       Lab sink tap handle

4       Lab sink tap spout

5       Classroom door handle

7       Toilet seat

9       Toilet sink tap

10      Toilet door handle

11      Toilet hand dryer nozzle

12      Mobile phone screen

13      Projector remote

14      Teacher’s computer keyboard

15      Teacher’s computer mouse

16      Inside of school bag

17      Inside of shoe

18      Your pencil

19      Your exercise book

20      Drinks bottle spout

21      Classroom floor

22

                                                Page 3 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?


Results
Draw the bacterial colonies (if any) which have grown on your agar plate.




                After 1 day                   After 2 days                     After 5 days

Count the bacterial colonies that have grown on the agar and complete the table below.
Tips for counting the colonies:
•   Dot each colony with a coloured marker as you count.
•   Use a different colour each time you examine to count the additional colonies only. Add this amount
    to the previous count.
•   Place the Petri dish on a piece of graph paper and count the colonies row by row.
•   If there are many colonies to count, divide the area into 2 using a marker pen, count the colonies in
    ½ then multiply by 2 to find the total.



    Location:

                              Day                                    Number of colonies




Compare your results with the other locations. Your teacher may ask you to add your results to a
collective data table.
You may be given the opportunity to take photographs as a means of recording and comparing the
bacterial growth from difference locations.
                                                                                  Where Do Bacteria Live?

Questions


1. Which location has the most number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
2. Which location has the least number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
3. Why is it important to use sterile nutrient agar for the investigation?
4. Describe the common environmental conditions where the highest bacterial growth was found.
   (Think about temperature, light, moisture etc.)
5. What does the control Petri dish show? Explain why.
6. What measures can you take to reduce your exposure to bacteria?
                                                                                   Where Do Bacteria Live?

Answers

1. Which location has the most number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
   This will depend on the locations used and the results the students have obtained.

2. Which location has the least number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
   This will depend on the locations used and the results the students have obtained.

3. Why is it important to use sterile nutrient agar for the investigation?
   It ensures that the culture(s) which grow on the agar after incubation, are only the ones from the
   swab, and therefore ensure that the investigation is valid.

4. Describe the common environmental conditions where the highest bacterial growth was found.
   (Think about temperature, light, moisture etc.)
   Bacteria are likely to be found in abundance in areas which are moist, and contain traces of food
   for nutrition. Also high traffic items or locations, e.g. mobile phones and door handles may also
   show high levels of bacteria.

5. What does the control Petri dish show? Explain why.
   The control dish will likely show some growth of bacterial cultures. These cultures will have
   come from the air around the Petri dish whilst it was left open.

6. What measures can you take to reduce your exposure to bacteria?

    • Wash your handles before and after eating or preparing foods, suing hot water and soap.

    • Bleaching and disinfecting worktops and surfaces regularly.

    • Ensuring that mouths and noses are covered, and then hands are washed after coughing
    and sneezing.

    • Drying and removing excess moisture from areas such as the bath tub, shower head and
    kitchen sink.

    • Other sensible suggestions.

Series and Parallel Circuits
 Aim: to make observations of current and voltage in series and parallel circuits.


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• 3 bulbs
                                                         Circuit components –
• Battery or other power source                          electrical shock.

• Voltmeter                                              Do not handle with wet hands.
                                                         Check all equipment for damage or faults.
• Ammeter

• Connecting wires

• Circuit photos




                                      Fig 1                                      Fig 2

Method (series circuit):
Step 1: Set up the series circuit as shown in figure 1 above.

Step 2: Complete the circuit and measure and record the current and voltage at the bulb.

Step 3: Reconstruct the series circuit to include 2 bulbs.

Step 4: Complete the circuit and measure and record the current and voltage at one of the bulbs.

Step 5: Reconstruct the series circuit to include 3 bulbs.

Step 6: Complete the circuit and measure and record the current and voltage at one of the bulbs.



Method (parallel circuit)
Step 1: Set up the parallel circuit as shown in figure 2 above.

Step 2: Complete the circuit and measure and record the current and voltage at one of the bulbs.

Step 3: Reconstruct the series circuit to include 3 bulbs.

Step 4: Complete the circuit and measure and record the current and voltage at one of the bulbs.


                                                 Page 1 of 2
                                                                                    Series and Parallel Circuits

Results:


                                     Current, A                                 Voltage, V
 Number of bulbs
                            Series                Parallel             Series                Parallel


           1



           2



           3




Questions:
 1. How was the current in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 2. How was the current in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 3. How was the voltage in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 4. How was the voltage in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 5. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the current of series and parallel circuits.

 6. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the voltage of series and parallel circuits.




                                                  Page 2 of 2
 Answers
1. How was the current in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current remains the same / unchanged in a series circuit.

2. How was the current in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current is shared between the number of branches / bulbs in the parallel circuit.

3. How was the voltage in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage is shared between the bulbs in a series circuit.

4. How was the voltage in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage remains the same for all bulbs in a parallel circuit.

5. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the current of series and parallel circuits.
   Changing the number of bulbs in a series circuit has no effect on the current, whereas in a
   parallel circuit the current is shared between the branches.

6. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the voltage of series and parallel circuits.
   Changing the number of bulbs in a parallel circuit has no effect on the voltage supplied to each
   bulb, whereas in a series circuit the voltage is shared between the bulbs.
                                                                                  Series and Parallel Circuits



Support: Measuring current and voltage in a circuit

What the circuit symbols mean




          Bulb                                                 Cell




        Ammeter                                              Battery




        Voltmeter




To measure the current in the circuit you need to attach the ammeter in series (in line with) with the
component.




To measure the voltage in the circuit you need to attach the voltmeter in parallel (branched around) the
component you are measuring.

Hooke’s Law
 Aim: to observe Hooke’s Law in different materials.


Equipment
                                                              Safety Information
• Retort stand
                                                              Masses – risk of injury
• Clamp

• Boss                                                        Ensure the equipment is well
                                                              secured on the desk.
• G clamp

• Metre ruler

• Mass hanger and 100g masses

• Spring

• Elastic band



Method
Step 1: Set up the retort stand, boss, clamp and spring as
        shown in the diagram.

Step 2: Fully secure the base of the retort stand to the desk
        and check it is firmly secure before continuing.

Step 3: Use the metre ruler to measure and record the original
        length of the spring (at 0g mass).

Step 4: Attach the mass hanger (with no masses on) to the
        spring. (The hanger should have a mass of 100g −
        check with your teacher if you are unsure).

Step 5: Measure the new length of the spring and record.

Step 6: Place a 100g mass onto the mass hanger. Measure
        and record the new length of the spring.

Step 7: Continue to repeat step 6 until you have added 1000g
        (the hanger + 9 masses).

Step 8: Carefully unload the spring and remove from the
        apparatus.

Step 9: Attach the elastic band to the clamp in place of the
        spring and repeat the investigation.


                                                Page 1 of 2                             visit twinkl.com
                                                                                                         Hooke’s Law


Results Table
Make sure you write the correct units for each heading.
                         Spring length             Spring              Elastic band          Elastic band
      Mass (g)
                             (cm)              extension (cm)          length (cm)          extension (cm)
          0
         100
         200
         300
         400
         500
         600
         700
         800
         900
        1000

Hooke’s Law states that an object will be stretched or squashed to an extension (e) which is directly
proportional to the force (F) applied. Hooke’s Law only applies within the elastic limit of the object.

                                                   F=k×e

The spring constant (k) varies for different materials. If a spring is stiff (not easily stretched), it will have
a greater value of k.




Questions
 1. Calculate the extension of the spring and the elastic band and complete the table. To do this you
    need to subtract the original length of the spring (at 0g mass added) from the length of the spring.
    e.g. if the spring measured 6cm before any masses were added, and then measured 13cm with
    100g added. The extension at 100g is 13 – 6 = 7cm.

 2. Plot a graph to show extension against force for the spring and the elastic band. The extension
    should be plotted on the x-axis, in metres, and the force on the y-axis, in Newtons.
    To convert cm to m you will need to divide by 100. 100cm = 1m.
    100g = 1N.

 3. Look at your graph. Does the spring obey Hooke’s Law? Explain how you know.

 4. Look at your graph. Does the elastic band obey Hooke’s Law? Explain how you know.

 5. Which part of the graph represents the spring constant?

 6. Which material, the spring or the elastic band, has the highest spring constant? Explain how you know.



                                                    Page 2 of 2                              visit twinkl.com
                                                                                                 Hooke’s Law



Answers
1. Check the student’s individual results.

2. Check the student’s individual results.

3. The spring should obey Hooke’s Law and this will be evident by a directly proportional
   relationship between the extension and force. A straight-line graph should have been drawn.
   Depending on the type of spring used and its elastic limit, the graph may not be linear to the 10N
   force and the spring may have deformed during the practical investigation.

4. The elastic band should obey Hooke’s Law and this will be evident by a directly proportional
   relationship between the extension and force. A straight-line graph should have been drawn.

5. The gradient of the line.

6. This will likely be the spring, and should be evident by a steeper gradient on the graph. (Or by
   a higher spring constant value if your students have calculated the spring constant for each
   material).

Refraction
 Aim: To observe the relationship between angle of incidence and refraction


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Ray box
                                                         Filament bulb – risk of burns
• Single slit plate
                                                         Handle with extra care. Rinse any
• Lab pack (if needed)                                   burns under cold running water for
                                                         10 minutes and inform the teacher immediately.
• Protractor

• Pencil and ruler

• Paper




                Figure 1. Set-up



                                                                 Figure 2. Measurements


Method:
Step 1: Place the glass block flat in the middle of the paper and draw around it.

Step 2: Direct the light from the ray box onto one of the longer sides of the glass block, at a diagonal
angle.

Step 3: Trace over the ray as it leaves the ray box and enters the glass box (the incidence ray). You can
tidy up the line with the ruler afterwards.

Step 4: Trace over the ray as it leaves the glass block on the other side (the emergent ray). You can tidy
up the line with the ruler afterwards.


                                                 Page 1 of 2
                                                                                                 Refraction

Step 5: Remove the glass block and join the incidence and emergent rays with a straight line.

Step 6: Use the ruler and protractor to mark normal lines at the point where the incidence ray enters
the glass block, and the point where the emergent ray leaves the glass block.

Step 7: Measure the angle of incidence (A), angle of refraction (r) and angle of emergence (B). Record
these in the table.

Step 8: Repeat steps 1 to 7 for at least four different angles of incidence.


Results:


      Angle of Incidence                 Angle of Refraction                   Angle of Emergence




Questions:

1. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction.

2. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of emergence.

3. What is the name of the type of wave by which light is transmitted?

4. Explain refraction in terms of density and wave speed.



                                                 Page 2 of 2
 Answers:
1. The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of refraction; A > r.

2. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal.

3. Transverse wave (electromagnetic spectrum wave).

4. The velocity of the light wave is decreased as it enters a denser medium (the glass block). As
   it enters at an angle, the ray is ‘bent’ (refracted). When the light ray emerges into the original
   medium again (air) it resumes the same velocity and angle as before it entered the glass block.

Chemical and Physical Changes
 Aim: To distinguish between chemical and physical change.

This investigation is split into four activities. Your teacher will instruct you of the order of the activities
and let you know when to swap.
                                            Safety Information
Activity 1 – Burning magnesium              Bunsen burner – risk of burns/scalds.
Equipment:                                  Handle with extra care. Rinse any burns under
                                            cold running water for 10 minutes and inform
• Bunsen burner
                                            the teacher immediately.
• heatproof mat
                                            Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• tongs                                     Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher immediately.
• magnesium (2cm strip)                     Magnesium – risk of eye damage.
                                            Do not look directly at the light created by the magnesium.
Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 3: Holding the magnesium with the tongs, carefully hold the magnesium in the flame until it ignites.


Activity 2 – Cooking a pancake
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner                • mini frying pan                 • small cooking spatula

• heatproof mat                • pancake shaker (made up         • cooking oil
                                 to a batter with water)
• gauze

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the frying pan onto the gauze.

Step 3: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 4: Add a small amount of cooking oil to the pan and heat gently.

Step 5: Reduce the heat from the Bunsen burner and add a small amount of pancake batter to the frying pan.

Step 6: As the edges of the pancake batter begin to solidify, gently loosen with the spatula until you can
loosen the whole pancake from the base of the pan.

Step 7: Flip the pancake and finish cooking on the other side.

     Check with your teacher before consuming anything in a lab – it may not be safe to do so.


                                                   Page 1 of 2
                                                                              Chemical and Physical Changes

Activity 3 – Boiling water
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner

• heatproof mat

• gauze

• beaker

• thermometer

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the beaker onto the gauze.

Step 3: Add 150ml of water to the beaker and place the thermometer into the water.

Step 4: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 5: Heat the water gently until you see bubbles begin to form and the water starts to boil.

Step 6: Switch off the Bunsen burner and leave the equipment to cool.


Activity 4 – Melting chocolate
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner

• heatproof mat

• gauze

• beaker

• square of chocolate

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the beaker onto the gauze.

Step 3: Add the piece of chocolate to the beaker.

Step 4: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 5: Heat the chocolate gently until you see that it is beginning to melt and become liquid.

Step 6: Switch off the Bunsen burner and leave the equipment to cool.

Magnetic Fields
 Aim: To observe magnetic field lines


Equipment:
                                                        Safety Information
• Sheet of white paper                                  Iron filings – rinse hands under cold
• Pair of bar magnets                                   water to remove from skin. Do not
                                                        rub your eyes.
• Small compass

• Iron filings

• Pencil




           Figure 1




           Figure 2




           Figure 3




Method:
Step 1: Set up the bar magnet as shown in figure 1 on the sheet of white paper.

Step 2: Gently scatter iron filings around the bar magnet. Allow them to settle.

Step 3: Draw the pattern of the magnetic field lines on your results sheet.

Step 4: Using the compass, position it at different points around the bar magnet, each time drawing an
arrow on your diagram to show which way the compass is pointing.

Step 5: Repeat steps 1 to 4 for the bar magnet set-ups shown in figures 2 and 3.



                                                Page 1 of 2
                                                                                            Magnetic Fields
Results:




   1




   2




   3




Questions:
 1. Do the magnetic field lines point from north to south, or from south to north around a bar magnet
    (figure 1)?

 2. Where is the magnetic field strength strongest around a bar magnet (figure 1)?

 3. Where is the magnetic field strength weakest around a bar magnet (figure 1)?

 4. Describe the magnetic field line pattern between two opposite poles of bar magnets (figure 2).
    What will the magnets do?

 5. Describe the magnetic field line pattern between two same poles of bar magnets (figure 3). What
    will the magnets do?


                                               Page 2 of 2
 Answers:
1. Magnetic field lines go from the north pole into the south pole.

2. The magnetic field strength is strongest at the poles.

3. The magnetic field strength is weaker the farther it is from the magnet.

4. The magnetic field lines go straight from the north pole of one magnet into the south pole of the
   other magnet. The magnetic field strength is strongest between the poles. The bar magnets will
   attract.

5. The magnetic field lines create a diamond between the poles. The magnetic field strength is
   weakest between the poles. The bar magnets will repel.

Teacher/Technician Notes
• Use fresh fruit (strawberry or kiwi works well). You may want this to peeled and chopped
  into chunks before the lesson to avoid the need for peelers and knives in the lab.

• Check for any fruit allergies to ensure you order fruit which is safe for all of your class to use.

• Pineapple juice is used as it contains an enzyme which removes the proteins from the DNA.
  If this is unavailable, contact lens cleaning solution may be used as an alternative.

• You may choose to mush the fruit in polystyrene cups to prevent damage to the glassware
  (or just if you don’t like the noise created by metal forks scraping glass!).

• First, test the fruit you are using with the method. If you find that the pulp is too
  thick to be filtered in a filter funnel, then you may wish to use a sieve lined with
  kitchen roll and press the liquid out using the back of the fork instead.

• Ethanol (alcohol) should be stored in the freezer and then kept on ice in the lab – ideally
  this should be requested halfway into the practical to ensure it remains ice cold.




                                                     Page 1 of 1                                visit twinkl.com
 Extracting DNA from Fruit
  Aim: To extract DNA from cells.

Equipment:
• fruit - peeled and          • boiling tube                      • spatula
  chopped into chunks
                              • boiling tube rack                 • pipette
• pineapple juice
                              • measuring cylinder
• table salt
                              • funnel
                                                                  Safety Information
• washing-up liquid                                               Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
                              • filter paper
• ice-cold alcohol                                                Apply pressure to wounds and
                              • glass rod
• 2 beakers                                                       inform teacher immediately.
                              • fork

Method:
Step 1: Roughly measure 80ml water into a beaker. Add 1 spatula of table salt and stir
well with the glass rod, until all the salt has dissolved.

Step 2: Add 10ml of washing-up liquid to the same beaker and stir gently to mix
together. Put this beaker to one side.

Step 3: Into the second beaker, place the chopped fruit and mush it carefully with a fork.

Step 4: Pour the contents of the first beaker (from steps 1 and 2) into the second
beaker with the fruit pulp.

Step 5: Stir it a little to mix the contents then leave at room temperature for 20 minutes.

Step 6: Rinse and clean the empty beaker.

Step 7: Set up the filter funnel over the clean beaker.

Step 8: Filter the fruit pulp mix. The filtrate should be a slightly coloured liquid. (The
colour of the liquid will depend on the type of fruit you used).

Step 9: Discard the filter paper and pour the filtrate into a measuring cylinder.

Step 10: Add pineapple juice to the filtrate in a ratio of 1:5 pineapple juice to filtrate.

Step 11: Leave at room temperature for 5 minutes.

Step 12: Pour out the mixture from the measuring cylinder into a boiling
tube and stand in the boiling tube rack.

Step 13: Carefully pour or pipette ice-cold alcohol down the inside of the
boiling tube, in a ratio of 1:1.

Step 14: Leave to separate for 5 to 10 minutes before observing the DNA.

 The Carbon Cycle Answers
1. How is carbon used by living things? [2]

    Carbon is used by plants (producers) [1] to make carbohydrates, proteins and fats [1]

2. Name two stores of carbon compounds. [2]

    Two from: fossil fuels, biomass, carbohydrates, food

3. Name two processes that return CO2 to the atmosphere. [2]

    Two from: combustion, respiration, dissolving/evaporation

4. Name a process that removes CO2 from the atmosphere. [1]

    Photosynthesis

5. Describe a human activity that affects CO2 levels in the atmosphere. [2]

    burning fossil fuels (for electricity) – increase

    deforestation (fewer plants to absorb CO2) – increase

    driving cars (fumes and emissions) - increases

        1 mark for naming the human activity

        1 mark for describing the effect i.e. increase or decrease in CO2 levels

Diffusion Quick Assessment Answers
1. Diffusion is:

   • the movement of liquid or gas particles;

   • from an area of high concentration;

   • to an area of low concentration;

   • down a concentration gradient;

   • requiring no energy/it is a passive process.

2. Diffusion can happen in liquids and gases.

3. Diffusion can happen in liquids and gases because the particles are free to move, whereas in a
   solid the particles are fixed and can only vibrate on the spot.

4. A teacher set up the following apparatus:

   a) The bromine gas particles would diffuse from a high to
      low concentration and so move upwards.

   b) The diffusion of this gas could be slower than expected due to any air particles
      colliding with the bromine gas particles and sending them off in another
      direction. This random movement of gases is known as Brownian motion.

   c) The teacher could speed up the rate of diffusion in this experiment by
      increasing the amount of bromine gas used to create a steeper concentration
      gradient or increasing the temperature. (Size of molecule and state of matter
      are not applicable in this experiment as bromine gas is being used.)

Edexcel GCSE Physics Student Progress Sheet
Name: 							                                                   Target:        				

GCSE Physics
Topic 6 Radioactivity


        I can describe an atom as a positively charged nucleus consisting of protons
        and neutrons. This is surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The nuclear
 6.1
        radius is much smaller than that of the atom and with almost all of the mass
        in the nucleus.

 6.2    I can recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.

        I can describe the structure of nuclei of isotopes using the terms atomic
        (proton) number and mass (nucleon) number, and using symbols in the
 6.3    format:
          6
          13C

        I can recall that the nucleus of each element has a characteristic positive charge,
 6.4    but that isotopes of an element differ in mass by having different numbers of
        neutrons.

        I can recall the relative masses and relative electric charges of protons, neutrons,
 6.5
        electrons and positrons.

        I can recall that, in an atom, the number of protons equals the number of
 6.6
        electrons and is therefore neutral.

        I can recall that, in each atom, the electrons orbit the nucleus at different set
 6.7
        distances from the nucleus.

        I can explain that electrons change orbit when there is absorption or emission
 6.8
        of electromagnetic radiation.

 6.9    I can explain how atoms may form positive ions by losing outer electrons.

        I can recall that alpha, β– (beta minus), β+ (positron), gamma rays and neutron
6.10
        radiation are emitted from unstable nuclei in a random process.

        I can recall that alpha, β– (beta minus), β+ (positron) and gamma rays are
6.11
        ionising radiations.




                                                Page 1 of 4
                                                                    Edexcel GCSE Physics Student Progress Sheet




6.12   I can explain what is meant by background radiation.

6.13   I can describe the origins of background radiation from Earth and space.

       I can describe methods for measuring and detecting radioactivity limited to
6.14
       photographic film and a Geiger–Müller tube.

       I can recall that an alpha particle is equivalent to a helium nucleus, a beta particle
6.15   is an electron emitted from the nucleus, and a gamma ray is electromagnetic
       radiation.

       I can compare alpha, beta and gamma radiations in terms of their abilities to
6.16
       penetrate and ionize.

       I can describe how and why the atomic model has changed over time, including
6.17   reference to the plum pudding model and Rutherford alpha particle scattering,
       leading to the Bohr model.

       I can describe the process of β– decay (a neutron becomes a proton plus an
6.18
       electron).

       I can describe the process of β+ decay (a proton becomes a neutron plus a
6.19
       positron).

       I can explain the effects on the atomic (proton) number and mass (nucleon)
6.20
       number of radioactive decays (α, β, γ and neutron emission).

       I can recall that nuclei that have undergone radioactive decay often undergo
6.21
       nuclear rearrangement with a loss of energy as gamma radiation.


6.22   I can use given data to balance nuclear equations in terms of mass and charge.


       I can describe how the activity of a radioactive source decreases over a period
6.23
       of time.

6.24   I can recall that the unit of activity of a radioactive isotope is the Becquerel, Bq.

       I can explain that the half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for half
6.25
       the undecayed nuclei to decay or the activity of a source to decay by half.

       I can explain that it cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay,
6.26   but that half-life enables the activity of a very large number of nuclei to be
       predicted during the decaying process.


                                                Page 2 of 4
                                                                    Edexcel GCSE Physics Student Progress Sheet




       I can use the concept of half-life to carry out simple calculations on the decay
6.27
       of a radioactive isotope, including graphical representations.

       I can describe uses of radioactivity, including:
       a) household fire (smoke) alarms;
       b) irradiating food;
6.28
       c) sterilisation of equipment;
       d) tracing and gauging thicknesses;
       e) diagnosis and treatment of cancer.

       I can describe the dangers of ionising radiation in terms of tissue damage and
6.29
       possible mutations and relate this to the precautions needed.

       I can explain how the dangers of ionising radiation depend on half-life and
6.30
       relate this to the precautions needed.

       I can explain the precautions taken to ensure the safety of people exposed to
6.31   radiation, including limiting the dose for patients and the risks to medical
       personnel.

       I can describe the differences between contamination and irradiation effects
6.32
       and compare the hazards associated with these two.

       I can compare and contrast the treatment of tumours using radiation applied
6.33
       internally or externally.

       I can explain some of the uses of radioactive substances in the diagnosis of
6.34
       medical conditions, including PET scanners and tracers.

6.35   I can explain why isotopes used in PET scanners have to be produced nearby.

       I can evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear power for generating
6.36   electricity, including the lack of carbon dioxide emissions, risks, public perception,
       waste disposal and safety issues.

       I can recall that nuclear reactions, including fission, fusion and radioactive
6.37
       decay, can be a source of energy.

       I can explain how the fission of U-235 produces two daughter nuclei and the
6.38
       emission of two or more neutrons, accompanied by a release of energy.

6.39   I can explain the principle of a controlled nuclear chain reaction.


                                                Page 3 of 4
                                                                  Edexcel GCSE Physics Student Progress Sheet




       I can explain how the chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor, including
6.40
       the action of moderators and control rods.

       I can describe how thermal (heat) energy from the chain reaction is used in
6.41
       the generation of electricity in a nuclear power station.

6.42   I can recall that the products of nuclear fission are radioactive.

       I can describe nuclear fusion as the creation of larger nuclei resulting in a loss
6.43   of mass from smaller nuclei, accompanied by a release of energy, and recognise
       fusion as the energy source for stars.

6.44   I can explain the difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.

       I can explain why nuclear fusion does not happen at low temperatures and
6.45
       pressures, owing to electrostatic repulsion of protons.

       I can relate the conditions for fusion to the difficulty of making a practical and
6.46
       economic form of power station.

Instructions: Label the parts of the microscope
 Name: ________________________                           Date: ______________________


HANDOUT 5.1-2: FUNCTIONS OF MICROSCOPE PARTS
Ocular: This is the eyepiece lens that usually magnifies by a power of 10. (Note: To determine
the power of the microscope, one multiplies the power of the ocular by the power of the
objective lens being used.)

High-power objective: It is located just above the stage. It is the longer of the objectives. Its
lens has a magnifying power usually of 43.

Low-power objective: It is located just above the stage. It is the shorter objective. Its lens has
a magnifying power usually of 10.

Stage: This is a horizontal platform just below the objectives that supports the microscope slide
for observation.

Revolving nosepiece: The objective lenses are attached to this part. It can be manually rotated
to select the objective lens that you wish to use.

Stage clips: They clamp over the edges of the microscope slide to secure it to the stage.

Diaphragm (or condenser): Located just below the stage, it can be hand adjusted to regulate
the amount of light entering the microscope. An image viewed through the microscope should
not be dark but should have plenty of light.

Mirror: This is adjusted to reflect light from the microscope lamp up into the microscope.
Although the mirror is sometimes used to regulate the amount of light entering the microscope,
this is not good technique.

Coarse adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is always used first, and it is used
only with the low-power objective.

Fine adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is used with the high-power objective
to “fine tune” the focus.

Arm: This is the back of the microscope and it is used along with the base to transport the
microscope.

Base: This is the bottom of the microscope and it is used along with the arm to transport the
microscope.

Note: Both eyes should be open when viewing through the microscope. This prevents eye
fatigue, which occurs when the non-viewing eye is kept closed. Keeping both eyes open does
take some practice, but it is highly recommended.

Definition of  chemical reaction label Key words DNA DNA is  D eoxyribo  N ucleic  A cid.    DNA  is a chemical .    DNA  is responsible for the production of proteins within a cell. Proteins are the `doers’ and  ` builders’ of  your body – so by controlling the proteins, DNA controls the way your body  looks and the way it functions. DNA molecules are found in the nucleus of every cell in your body. The DNA in each cell carries the blueprint for making all the proteins in your body. However, cells  in your body are usually specialised so they do not need to make all the possible proteins. This means your cells  usually use only parts of  the to  make the proteins they need. Structure  of DNA Double helix structure – like a twisted ladder. The ladder uprights are made of a chain of alternating sugar and phosphate units.  T hey provide support to the rungs  of the “ladder” and do not provide any genetic code . The “ ladder’s ”  rungs are made of pairs of special molecules called nitrogen bases . There are only  4  different  base units: A = adenosine T = thymine C = cytosine G = guanine Each rung is a pair of bases. A is always paired to T, but the rung can be AT or TA. C is always paired with G, but the rung can be CG or GC. A and T are said to be complementary bases, as are C and G 2.  (A) DNA Terminology A section  of  a  DNA  molecule  which  provides c ode s  for a certain trait  is  called  a gene . A single strand of DNA may have 1000’s of genes along its length. A chromosome is  simply  a strand of DNA . A cell will have several or many chromosomes  Chromosomes  are actually quite long so they are “folded up” on themselves four times (called quaternary  folding )  to fit in the nucleus of the cell. Humans have 46 chromosomes. 23 chromosomes are received from each parent – thus two very important points about your DNA are obvious. Your DNA is a 50% combination of your  dad’s  DNA  and 50% of your Mum’s DNA . . Each chromosome from your parent (each one of the 23) has a match ing  chromosome from the other parent. You don’t have 46 different chromosomes – you have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Each one of the pairs of chromosomes will be virtually identical – so there are two copies of each gene.  This is very useful because if one copy of a gene does not work, you will have a backup copy which hopefully will make the correct protein.

uploads/science/year-8/earth-and-space-s.searchText: Continental Drift  Continent=One of the Large landmasses on the Earth.   E.g.  Africa Continental drift=the Earths continents are moving . Wegener first  suggested this. He based his ideas on the following.  The continents fit together like parts of a jigsaw puzzle, so perhaps  they  were once joined. Fossils of long dead animals  were  fo und on continents that are  far apart. Later evidence.  Ocean ridges and rifts suggest that the seafloor may be spreading in some places(ridges) and sinking in other places(trenches) Magnetic striping.   Symmetrical  magnetic  patterns form along the ocean ridges Sediment thickness.  As you move away from an ocean ridge the sedimentary rock layers become thicker, suggesting that they are older.  So the ridges show new rock forming. So what does the theory of plate tectonics suggest? Plate tectonics=  the  Earth's surface is broken in to a number of shifting  plates   Key Words Word Meaning  Continent Ocean ridge Ocean trench Subduction Sediment M atter that s ettles to the bottom of a river, ocean or lake. Sedimentary rock  Rock  that  has formed through  sediment falling to the bottom of an ocean or lake or sea. The sediment builds up in layers and turns to solid rock over time.

uploads/science/2013 10 EVOLUTION ANSWER.searchText: Evolution Offspring =the  children. Mate =to have sex.   Fertile =able to mate and produce offspring. Ancestors =the relatives of a person that lived  before  them.  Your Great Grandad is one of your ancestors. Generation =the time between the birth of one animal and the  time  when that animal produces it s  own offspring. Species =one type of living thing with shared characteristics.  Members of the same species are able to mate with other members of that species and produce fertile offspring. For example male horses can mate with female horses to produce young  horses ( offspring).  These young horses can grow up to mate and have their own offspring.  So horses are in the same specie s . A Zebra and a Horse can mate to produce a Zeedonk.  A Zeedonk cannot reproduce.  A zeedonk is not fertile.  A Zebra and hose are not in the same species. Example  Same species?  Yes or no. A horse and a donkey can mate to give an offspring called a Mule.  Mules are not fertile.  Mules cannot have baby mules. Poodle dog and German S hepard dog can mate to give offspring.  The offspring are fertile and can grow up to have offspring of their own. A lion and a tiger can reproduce to give a Liger.   A Liger is not fertile.  It cannot have babies. Evolution Evolution is the change in a species over many generations resul ting in new species being made. For examples the  horses we see today evolved fro m a much  smaller animal .  This took millions of years to happen. The idea of evolution was thought up by Charles Darwin. Not everyone agrees with his theory.  Here is a cartoon that was drawn of him, at the time his theory was released. You do not need to believe his theory, but you should understand it. Evidence for Evolution  Fossils.  By looking at fossils it is possible to see the gradual change in species over time.   Fossils are  the remains (or an impression) of a plant or animal that existed in a past  and has been dug out from the ground. Here we can see the fossil record of horse skulls.      Homologous  structures .  This means that some animals share some characteristics parts to their bodies.  This suggests that they may have all come from one common ancestor. Count how many finger the human hand has.  Now count the number of finger like bones in the flipper of the Whale.  The idea is that they  both  come from a common  ancestor  that had 5 “finger” bones. Key words Match the word with the correct definition Word  Meaning(definition) Mate      the children Species able to mate and produce offspring Fertile  the relatives of a person that lived before them Generation the time between the birth of one animal and the time when that animal produces its own offspring Ancestors To have sex fossil one  type of living thing with shared characteristics.  Members of the same species are able to mate with other members of that species and produce fertile offspring Offspring the change in a species over many generations resulting in new species being made Evolution the remains (or an impression) of a plant or animal that existed in a past geological age and that has been excavated from the soil Fossils the of a plant or animal that existed in a past   has been dug out of the ground

uploads/science/2013 10 FACTORS AFFECTIN.searchText: Name: Rates of Chemical Reactions The speed at which a chemical reaction occurs is called the _________ of ____________.  ___________ are an example of a reaction occurring quickly. ______________ is an example of a reaction that occurs slowly. Factors that affect the rate of a reaction include:           You will conduct the following reaction under different conditions to see how they affect the rate of reaction.  Write the balanced formula equation below  the word equation . Magnesium    +     Sulfuric  Acid  Magnesium  Sulfate     +    Hydrogen Gas Control A control is an experiment you do to use as a comparison.  For this experiment you will not change any of the above factors. Why is it important to have a control? Put 2cm of 2M H 2 SO 4  in a test tube.  Place the test tube in a test tube rack. Get your timer ready. Start the timer when you place your magnesium strip in the acid. Stop the timer when the magnesium has all reacted. Record your results in the table. Temperature Read the temperature section on page 163 Half fill a beaker with boiling water from the kettle. Half fill another beaker with iced water Put 2cm of  2M  Sulfuric  acid in the bottom of two test tubes. How do you think the reaction rates of the hot and cold test tubes will compare to the room temperature one you did previously? What  is your independent variable for this experiment? What is your dependent variable? Write a hypothesis Place one of these test tubes in the beaker of boiling water and the other in  the beaker of iced water . Get your timer ready. Start your timer when you place the strips of magnesium in the acid. Record how long it takes the magnesium to disappear from each test tube on the table . Write a conclusion regarding the effect of temperature on reaction rate. Concentration Read the concentration section on page164 The more concentrated a solution the _____________  the  rate of reaction. Use a diagram to explain why this is the case. The concentration of acids is measured in moles (M).  The higher the number the more concentrated the acid is.  In the previous experiments the concentration of the acid used was ______M, in this experiment we will use 0.2M sulphuric  acid.  0.2M H 2 SO 4  is more __________ than 2M H 2 SO 4. uploads/science/2013 Classifying volcano.searchText: Classifying volcanoes Volcanoes are classified according how to how they erupt.   These  6 main types  are listed  below.  They go form least  explosive( Icelandic) to most explosive( Pel e an ) 1 )   Icelandic  - This type of eruption emits large amounts of lava from fissures, often miles in length and spread in sheets over the land. The lava is very fluid and can flow for long distances.    Forms low broad dome like cones .   2 ) Hawaiian  - T hese eruptions come with lots of lava. These are  rarely explosive , but fountains of lava can be shot up to 1,000 feet or more by jets of gas. The lava forms  flat la va cones .   3 )  Strombolian   These  form  moderate explosions  accompanied by scoria  and a white  vapor  cloud. Every so often, gases escape with small  explosions, throwing scoria .    They form  Steep sided cones called cinder cones. 4   and 5 )  Plinian /Vulcanian .  It forms a solid crust over the crater between infrequent eruptions. Accumulated gases then blow out these obstructions with  strong explosions . Broken fragments, fresh lava, and scoria are hurled out of the crater. These eruptions come with a large “cauliflower-shaped” ash cloud.  Forms steep sided and very symmetrical cones. 6)   Peléan   - greatest explosions . Its distinguishing feature is the  nuée   ardente , or “glowing cloud,” a highly heated gas charged with glowing ash particles that rushes down mountain slopes with hurricane force.  The magma in these eruptions is  usually blocked, so that explosions blast out horizontally beneath the plug. uploads/science/2014 DNA Cut colour and.searchText: DNA Bases DNA  molecule has  a twisted double strand (double helix)  shape.  It looks a bit like a ladder.   The sides of the ladder are made out of  Phosphate( P) and sugar(S)  moleclues .  This is called the sugar phosphate backbone. The steps of the ladder are made  of special chemicals called nitrogen bases.   The nitrogen bases come in pairs called nitrogen base pairs. Adenine bases  (A) always join to  Thymine(  T ) bases. Thymine bases (T)  always join to  Adenine ( A ) bases. Cytosine b ases always join to  Guanine ( G  ) bases. Guanine ba ses always join to Cytosine  ( C ) bases. This is called complimentary base pairing. Building a DNA Molecule   On the large A3 sheet of paper:  Colour  all of the  letter A and T Parts red. Colour  all of the  letter C and G parts Green.   On the smaller A4 sheet: Colour  all of the  letter A and T Parts red. Colour  all of the  letter C and G parts Green.   Cut out  all of the  letter Ts from the small A4 sheet.  Stick the letter Ts that you have cut out so that they join with the letter  As  on the big A3 sheet.   Cut out  all of the  letter As from the small A4 sheet.  Stick the letter  As  that you have cut out so that they join with the letter Ts on the big A3 sheet.   Cut out  all of the  letter Cs from the small A4 sheet.  Stick the letter Cs that you have cut out so that they join with the letter Gs on the big A3 sheet.   Cut out  all of the  letter Gs from the small A4 sheet.  Stick the letter Gs that you have cut out so that they join with the letter Cs on the big A3 sheet.   Now cut out all of the letter S form the smaller A4 sheet.  Glue them onto the A3 sheet.   Cut out  all of the  letter Ps from the smaller A4 sheet.  Glue them to the A3 sheet.

uploads/science/2014 Earthquakes.docx.searchText: Earthquakes Information Earthquake= a sudden and rapid movement of the ground. Measuring Earthquakes are measured by machines called Seismometers.  The unit of measure is points on the Richter scale.  Each time the Richter scale increases by one the force of the earthquake increases by ten. Waves  The shaking occurs in waves.  These waves are called Seismic waves.  There are three types of Seismic wave: P-waves= these  waves move backwards and  forwards ( longitudinally) in the Earth. S-waves= these  waves move up and  down ( transversely) in the Earth. Surface waves=waves moving along the  Earth’s  surface.  These cause the most damage. Where they start Earthquakes occur most often at fault lines. Focus=the place a nd earthquake starts under the g round. Epicentre=the  place on the surface of the Earth directly above the focus.   This is where most of the energy is released. Effects The ground surface deforms (changes shape). Buildings fall down.  Most earthquake-related deaths are caused by the collapse of  structures. Bridges fall down. Landslides  where large pieces of land slide downwards T sunamis, which is when large waves are caused by the earth moving under water Fires started by gas and other fuel lines being broken. Sewage pipes burst.  Apart from being smelly this increases the chances of people getting sick after the earthquake. Water pipes for drinking water burst. Flooding caused as dams burst. Breakdown  in communication systems , both because wires are damaged and there is no power . Transport networks disrupted.   Power supplies disrupted. Looting . uploads/science/2014 Haiti Earthquake 20.searchText: Name: Hundreds feared dead in Haiti earthquake ABC Report On  January 12th,  2010  the worst earthquake in 200 years - 7.0 in magnitude - struck less than ten miles from the Caribbean city of Port-au-Prince, Haiti. The initial quake was later followed by twelve aftershocks greater than magnitude 5.0. Structures of all kinds were damaged or collapsed, from shantytown homes to national landmarks. Major buildings including offices, hotels and shops collapsed when a massive earthquake hit Haiti's capital, burying hundreds, possibly thousands of people beneath rubble, an aid worker with a US charity said. "The whole city is in darkness, you have thousands of people sitting in the streets, with nowhere to go," Rachmani Domersant, an operations manager with Food for the Poor, told Reuters from Port-au-Prince. "I've seen seven to eight buildings, from office buildings to hotels and shopping stores, collapsed  or burning  ... I think hundreds of casualties would be a serious understatement," he added. Haiti's ambassador to the US says the earthquake has caused a "catastrophe of major proportions" and there are reports of mass panic, with screaming people rushing into the streets as buildings collapsed,  throwing a pall of dust over the city . This morning a local doctor told AFP that he feared the death toll would be significant. "When we get an idea of the toll it will be measured in the hundreds," the doctor said. The  epicenter  of the quake was located inland, just 16  kilometers  from the capital, and was a shallow 10km deep, intensifying its impact, and significant casualties are expected. Reuters  reporter Joseph Guyler Delva says he saw dozens of people apparently dead or injured lying under rubble, which blocked roads.  "Everything started shaking, people were screaming, houses started collapsing...  it's  total chaos," he said The national director of World Vision in Haiti, Frank Williams, is just outside Port-Au-Prince.  "People are screaming all around and walls from buildings and private residences have fallen into the streets, so that has pretty much blocked off most of the traffic," he said.  "We have some aftershocks that we've experienced... people are wailing... [are] very frightened. Most of the people are out on the streets." The earthquake hit at 4.53pm (local time) in an extremely populated area. A US Geological Survey official told CNN that significant casualties were expected. Haiti's ambassador to the US Raymond Alcide Joseph told CNN he was heartbroken as he had just spoken by telephone with a senior presidential aide who described scenes of chaos and devastation. "He had to stop his car just about half an hour ago, and take to the streets, start walking, but he said houses were crumbling on the right side of the street and the left side of the street," Mr Joseph said. "He does not know whether he would reach his home, not knowing what he would find, because he had a bridge to cross to get there." The presidential palace in Port-Au-Prince collapsed and many other public buildings across the capital were destroyed, Haitian television streaming online reported Tuesday. "The presidential palace, the finance ministry, the ministry of public works, the ministry of communication and culture," were all affected by the quake, a Haitian reporter said, adding that the parliament building and a cathedral in the capital were also crumbling. Earthquakes are the shaking, rolling or sudden shock of the earth’s surface. They are the Earth's natural means of releasing stress. More than a million earthquakes rattle the world each year. Location of Haiti and  Epicentre   Map showing plate boundaries An  earthquake  is what happ ens when two tectonic plates of the Earths crust  suddenly slip past one another. The surface where they slip is called the  fault  or  fault plane . The location below the earth’s surface where the earthquake starts is called the  focus  ,  the location directly above it on the surface of the earth is called the  epicenter . Why did he need to do that? Give at least 2 reasons why  you think  it would be difficult for the government to control a rescue and response plan to the disaster? Since the earthquake there has been an outbreak of the disease  Cholera.  Can you think of why . Look at the maps showing the location of the quake and the location of the plate boundaries.
